compound_name: Pyridine, valence isomerization to prefulvene through a conical intersection
point_group: C2v for the Kekule ground and S2 structures, Cs for the S2 transition state and the conical intersection, C1 for the ground state transition state
geometry_source: Reaction path optimized at CASSCF(8,7)/STO-3G following the intrinsic reaction coordinate from the transition state to reactants and products; transition state and prefulvene geometries optimized at CASSCF(8,7)/6-31G*; conical intersection geometry optimized at CASSCF(8,7)/STO-3G; the S1(n,pi*) boat geometry optimized at CIS/6-311G(d,p)
method: CASSCF for the reaction path, stationary points and conical intersection, with time-dependent DFT B3LYP and CIS used for states the active space could not handle
basis_set: STO-3G and 6-31G* for the CASSCF calculations; 6-311G(d,p) for the TD-DFT and CIS calculations
active_space_orbital_description: Eight active electrons in seven active orbitals: three occupied pi orbitals, one occupied nitrogen lone pair n, and three pi* orbitals. Larger (8,8) and (10,8) spaces were also tried in a few instances.
active_space_protocol: The (8,7) space was used throughout for the ground and pi-pi* states. In a few instances larger (8,8) or (10,8) spaces were used as a check, and these showed that the seven-orbital space is saturated for pyridine. The n-pi* state was not treated with CASSCF at all: its boat-type geometry would require a large number of mixed n and pi orbitals and converged slowly, so CIS/6-311G(d,p) was used for that geometry with TD-DFT/6-311G(d,p) vertical emission energies.
electronic_structure_description: Table 2 gives, from CASSCF(8,7)/6-31G*, the angle alpha at the nitrogen atom formed by its two bonds to the carbons at positions 2 and 6, and the distance d between those two carbons, for six points along the path: Kekule S0 in C2v, 114.8 degrees and 2.321 Angstrom; Kekule S2 in C2v, 112.8 degrees and 2.388 Angstrom; the S2(pi,pi*) transition state in Cs, 91.8 degrees and 2.103 Angstrom; the S0-S2 conical intersection in Cs, 80.9 degrees and 1.903 Angstrom; the S0 transition state in C1, 69.4 degrees and 1.643 Angstrom; and prefulvene in S0 and Cs, 55.7 degrees and 1.478 Angstrom. The reaction path from the Kekule form to the prefulvenic form was mapped as an intrinsic reaction coordinate, and because symmetry breakage is involved the path is quantified by the two monotonically varying coordinates above. The lowest-energy path in the potential energy diagram is the adiabatic ground state path; the S2(A'') path is the lowest-energy path on the S2(pi,pi*) surface, while the higher S0(A') curve gives the ground state energy along that path at the vertical transition energy. At this level of theory the n-pi* state lies at higher energy than the lowest pi-pi* state, though the authors state that the accurate energy position is not their focus and that excited state energies can easily be off by 10 kcal/mol. The S1(n,pi*) state has a nonplanar boat-shaped geometry and its lowest electronic transition is shifted to lower energy by approximately 7000 per cm, in agreement within the approximations used with the experimentally observed fluorescence Stokes shift.
Other: This is one of the few papers that reports an explicit saturation test and states its conclusion in those terms. The working space is (8,7) -- three occupied pi orbitals, one occupied nitrogen lone pair n, and three pi* orbitals. In a few instances a larger (8,8) or (10,8) space was also used, and those calculations showed that the space of seven orbitals is saturated in the case of pyridine, allowing the essential details relevant to the description of this system to be captured. So the (8,7) numbers are not merely the affordable choice; enlargement was tried in both directions, one more orbital and two more electrons with one more orbital, and neither changed the picture. The counterpart to that success is an equally explicit failure, recorded in the same paper. Pyridine in the n-pi* state assumes a boat-type geometry, and the authors state that treating this kind of geometry with the CASSCF method requires inclusion of a large number of mixed n and pi orbitals -- a space that upon trial was found to converge slowly with the available computation speed. They therefore abandoned CASSCF for that state and optimized its geometry with single-excitation configuration interaction instead, with vertical emission energies from time-dependent DFT. The pair of results is instructive: the same seven-orbital space that is saturated for the pi-pi* isomerization path is not even the right kind of space for the n-pi* minimum, because out-of-plane distortion mixes n and pi character and destroys the clean separation the space was built on. A space can be converged for one region of a surface and inapplicable in another region of the same molecule. Two further caveats attach to the reported energetics. The authors state plainly that within the level of ab initio theory used, the energies of the excited states can easily be off by 10 kcal/mol, and they note that at this level the n-pi* state lies above the lowest pi-pi* state while disclaiming any focus on the accurate energy position -- which matters because the experimental interpretation rests on distinct dynamics following S1(n,pi*) and S2(pi,pi*) excitation. And the geometries are not all from one basis: the transition state and prefulvene structures are optimized at CASSCF(8,7)/6-31G* while the conical intersection geometry is optimized at CASSCF(8,7)/STO-3G, as is the whole reaction path in the potential energy diagram, so the minimal-basis intersection sits on a path whose endpoints were characterised in a polarized double-zeta basis.
reference_short: Chachisvilis & Zewail, J. Phys. Chem. A 1999, 103, 7408
notes: Experimentally, excitation to S1(n,pi*) gives a 23 ps component with the 2.2 ps component drastically reduced, while excitation to S2(pi,pi*) gives a pronounced 2.2 ps component alongside the 23 ps one; the pyridinium ion, where the n-pi* transition is absent, shows only the fast component. The fast decay is assigned to motion on the pi-pi* reaction path forming isomers and the slow one to nonradiative, nonreactive decay after S2 to S1 relaxation.
correlation_correction: None applied to the CASSCF results

geometry_source: Geometries fully optimized at the density functional level with harmonic frequencies obtained analytically at the optimized structures; CASSCF/CASPT2 calculations performed to describe the multiconfigurational nature of selected molecules and analyse the bonding
method: CASSCF/CASPT2 with spin-orbit coupling added through the complete active space state interaction (CASSI) method, which uses an effective one-electron spin-orbit Hamiltonian based on the mean field approximation of the two-electron part; B3LYP, BPW91 and PBE density functional calculations alongside
software: Gaussian 09 for the density functional calculations
basis_set: ANO-RCC-VTZP for the CASSCF/CASPT2 calculations; 6-311+G(3df) for phosphorus with the 60-electron SDD pseudopotential for uranium in the DFT calculations
relativistic_treatment: Uranium described with the ANO-RCC-VTZP basis in the wave function calculations; a 60-electron SDD pseudopotential in the DFT calculations
soc_included: yes, through CASSI with an effective one-electron spin-orbit Hamiltonian in the mean field approximation
active_space_orbital_description: Nine electrons in sixteen orbitals, the sixteen being linear combinations of the U 7s, 6d and 5f atomic orbitals with the P 3p atomic orbitals.
active_space_protocol: The full composition rule, all combinations of U 7s, 6d and 5f with P 3p, is affordable for the diatomic and was used without truncation. The same spaces were applied to the nitrogen analogue NU for a systematic comparison. Doublet, quartet and sextet states were explored, and spin-orbit coupling was then added by CASSI.
electronic_structure_description: Table 2 compares electronic states, effective bond orders and bond distances for the uranium pnictides: PUP 3Phi_u, 2.54, 2.36 Angstrom; PUP 1Sigma_g+, 2.75, 2.31 Angstrom; PU 4Gamma, 2.76, 2.38 Angstrom; NUN 1Sigma_g+, 2.87, 1.73 Angstrom; NU 4Gamma, 2.85, 1.76 Angstrom. The ground state is an Omega = 1.0 state dominated by quartet states as found in the CASSI calculations, with the largest contributions being 47 percent from the 4Gamma and 32 percent from the 4Phi states. Because both contribute substantially, fundamental frequencies were computed for each: 484 and 481 per cm respectively, both higher with CASSCF/CASPT2 than with the density functionals. Table 1 gives the CASPT2 bond length as 2.38 Angstrom with a 4Gamma frequency of 484 per cm and intensity 43 km/mol, against B3LYP 2.38 Angstrom and 405 per cm, BPW91 2.33 Angstrom and 425 per cm, and PBE 2.33 Angstrom and 428 per cm. The effective bond order is 2.76. The CASSCF/CASPT2 molecular orbitals with occupation numbers for the major quartet component show unpaired electrons in ten partially occupied molecular orbitals localized mostly on the uranium atom. The hybrid density functional bond lengths are longer, suggesting that functional underestimates the U-P bonding.
Other: The active space here is built by a stated composition rule and then cut down by a stated occupation criterion, and the paper is explicit about both steps and about why the cut was forced. For the diatomic UP the space is nine electrons in sixteen orbitals, the sixteen being linear combinations of the U 7s, 6d and 5f atomic orbitals with the P 3p atomic orbitals -- that is, everything that could plausibly bond, with nothing left out. Applying the same rule to the triatomic PUP would give twelve electrons in nineteen orbitals, and the authors state flatly that this active space is too large to be treated with current implementations of the CASSCF/CASPT2 code. The truncation is then principled rather than arbitrary: orbitals which are either almost doubly occupied or almost empty were removed, leaving twelve electrons in thirteen orbitals, in analogy with the same group's earlier treatment of NUN. Removing near-integer-occupation orbitals is the standard occupation-number criterion, and it works precisely because those orbitals contribute little correlation while costing full combinatorial weight. What makes this paper unusually useful is the control it runs on that truncation. Rather than assuming the comparison across systems survives the cut, the authors performed calculations on NU and NUN with the same active spaces as PU and PUP -- so the nitrogen analogues carry the same (9,16) and (12,13) spaces as their phosphorus counterparts. The central chemical conclusion is a difference of effective bond orders between those pairs: 2.54 for the PUP triplet ground state against 2.87 for the NUN singlet, and 2.76 for PU against 2.85 for NU, supporting the claim that third row elements are less effective than second row elements for pi bond formation. That comparison is only meaningful because the spaces were matched deliberately, and it would have been unreadable had the phosphide been truncated and the nitride not. The bicyclic U(P2)2 adduct sits outside this scheme entirely, computed in C2v with a (12,12) space, so its energies are not on the same footing as the diatomic and triatomic series. Two further points bear on interpretation. Effective bond orders are defined here as bonding minus antibonding occupancies divided by two, read off the active space occupation numbers, so they are a property of the chosen space, not an observable -- a truncated space cannot report antibonding occupancy in an orbital it has discarded. And spin-orbit coupling, added through the CASSI method with an effective one-electron spin-orbit Hamiltonian in the mean-field approximation, changes the character of the answer rather than merely shifting it: the UP ground state is an Omega = 1.0 state with 47 percent 4Gamma and 32 percent 4Phi character, so no single spin-free state is the ground state at all, and the fundamental frequencies had to be computed for both components. For PUP, where the singlet and triplet are close, a CASSI calculation was needed to confirm that the spin-orbit ground state is a mixture of triplets, with the state analysed in the bonding discussion contributing 95 percent of it.

The same spaces were applied to the nitrogen analogue NUN for a systematic comparison.
electronic_structure_description: Table 2 compares electronic states, effective bond orders and bond distances for the uranium pnictides: PUP 3Phi_u, 2.54, 2.36 Angstrom; PUP 1Sigma_g+, 2.75, 2.31 Angstrom; PU 4Gamma, 2.76, 2.38 Angstrom; NUN 1Sigma_g+, 2.87, 1.73 Angstrom; NU 4Gamma, 2.85, 1.76 Angstrom. A linear triplet is the ground state, 7 kcal/mol below the lowest-energy linear singlet at the CASSCF/CASPT2 level; the triplet is the U(IV) molecule and the singlet the U(VI) analogue. Because the two are close in energy a CASSI calculation was performed, confirming that the spin-orbit ground state is a mixture of triplets, with the state described in the bonding analysis contributing 95 percent of it. The density functionals place the triplet lower by 19 and 16 kcal/mol, a much larger gap. Table 1 gives, for the 3Phi_u state, a CASPT2 bond length and angle of 2.36 Angstrom and 180 degrees with frequencies 489 per cm (sigma_u, intensity 7), 427 (sigma_g, 0) and 131 (pi_u, 17 doubly degenerate), against B3LYP 2.33 Angstrom and 180 degrees, BPW91 2.34 and 180, PBE 2.34 and 180. For the 1Sigma_g+ state the CASPT2 values are 2.31 Angstrom and 180 degrees with 523 per cm (sigma_u, 65), 459 (sigma_g, 0) and 142 (pi_u, 10 doubly degenerate), while the functionals give bent structures at 156, 129 and 126 degrees. The important diagnostic antisymmetric P-U-P stretching fundamental for the triplet is calculated at 489, 468 and 457 per cm by the three DFT methods and for the singlet at 523, 485 and 455 per cm. The triplet effective bond order of 2.54 compares with 2.87 for the NUN singlet ground state, supporting the conclusion that third row elements are less effective than second row elements for pi bond formation. The sought-after molecule probably absorbs under the intense P4 precursor band near 465 per cm, where it cannot be observed.
Other: The active space here is built by a stated composition rule and then cut down by a stated occupation criterion, and the paper is explicit about both steps and about why the cut was forced. For the diatomic UP the space is nine electrons in sixteen orbitals, the sixteen being linear combinations of the U 7s, 6d and 5f atomic orbitals with the P 3p atomic orbitals -- that is, everything that could plausibly bond, with nothing left out. Applying the same rule to the triatomic PUP would give twelve electrons in nineteen orbitals, and the authors state flatly that this active space is too large to be treated with current implementations of the CASSCF/CASPT2 code. The truncation is then principled rather than arbitrary: orbitals which are either almost doubly occupied or almost empty were removed, leaving twelve electrons in thirteen orbitals, in analogy with the same group's earlier treatment of NUN. Removing near-integer-occupation orbitals is the standard occupation-number criterion, and it works precisely because those orbitals contribute little correlation while costing full combinatorial weight. What makes this paper unusually useful is the control it runs on that truncation. Rather than assuming the comparison across systems survives the cut, the authors performed calculations on NU and NUN with the same active spaces as PU and PUP -- so the nitrogen analogues carry the same (9,16) and (12,13) spaces as their phosphorus counterparts. The central chemical conclusion is a difference of effective bond orders between those pairs: 2.54 for the PUP triplet ground state against 2.87 for the NUN singlet, and 2.76 for PU against 2.85 for NU, supporting the claim that third row elements are less effective than second row elements for pi bond formation. That comparison is only meaningful because the spaces were matched deliberately, and it would have been unreadable had the phosphide been truncated and the nitride not. The bicyclic U(P2)2 adduct sits outside this scheme entirely, computed in C2v with a (12,12) space, so its energies are not on the same footing as the diatomic and triatomic series. Two further points bear on interpretation. Effective bond orders are defined here as bonding minus antibonding occupancies divided by two, read off the active space occupation numbers, so they are a property of the chosen space, not an observable -- a truncated space cannot report antibonding occupancy in an orbital it has discarded. And spin-orbit coupling, added through the CASSI method with an effective one-electron spin-orbit Hamiltonian in the mean-field approximation, changes the character of the answer rather than merely shifting it: the UP ground state is an Omega = 1.0 state with 47 percent 4Gamma and 32 percent 4Phi character, so no single spin-free state is the ground state at all, and the fundamental frequencies had to be computed for both components. For PUP, where the singlet and triplet are close, a CASSI calculation was needed to confirm that the spin-orbit ground state is a mixture of triplets, with the state analysed in the bonding discussion contributing 95 percent of it.

compound_name: Previtamin D (precalciferol), S1 minimum and S1/S0 conical intersection by ONIOM
geometry_source: S1 minimum and S1/S0 conical intersection geometries optimized by ONIOM, by a full non-ONIOM Target calculation, and for the bare model system alone, for comparison
method: ONIOM two-layer hybrid with CASSCF/4-31G as the high-level method on a hexatriene model system embedded in the full molecule, with a range of low-level methods; conical intersection optimization within ONIOM
software: A development version of the Gaussian program
basis_set: 4-31G for all CASSCF calculations; STO-3G for the low-level methods unless otherwise indicated
active_space_orbital_description: Six electrons in the six orbitals of the pi system of hexatriene. The model system is C6H8 embedded in the real system C28H44O, so the C=C in the -R group of the real molecule is excluded from the active space.
active_space_protocol: The same active space, the six-electron six-orbital hexatriene pi system, was used for all CASSCF calculations: the Target calculation on the full molecule, the ONIOM model system, and the case where the low-level method describing the ONIOM real system is also CASSCF. Holding it fixed is what makes the ONIOM and Target numbers comparable. State-averaged orbitals were used for the conical intersection and state-specific orbitals for the S1 minimum. The nocpmcscf approximation was used for the crossing search, a small approximation to the orbitals and hence the gradient in the region of degeneracy, accepted here because ONIOM is being compared to a Target calculation run with the same approximation. The choice of space and the modest 4-31G basis are justified by reference to other studies as sufficient to describe the structures adequately.
nroots_per_mult: state-averaged over two states for the conical intersection, state-specific for the S1 minimum
electronic_structure_description: Table 3 gives the S1-S0 energy difference at the S1 minimum geometry in kcal/mol, together with the dihedral angle describing the C6-methyl orientation, for each low-level method. Under ONIOM-CLS: CAS(S0) 64.30 with error -1.54 against the Target and dihedral 35.6 degrees; RHF 57.27, error -8.57, 53.8 degrees; ROHF triplet 65.43, -0.41, 21.6; ROHF quintet 66.32, +0.48, 15.2; UHF singlet 66.53, +0.69, 22.8; UHF triplet 66.06, +0.22, 22.7; UHF quintet 66.84, +1.00, 15.2; UFF 59.77, -6.07, 43.4; AM1 64.86, -0.98, 25.6. Under ONIOM-CLS*: CAS(S1) 67.53, +1.69, 17.1; CAS(S1)/4-31G 69.30, +3.46, 5.7; model-only 68.76, +2.92, 5.5; and the Target 65.84 with dihedral 5.7 degrees. The all-CASSCF ONIOM combination overestimates the gap by about 3 kcal/mol even though its geometry is identical to the Target, so that error comes entirely from the localized description of the excitation rather than from the low-level method, and no other combination can be expected to do better. The residual error correlates with the out-of-plane orientation of the methyl group attached to C6, the linear best fit crossing the y axis at 3.5 kcal/mol, close to the localization error itself. That dependence is attributed to the C5-C6 bond being near-single at about 1.48 Angstrom in the excited state and therefore easily deformed, while formally double in the ground state where small deformations cost significant energy; the largest errors accordingly occur with low-level methods that describe the ground state, namely CAS(S0), RHF, UHF singlet, UFF and AM1, since the Target geometry is an S1 structure. For the conical intersection geometry the model-only structure represents the Target better than it did for the S1 minimum, but is still markedly worse than every ONIOM calculation, especially in the (4,5,6) angle and the dihedrals, one of which differs by nearly 10 degrees; absence of the cyclic substituent means the bare model cannot reproduce the Target geometry. Most ONIOM combinations reproduce the Target well and slightly better than at the S1 minimum, presumably because the open-shell low-level methods emulate the electronic structure of the conical intersection better than that of the S1 minimum; the best are triplet UHF and ROHF and singlet UHF, while RHF and UFF perform worst, followed by AM1. For the conical intersection minus S1 minimum energy difference, most ONIOM methods with quantum mechanical low levels come close to the Target; UFF in the low level gives a significantly larger error and places the crossing below the minimum, while AM1 gives a small error of opposite sign to all the others, and the correlation with methyl orientation disappears.
Other: The active space is the fixed quantity in this study rather than the variable, and that is the point: a six-electron, six-orbital hexatriene pi space is used identically for the ONIOM model system, for the full-molecule Target calculation, and for the case where CASSCF also serves as the low-level method on the real system. Only with the space held constant can the differences in Table 3 be attributed to the ONIOM partitioning rather than to the reference. What the paper then measures is a cost that has no analogue in ordinary active-space error: the cost of localizing the excitation. The cleanest number is the all-CASSCF ONIOM combination, whose geometry is identical to the Target by construction and which still overestimates the S1-S0 gap by about 3 kcal/mol. The authors state the inference explicitly -- that error results completely from the localized description of the excitation and not from the level of theory used as the low level, and since every other combination also uses the localized description, none can be expected to do better. That establishes a floor on accuracy set by where the active space is placed in the molecule rather than by how big it is. The complementary finding is that the space cannot be placed on the model system in isolation: the model-only calculation, the same six-electron six-orbital pi space on bare hexatriene, reproduces neither the S1 minimum nor the conical intersection geometry properly, because the absence of the cyclic substituent leaves the geometry wrong. So the environment matters geometrically even though the correlated wave function never leaves the fragment. A third observation concerns what kind of low-level wave function is compatible with an active space describing a crossing. The conical intersection geometries come out better than the S1 minimum geometries across the board, which the authors attribute to the open-shell low-level methods emulating the electronic structure of the intersection better than that of the S1 minimum, and the best performers are triplet UHF and ROHF and singlet UHF, while closed-shell RHF is as bad as molecular mechanics. Since the exclusion of the -R group C=C from the active space is what forces this partitioning in the first place, the choice of which double bond to correlate propagates all the way to which single-reference method can sit outside it. One methodological caveat is recorded by the authors: the nocpmcscf approximation was used in the crossing search, a small approximation to the orbitals and hence the gradient near the degeneracy, accepted because ONIOM and Target were run with the same approximation, so the comparison is internally fair but the absolute intersection geometry carries that approximation.
reference_short: Bearpark, Larkin & Vreven, J. Phys. Chem. A 2008, 112, 7286
notes: The model system is C6H8 and the real system C28H44O. Low-level methods tested were CAS(S0), CAS(S1), RHF, ROHF triplet and quintet, UHF singlet, triplet and quintet, UFF and AM1, in an STO-3G basis unless otherwise indicated. Enlarging the high-level region to include the methyl group and perhaps the second carbon attached to C6 would be expected to improve agreement, but was not pursued because the errors in the gap arise from the S0 energy not corresponding to an optimized structure on that surface, and the study's goal concerns two critical points.
correlation_correction: None; CASSCF only, with no perturbative correction

point_group: D-infinity-h; the symmetrical linear structure was verified experimentally using isotopically scrambled dinitrogen
geometry_source: Geometries optimized with the B3LYP and BPW91 density functionals and, for the hydride, by full CASPT2 optimization both with linear symmetry imposed and without any symmetry constraint
method: CASSCF/CASPT2 to describe the multiconfigurational nature of the molecules and analyse the U-N bonding, alongside hybrid B3LYP and pure BPW91 density functional calculations; matrix infrared spectroscopy of laser-ablated uranium atom reaction products
software: MOLCAS 7.2 for the CASSCF/CASPT2 calculations; Gaussian 09 for the density functional calculations
basis_set: ANO-RCC-VTZP for the CASSCF/CASPT2 calculations; 6-311++G(3df,3pd) for H and N with a 30-electron-core SDD pseudopotential for U in the DFT calculations
relativistic_treatment: ANO-RCC-VTZP basis for uranium in the wave function calculations; a 30-electron-core SDD pseudopotential in the DFT calculations
active_space_orbital_description: Twelve electrons in twelve orbitals, containing two sigma bonding and antibonding pairs and two sets of pi bonds, amounting to four pi bonding orbitals and four pi* antibonding orbitals in total.
active_space_protocol: A bond-inventory space covering every U-N sigma and pi bonding orbital together with its antibonding partner, so that the multiconfigurational character of the two equivalent triple bonds is captured symmetrically.
electronic_structure_description: The uranium-nitrogen bonds are equivalent by symmetry. Mulliken bond orders based on the CASSCF orbitals are N-2.89-U-2.89-N, and the CASSCF Mulliken partial charges are -0.25 on each nitrogen and +0.50 on uranium. The molecule is formed directly from the reaction of a laser-ablated excited uranium atom with molecular nitrogen; this requires electronically excited uranium, since annealing does not increase the yield but ultraviolet irradiation to excite U increases the signal threefold, consistent with a separate CASSCF/CASPT2 study of the reaction path that found a 25 kcal/mol barrier for this 59 kcal/mol exothermic reaction. Infrared spectra of laser-ablated uranium with nitrogen in excess argon at 5 K gave strong NUN and weak UN absorptions.
Other: The active space here is defined by bond inventory and then extended by exactly one electron and one orbital when a hydrogen atom is added, which makes the comparison between the two molecules unusually clean. For NUN the space is twelve electrons in twelve orbitals containing two sigma bonding/antibonding pairs and two sets of pi bonds, four pi bonding and four pi* antibonding orbitals in total. For NUNH one electron in a hydrogen 1s orbital is added, giving (13,13): the same bonding and antibonding orbitals as in NUN plus one nonbonding orbital localized on uranium. Because nothing else changes, the differences in Mulliken bond orders read off the CASSCF orbitals -- N-2.89-U-2.89-N for the symmetric molecule against N-2.91-U-2.19-N-1.05-H for the hydride -- reflect the chemistry rather than a re-tuned reference, and the conclusion that the two N-U bonds in NUNH differ by nearly a bond order rests on that. ligand_set: Methylenediphosphonic acid (C1P2) phosphonate ligands with sodium counterions, from hydrothermal reaction of the actinide trichloride with the acid in the presence of NaOH or NaNO3

method: CASSCF and CASPT2, with DFT-PBE natural bond orbital and natural population analyses alongside
basis_set: Relativistic all-electron ANO-RCC of double-zeta quality (ANO-RCC-VDZP) with contractions [8s7p5d3f1g] for Pu and Am and [3s2p1d] for O; ANO-RCC-MB for P, Na, C and H with contractions [3s2p], [3s2p], [2s1p] and [1s] respectively; def-TZVP for the DFT calculations

active_space_orbital_description: Ten electrons in fourteen An 5f orbitals, the electron count following from the Pu 5f5 configuration per actinide atom. The space was then expanded below the valence 5f orbitals by one doubly occupied orbital and its corresponding antibonding partner, the added orbital being an An 6p in both complexes.
active_space_protocol: The initial space comprised all fourteen actinide 5f orbitals with their ten electrons. Because that space showed the 5f orbitals localized on the metal with no evident interaction with the coordinating phosphonate oxygens, it was expanded below the valence 5f orbitals to admit an additional doubly occupied orbital and the corresponding antibonding orbital, which turned out to be an An 6p; that orbital also showed no interaction with the coordinating ligands. The ground state electronic configuration was described as slightly complex because of the unpaired f electrons per actinide atom.
electronic_structure_description: The An 5f orbitals are localized on the metal site with no evident interaction with any coordinating oxygen atoms of the phosphonate ligands, and the An 6p orbital admitted by expanding the space likewise shows no interaction with the coordinating ligands. At the DFT-PBE level the ten highest singly occupied alpha spin orbitals are localized Pu 5f orbitals, with a little electron density delocalized onto the O 2p orbital of select coordinating PO3 groups; just below the localized valence 5f orbitals lie O 2p orbitals of those PO3 groups. Partial atomic charges per actinide are 2.87 by Mulliken and 2.45 by LoProp at CASSCF, against 1.10 by Mulliken and 1.57 by natural population analysis at DFT-PBE. Natural population analysis gives Pu 5f5.38 and Pu 6d0.79, and Mulliken gives Pu 5f5.04 and Pu 6d0.54. Atomic populations from the total density at DFT-PBE give, by Loewdin, Pu 6s 4.185, 6p 12.440, 5d 11.467 and 5f 5.895; by natural population analysis 4.165, 11.994, 10.844 and 5.423; by Mulliken 4.267, 12.301, 10.906 and 5.404. Total alpha minus beta spin densities are 5.030 by Loewdin, 5.096 by natural population analysis and 5.066 by Mulliken, with the 5f contribution being 4.927, 4.915 and 4.949 respectively.
Other: The active space is chosen to answer one question -- whether the actinide 5f orbitals are involved in bonding to the phosphonate ligands -- and the paper's result is a negative that the space is deliberately structured to be able to detect. The initial spaces contain all fourteen An 5f orbitals with the electrons that occupy them, ten for the plutonium complex from Pu 5f5 and twelve for the americium complex from Am 5f6. Irrespective of structure and actinide metal, those 5f orbitals come out localized on the metal site, with no evident interaction with any coordinating oxygen atom of the phosphonate ligands. The important methodological step is what follows: rather than accepting a null result from the first space, the authors expanded the space below the valence 5f orbitals, adding one doubly occupied orbital and its corresponding antibonding partner, which in both complexes turned out to be an An 6p. That orbital also shows no interaction with the coordinating ligands. Enlarging downward is the right test here, because a space containing only metal-localized f orbitals cannot by construction show metal-ligand mixing -- there is no ligand orbital in it to mix with -- so the absence of covalency in the small space is uninformative until an orbital that could have shown it is admitted and still does not. A caution for anyone reusing these numbers: the arithmetic of the final space is not stated consistently. The text gives initial spaces of ten and twelve electrons in fourteen orbitals and describes the expansion as adding one doubly occupied orbital plus its antibonding partner, which would give twelve electrons in sixteen orbitals for the plutonium complex and fourteen in sixteen for the americium one, whereas the caption to the figure showing the americium bonding orbitals labels it a (16,16) active space. The initial spaces as explicitly stated are recorded in the electron and orbital columns here and the expansion is described in the protocol, rather than reconciling the two statements. A second and independent caveat concerns what the space says about charge. At the CASSCF level the Mulliken and LoProp methods give similar actinide partial charges, but the Mulliken values are on average 0.4e larger than the LoProp ones and closer to the formal trivalent state, and the DFT Mulliken and natural population charges are further from +3 still. Since the localization conclusion is read off orbital plots and the covalency discussion off partial charges, and those charges vary by more than an electron between analysis schemes on the same wave function, the qualitative orbital result is the more robust of the two. Notably the DFT analyses, not the CASSCF ones, are what reveal occupancy of the An 6d orbitals -- Pu 6d0.79 versus Am 6d0.84 from natural population analysis, marginally reversed at the Mulliken level with Pu 6d0.54 versus Am 6d0.51 -- and the 6d orbitals were never in the active space at all, so that part of the electronic structure lies entirely outside the multiconfigurational treatment.

Every state shares a common core configuration not tabulated. Table 3 gives CASPT2 vertical energies at the ground-state geometry with oscillator strengths for eleven states: 1A' 0.938 eV, 1A'' 1.113, 2 1A' 2.329, 2 1A'' 3.850, all with f below 1e-10; 2 3A'' 4.179 eV with f 0.0148; 3A' 4.395 with 0.000180; 3 3A'' 4.579 with 0.0143, assigned to 7a' to 9a'; 2 3A' 4.727 with 0.000908; 3 3A' 5.056 with 0.00597, assigned to 1a'' to 9a', 2a'' to 11a' and 8a' to 2a''; 3 1A'' 5.274 and 3 1A' 5.397, both below 1e-10. Other: The active space is a full-valence space, defined once and then carried unchanged across all three charge states -- the same active orbitals were chosen for the anion and cation as for the neutral radical, with the active electron count simply increased or decreased by one. That is the cleanest possible arrangement for the quantities this paper reports, because ionization potentials and detachment energies are differences of total energies between charge states, and any change in the orbital set between them would contaminate those differences with a change of reference rather than a change of physics. The space is fourteen valence electrons in thirteen molecular orbitals for the neutral, corresponding to the valence atomic sp orbitals of the carbon and nitrogen atoms plus the hydrogen 1s, comprising ten a' and three a'' orbitals under the assumed planar Cs symmetry; the anion carries fifteen electrons and the cation thirteen in the same thirteen orbitals. Because it is the full valence space, no orbital-selection judgement is involved and there is nothing to converge -- the only remaining question is dynamic correlation, and the paper is explicit that comparing the CASSCF and CASPT2 energies shows the dynamical correlation effect must be considered. The magnitude is large and state-dependent, which is the substantive active-space-related finding here: for the neutral, CASSCF and CASPT2 adiabatic energies are 0.702 against 0.738 eV for the 1A' state, essentially agreeing, but 2.041 against 1.556 eV for the 2 1Sigma+ state, 3.822 against 3.315 for 2 1A'', and 5.307 against 4.824 for 3 1A' -- shifts approaching half an electronvolt that reorder nothing but change every transition energy well beyond spectroscopic tolerance. So a full valence space is a necessary but not sufficient reference here; the authors correspondingly compute transition moments at CASSCF but excitation energies, which they describe as very sensitive to dynamic correlation, at CASPT2, mixing the two levels within a single oscillator strength. A second point concerns what the space has to accommodate. The states are far from uniformly single-reference: for the neutral, 2 1A'' is described by three configurations with coefficients -0.435, -0.428 and 0.504, 2 3A' by 0.448 and 0.833, and 3 1A' by 0.341 and 0.809, while the ground state sits at -0.939. For the cation the authors state the criterion explicitly, noting that the leading-configuration coefficients for X 2A', 2Pi(2A''), 4Pi(4A') and 4A' are all above 0.90, indicating single-reference character, while the other states show obviously multireference character. A space that could not have carried those multiple configurations would have failed selectively, on exactly the excited states the paper is about. Finally, a caveat on the geometries the space was optimized under: all states of all three species were assumed to have planar Cs symmetry, and several stationary points turn out not to be minima under that assumption. The 2 2A' state of the anion has an imaginary frequency of 474.3i and is unstable, and linear configurations of both ions carry imaginary bending frequencies that resolve into Renner-Teller pairs -- for the cation, X 2A' and 2Pi(2A'') are separated by only 0.009 eV, degenerate at linearity. Energies read from this table are therefore tied to a symmetry assumption that the vibrational analysis partly contradicts.

Following the analysis of linear triatomic Renner-Teller molecules, the anion is classified as a type D Renner-Teller molecule: following the in-plane imaginary bending eigenvector stabilizes the 2A'' component of the 2Pi state to the nonlinear X 2A'' ground state, and following the out-of-plane one stabilizes the 2A' component to a nonlinear geometry, with the larger in-plane imaginary frequency implying greater distortion from linearity for the X 2A'' state. The ground state is strongly bent at 109.3 degrees with a barrier to linearity of 0.575 eV, while the excited 2A' state has an obtuse angle of 143.3 degrees and may be termed quasilinear, its barrier to linearity being only 0.006 eV. Calculated harmonic frequencies for X 2A'' are 2845.5, 1975.0, 1031.9, 1001.5, 493.7 and 494.9 per cm, agreeing well with earlier theoretical values. All frequencies are real and the optimized states are confirmed stable except 2 2A', which has an imaginary frequency of 474.3i and is therefore unstable. That is the cleanest possible arrangement for the quantities this paper reports, because ionization potentials and detachment energies are differences of total energies between charge states, and any change in the orbital set between them would contaminate those differences with a change of reference rather than a change of physics. The states are far from uniformly single-reference: for the neutral, 2 1A'' is described by three configurations with coefficients -0.435, -0.428 and 0.504, 2 3A' by 0.448 and 0.833, and 3 1A' by 0.341 and 0.809, while the ground state sits at -0.939. compound_name: Cyclobutane photodissociation to two ethylenes via the tetramethylene diradical
geometry_source: Nuclear positions at each time step taken from a semiclassical electron-radiation-ion dynamics (SERID) trajectory; the potential energy curves are one-dimensional cuts corresponding to those classical nuclear trajectories determined on the fly rather than optimized stationary points. A single trajectory was examined.
method: CASSCF followed by multireference second-order perturbation theory (CASSCF/MRPT2), computed along a semiclassical electron-radiation-ion dynamics trajectory
active_space_orbital_description: Four electrons in four orbitals. For the tetramethylene intermediate this space yields states of the same symmetry and spin multiplicity, so states outside the active space were included to break the degeneracy.
active_space_protocol: Potential energy surfaces of both the electronic ground state and the first excited state were computed with four electrons and four orbitals in the active space, with no symmetry restriction. Because the tetramethylene intermediate then has states of the same symmetry and spin multiplicity within that space, the degeneracy was broken by including states outside the active space; energies and eigenvectors were first obtained in standard CASSCF calculations and Rayleigh-Schrodinger perturbation theory was then applied iteratively, each iteration using the energies from the previous one, to obtain the nondegenerate energies.
multiplicities_studied: singlet; ground state and lowest excited state
electronic_structure_description: When a femtosecond-scale laser pulse is applied there is a HOMO to LUMO excitation during the first 200 fs, after which one C-C bond breaks to form the tetramethylene diradical intermediate, which then moves on its lowest surface before a second nonadjacent C-C bond breaks to give two ethylene molecules. The forces on the nuclei are large enough to break two nonadjacent C-C bonds successively but not large enough to break any C-H bond. The computed surfaces show a reaction intermediate between 200 and 450 fs, with two well-defined wells in the ground-state curve at 330 fs and 410 fs. Those wells are associated with C-C-C angles near 90 degrees, the initial value in cyclobutane, while the higher-energy regions correspond to C-C-C angles substantially different from 90 degrees; large deviation of the C1-C2-C4-C3 torsional angle from its initial value of 0 degrees is likewise associated with the intermediate state. The C-C-C angles and that torsional angle are identified as the main internal reaction coordinates defining the ground-state surface in the intermediate region: expanding the C-C-C angle raises the ground-state energy while rotating about the C2-C4 bond away from 0 degrees lowers it, and the first excited state behaves the same way.
Other: The interesting active-space feature here is a degeneracy that the space itself creates and that has to be repaired from outside it. A four-electron, four-orbital space is the natural minimal choice for breaking two C-C bonds, but the authors report that for the tetramethylene intermediate this space produces states of the same symmetry and spin multiplicity, and they broke that degeneracy by including states outside the active space, labelled by a distinct symbol in their equations. The repair is not an enlargement of the space but an iterative Rayleigh-Schrodinger perturbation treatment in which the previous iteration's energies enter the denominators, converging to nondegenerate energies. This is worth flagging for anyone reusing the numbers: the reported ground and first excited state energies for the intermediate are not plain CASSCF or plain single-shot perturbation values but the fixed point of that iteration, and the degeneracy being lifted is an artefact of the small space rather than a physical near-degeneracy of the diradical. A diradical is exactly the case where a minimal space is most tempting and least safe, since the two singly occupied orbitals are nearly degenerate by construction. The second caveat is about what these surfaces are. The authors emphasise that the curves are one-dimensional potential energy surfaces corresponding to the classical nuclear trajectories determined on the fly in the semiclassical simulation, not optimized paths, and that a single trajectory was examined. The CASSCF/MRPT2 energies are therefore evaluated at geometries generated by a separate and much cheaper electronic description, a tight-binding-like semiclassical treatment in a basis of s and p atomic orbitals, so the reference wave function never influenced the geometries it is being used to score. Whether the four-orbital space is adequate along that whole path is not tested anywhere in the paper -- no larger space is reported for comparison, and no occupation numbers are given.
reference_short: Dou, Lei, Li, Wen, Torralva, Lo & Allen, J. Phys. Chem. A 2007, 111, 1133
notes: The tetramethylene diradical intermediate has been reported experimentally to decay on timescales of a few hundred femtoseconds. The semiclassical dynamics uses a nonorthogonal basis with s and p atomic orbitals and is coupled to the radiation field within time-dependent perturbation theory; the CASSCF/MRPT2 calculations are described as completely independent of that simulation.
correlation_correction: Multireference second-order perturbation theory applied iteratively via Rayleigh-Schrodinger perturbation theory, with states outside the active space included to remove the same-symmetry same-multiplicity degeneracy for the tetramethylene intermediate

compound_name: 1-H, the smallest hydrogen-terminated phenylacetylene dendron building block
point_group: Single-point calculations and optimizations run without symmetry constraints
geometry_source: Relaxed ground and excited state geometries optimized with SA-3-CASSCF(4/4)
method: State-specific and state-averaged CASSCF, with internally contracted CASPT2 where feasible; state-averaged calculations denoted SA-N-CASSCF(n/m) for N states averaged, n active electrons and m active orbitals, all states equally weighted
software: MOLPRO for the ab initio calculations; Jaguar for the B3LYP-DFT ground state geometries of the phenyl-terminated series
basis_set: 6-31G for the CASSCF and CASPT2 calculations; 6-31G** for the B3LYP-DFT geometries
active_space_orbital_description: Four active electrons in four active orbitals, averaged over three states.
active_space_protocol: SA-3-CASSCF(4/4) for both the relaxed ground and excited state geometries, the number of averaged states being the fewest that still describe all the low-lying bright states of interest, all equally weighted. CASPT2 single points use the same state-averaging and active space, with the carbon 1s orbitals left uncorrelated and a level shift of 0.1 au.
nroots_per_mult: three states, equally weighted
electronic_structure_description: Table 2 gives the components of the Stokes shift in per cm from CASPT2, compared with experiment, for the three hydrogen-terminated compounds. Ground state destabilization on relaxation: 816, 675 and 3416 for 1-H, 2-H and 3-H. Excited state relaxation: 4228, 2792 and 594. Splitting of the emitting state: 0, 1986 and 3130. Total CASPT2 Stokes shift: 5044, 5453 and 7139, against experimental values of 5928, 6788 and 8627. For this compound the splitting contribution to the Stokes shift is zero, so the shift comes entirely from ground state destabilization and excited state relaxation, the latter dominating at 4228 per cm. The excited state relaxation decreases with increased conjugation across the series, as in linear alkenes. The sum of the absolute C-C bond length changes between the absorbing and emitting geometries is 0.31 Angstrom. The absorbing state is taken as the lowest lying bright state at the optimized ground state geometry and the emitting state as the lowest lying state with significant oscillator strength at the relaxed excited state geometry.
Other: Two distinct active-space decisions are at work here and they pull in opposite directions. The first is sizing: the number of states averaged over and the size of the space both vary from molecule to molecule according to a single stated criterion -- that the lowest-lying bright states be well described -- and the number of states is chosen to average over the fewest states that still describe all the low-lying bright states of interest, all equally weighted. So the space is not held fixed across the series whose trend is being reported; the hydrogen-terminated series runs SA-3-CASSCF(4/4), SA-4-CASSCF(4/4) and SA-7-CASSCF(6/6) for the one-, two- and three-unit compounds. That is defensible for a property defined relative to each molecule's own bright manifold, but it means the Stokes-shift components in the table are not differences taken at a common level. The authors address this indirectly rather than by convergence testing: they check that a large active space CASSCF on the phenyl-terminated one- and two-unit compounds reproduces the same lack of shift in absorption energies and the same excited-state orderings as the CASPT2 results on the hydrogen-terminated series, and use that correspondence to justify concentrating the expensive treatment on the smaller molecules. CASPT2 itself is only possible on the hydrogen-terminated series because of the size of the phenyl-terminated molecules, and it reuses the same state-averaging and active spaces as the corresponding CASSCF calculation, with carbon 1s left uncorrelated and level shifts of 0.1 and 0.3 au applied to the one- and three-unit compounds respectively. A level shift that differs by a factor of three between two members of a series is worth noting when their computed Stokes shifts are being compared. The second decision is the more interesting one, and it exploits a property of the active space rather than its size. The natural orbitals from a CASSCF calculation are just one of many equivalent sets: any unitary transformation of orbitals within the active space leaves the wave function and the energy unchanged. The orbitals that emerge here are generally delocalized and therefore unsuited to interpreting excitonic states in terms of localized chromophores, so the authors deliberately rotate within the space to construct chromophore-localized orbitals -- taking linear combinations of four orbitals from an SA-6-CASSCF(12/12) calculation to form two localized orbitals on each branch of the meta-substituted molecule, and rotating the orbitals of an SA-4-CASSCF(4/4) calculation for the para isomer. Those localized orbitals then furnish the configurations of an exciton model and the resulting Hamiltonian matrix, recomputed at each point of a linearly interpolated path between the absorbing and emitting geometries. This is an active space used as an interpretive basis rather than only as a correlation treatment, and the invariance argument is what makes it legitimate. One numerical discrepancy should be flagged: the text gives the Coulomb integral J for the para isomer as 939 per cm in the absorbing geometry, while the table gives 1021 per cm for the same quantity; the emitting values, 1466 against 1471, are also not identical. Both are reproduced here as printed.
reference_short: Thompson, Gaab, Xu, Bardeen & Martinez, J. Phys. Chem. A 2004, 108, 671
notes: The corresponding phenyl-terminated compound absorbs at 34700 per cm and fluoresces with its 0-0 peak at 32600 per cm.

electronic_structure_description: Table 3 gives the coupling terms and Coulomb and exchange integrals in per cm. The authors address this indirectly rather than by convergence testing: they check that a large active space CASSCF on the phenyl-terminated one- and two-unit compounds reproduces the same lack of shift in absorption energies and the same excited-state orderings as the CASPT2 results on the hydrogen-terminated series, and use that correspondence to justify concentrating the expensive treatment on the smaller molecules. method: CASSCF with the active space selected by the CAS-UNO natural orbital occupation method, used for conical intersection and intersystem crossing searches; TD-DFT for the absorption spectra and B3LYP geometry optimizations on the ground-state surface

relativistic_treatment: SDD effective core potential on chromium
active_space_orbital_description: Nine electrons in ten orbitals, generating 25200 quartet Slater determinant configurations. The minimal space covering all the metal d orbitals for a chromium(III) complex would be (3,5); the extra orbitals account for dative metal-ligand bonding. The five metal d orbitals whose occupations are reported are dxz, dyz, dxy, dz2 and dx2-y2.
active_space_protocol: The expanded active space was chosen from the UNO occupation numbers using the CAS-UNO method, with initial guess natural orbitals generated from a UHF wave function; the best balance was found to be nine electrons in ten orbitals. The space was further expanded and a couple of selected geometries were reoptimised, with only a very small effect on geometrical parameters observed. For conical intersection optimization the orbital rotation terms were neglected in the solution of the coupled perturbed multiconfigurational SCF equations. Intersystem crossing searches between quartet and doublet states used the same optimization algorithm, with a many-electron basis of MS = 1/2 Slater determinants capable of describing all spin states sharing that MS eigenvalue.
electronic_structure_description: The ground-state minimum and all the photoaquation products have quartet spin states. Metal d orbital occupations from the CASSCF wave function are, on the ground-state surface, dxz 0.9999, dyz 0.9999, dxy 0.9999, dz2 0.0180 and dx2-y2 0.0185; at the minimum energy Q0/Q1 conical intersection they become dxz 1.0001, dyz 0.9999, dxy 0.5039, dz2 0.0212 and dx2-y2 0.5001. A conical intersection seam was located between the quartet ground state of (dxz)1(dyz)1(dxy)1 configuration and the quartet excited state of (dxz)1(dyz)1(dx2-y2)1 configuration, involving rupture of a single Cr-N bond from a tn ligand in the twist boat conformation and rearrangement of the remaining ligands to a trigonal bipyramidal geometry at the metal, where the dxy and dx2-y2 orbitals become degenerate and equally populated, with almost 50 percent of the electron density in each. The derivative coupling and gradient difference vectors that lift the degeneracy essentially involve rearrangement of the bonded ligands toward a more square pyramidal coordination. Geometry optimizations started on the ground state displaced along the gradient difference vector gave two stable square pyramidal minima, each with a coordination hole at the axial position and one tn ligand hanging loose, to which water can then coordinate, giving both cis and trans isomers of the aquated product. The Q0/Q1 conical intersection lies on a ridge connecting those isomers, so decay through it involves downhill passage to either minimum in the surrounding moat. From TD-DFT the absorption bands are at 420 and 345 nm, both of ligand field character with zero oscillator strength, and 240 nm of ligand-to-metal charge transfer character, against experimental ligand field bands at 457 and 351 nm.
Other: The active space is chosen algorithmically rather than by inspection, and the paper states both the minimum that would suffice formally and the reason it is not enough. For a chromium(III) complex the minimal space covering all the metal d orbitals is (3,5), but larger spaces are generally required to account for dative metal-ligand bonding; such expanded spaces account for additional dynamic correlation and give qualitative wave functions capable of producing good geometries and reasonable relative energetics such as barrier heights. The expansion is driven by data: the CAS-UNO method is used, with initial guess natural orbitals generated from a UHF wave function, natural orbitals being those that diagonalize the one-electron density matrix with occupation numbers measuring each orbital's importance in a multiconfigurational wave function. This approach is noted as successful where the initial choice of orbitals is unclear or problematic because of system size. Choosing from the UNO occupation numbers, the best balance was found to be nine electrons in ten orbitals, generating 25200 quartet Slater determinant configurations. A convergence check is reported, though only a partial one: the space was further expanded and a couple of selected geometries reoptimised, with only a very small effect on geometrical parameters observed. That tests geometry, not relative energies, and the paper is explicit elsewhere that energies are the weak point -- for accurate spectroscopy and comparison of relative energetics between, for example, ligand-to-metal charge transfer and ligand field states, multireference perturbation corrections such as CASPT2 are described as essential, yet no CASPT2 is applied here. The spectroscopy is instead taken from TD-DFT and the CASSCF is used for what it is good at: analytical gradients, Hessians and nonadiabatic couplings are available for these wave functions, which is what makes conical intersection and intersystem crossing searches feasible. Readers should therefore treat the CASSCF energies as mechanistic rather than spectroscopic. The active space earns its keep in a specific and checkable way at the crossing. At the quasi-trigonal-bipyramidal conical intersection the dxy and dx2-y2 orbitals become degenerate and should be equally populated, and the CASSCF occupations confirm it directly -- 0.5039 and 0.5001 for the tris complex and 0.5025 and 0.5049 for the bis complex, against essentially integer occupations of about 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 and near zero on the ground-state surface. Half-integer occupations of exactly the two orbitals predicted to cross are the kind of evidence only an active space containing both of them can supply. Two technical caveats: the orbital rotation terms were neglected in solving the coupled perturbed multiconfigurational SCF equations for the conical intersection optimizations, and for the intersystem crossing searches the many-electron basis consisted of MS = 1/2 Slater determinants, which can describe all spin states sharing that MS eigenvalue; at such crossings the derivative coupling vector vanishes by spin symmetry so only the gradient difference vector is nonzero.

active_space_protocol: The space was chosen because the single-point CASSCF calculations along the reaction path require a balanced description of states with different electronic structure -- ground state, npi*, pipi* and the dissociative pisigma* -- so a fairly large space covering all three orbital types was used. The same (14,11) space carries the CASPT2 vertical excitation energies, there in a 6-31G(d,p) basis, and one-dimensional cuts were computed at the state-averaged CASSCF level.
electronic_structure_description: Vertical excitation energies, oscillator strengths and dipole moments from CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ at MP2/aug-cc-pVDZ ground-state geometries, with CASPT2(14,11)/6-31G(d,p) values in parentheses: S0 at 0.0 eV with a dipole moment of 3.19 debye; npi* at 4.67 eV (CASPT2 5.20), oscillator strength 0.0002, dipole 0.72 debye; pipi* at 4.74 eV (CASPT2 4.53), f 0.085, dipole 6.39 debye; pipi* at 6.00 eV (CASPT2 6.22), f 0.165, dipole 6.43 debye; pipi* at 6.14 eV, f 0.025, dipole 0.98 debye; and pisigma* at 5.90 eV, f 0.0007, dipole 6.94 debye. The oxo form absorbs at longer wavelengths than the hydroxy tautomer, consistent with experiment. The experimental gas-phase absorption maximum for this tautomer is at 4.51 eV, fairly well reproduced by the vertical transitions to the lowest npi* and pipi* states at both the CC2 and CASPT2 levels. At the minima of the excited states the CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ energies are 3.41 eV for npi* and 3.93 eV for pipi*, relative to the ground state. In the CASSCF profiles the npi* state lies vertically below the corresponding pipi* state, in qualitatively satisfactory agreement with the CC2 picture.
Other: The active space is justified explicitly by the balance it has to strike rather than by size alone. Single-point CASSCF calculations along the reaction path have to describe states of quite different electronic structure at once -- the ground state, two locally excited valence states of npi* and pipi* character, and a dissociative pisigma* state -- and the authors state that a balanced description of states with different electronic structure is required, which is why they employed a fairly large space of fourteen electrons correlated over eleven molecular orbitals: six pi orbitals, three lone pair n orbitals, and two sigma* orbitals. Each block earns its place against a specific state. Omitting the lone pairs would drop the npi* states; omitting the two sigma* orbitals would remove the pisigma* state entirely, and that state is the whole mechanism, since the model is hydrogen detachment driven by the repulsive pisigma* state, nonadiabatic relaxation to the ground state at the seam of intersection between pisigma* and S0, and hydrogen attachment to a vicinal heteroatom on the ground-state surface. A space chosen from the pi system alone would have reproduced the absorption spectrum and missed the photochemistry completely. Two sigma* orbitals rather than one is the specific detail that makes the tautomerization tractable: the reaction transfers hydrogen between two heteroatoms, so one O-H and one N-H antibonding orbital must both be present, and the figures accordingly show the sigma* natural orbital changing character between the oxo form, the intersection seam, and the hydroxy form. The crossing itself is located by a diagnostic that only this space can provide. Rather than optimizing a minimum energy crossing point, the authors take a geometry with both the OH and NH distances at 2.05 Angstrom, taken from an MP2 optimization of the corresponding radical, and demonstrate computationally that at that geometry the CASSCF(14,11)/cc-pVDZ energies of the pisigma* and S0 states are nearly the same while for other OH and NH distances they are clearly distinct -- so the point serves as a representative member of the extended intersection seam. The path is then a linear synchronous transit in which all bond lengths and angles vary proportionally between the ground-state equilibrium geometry and that seam point, with single-point CASSCF energies along it. Two caveats for reuse follow from this construction. First, the profiles are not relaxed paths, so barriers read off them are upper bounds tied to the interpolation. Second, and more important for the numbers, the vertical excitation energies are reported at two different levels with two different bases: CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ in the main table, with CASPT2(14,11)/6-31G(d,p) values in parentheses at MP2/aug-cc-pVDZ geometries. The same fourteen-electron eleven-orbital space thus appears with a Pople double-zeta basis for the perturbative energies and a correlation-consistent double-zeta basis for the surface scans, and the two sets of numbers should not be mixed. The agreement between the CASSCF and CC2 photophysical pictures is described by the authors as qualitatively satisfactory rather than quantitative.

electronic_structure_description: Vertical excitation energies, oscillator strengths and dipole moments from CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ at MP2/aug-cc-pVDZ ground-state geometries, with CASPT2(14,11)/6-31G(d,p) values in parentheses: S0 at 0.0 eV with a dipole moment of 1.35 debye; npi* at 4.84 eV (CASPT2 4.91), oscillator strength 0.001, dipole 0.87 debye; pipi* at 5.28 eV (CASPT2 4.81), f 0.370, dipole 2.03 debye; pipi* at 6.36 eV (CASPT2 6.43), f 0.043, dipole 1.87 debye; pipi* at 6.41 eV, f 0.090, dipole 1.90 debye; and pisigma* at 6.67 eV, f 0.00005, dipole 4.17 debye. The experimental absorption maximum at 4.86 eV is fairly well reproduced by the vertical transitions to the lowest npi* and pipi* states at both levels. At the minima of the excited states the CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ energies are 4.17 eV for npi* and 4.97 eV for pipi*. As for the oxo form, the npi* state lies vertically below the pipi* state in the CASSCF profiles. The pisigma* state of this tautomer lies considerably higher than that of the oxo form, 6.67 against 5.90 eV.
Other: The active space is justified explicitly by the balance it has to strike rather than by size alone. Single-point CASSCF calculations along the reaction path have to describe states of quite different electronic structure at once -- the ground state, two locally excited valence states of npi* and pipi* character, and a dissociative pisigma* state -- and the authors state that a balanced description of states with different electronic structure is required, which is why they employed a fairly large space of fourteen electrons correlated over eleven molecular orbitals: six pi orbitals, three lone pair n orbitals, and two sigma* orbitals. Each block earns its place against a specific state. Omitting the lone pairs would drop the npi* states; omitting the two sigma* orbitals would remove the pisigma* state entirely, and that state is the whole mechanism, since the model is hydrogen detachment driven by the repulsive pisigma* state, nonadiabatic relaxation to the ground state at the seam of intersection between pisigma* and S0, and hydrogen attachment to a vicinal heteroatom on the ground-state surface. A space chosen from the pi system alone would have reproduced the absorption spectrum and missed the photochemistry completely. Two sigma* orbitals rather than one is the specific detail that makes the tautomerization tractable: the reaction transfers hydrogen between two heteroatoms, so one O-H and one N-H antibonding orbital must both be present, and the figures accordingly show the sigma* natural orbital changing character between the oxo form, the intersection seam, and the hydroxy form. The crossing itself is located by a diagnostic that only this space can provide. Rather than optimizing a minimum energy crossing point, the authors take a geometry with both the OH and NH distances at 2.05 Angstrom, taken from an MP2 optimization of the corresponding radical, and demonstrate computationally that at that geometry the CASSCF(14,11)/cc-pVDZ energies of the pisigma* and S0 states are nearly the same while for other OH and NH distances they are clearly distinct -- so the point serves as a representative member of the extended intersection seam. The path is then a linear synchronous transit in which all bond lengths and angles vary proportionally between the ground-state equilibrium geometry and that seam point, with single-point CASSCF energies along it. Two caveats for reuse follow from this construction. First, the profiles are not relaxed paths, so barriers read off them are upper bounds tied to the interpolation. Second, and more important for the numbers, the vertical excitation energies are reported at two different levels with two different bases: CC2/aug-cc-pVDZ in the main table, with CASPT2(14,11)/6-31G(d,p) values in parentheses at MP2/aug-cc-pVDZ geometries. The same fourteen-electron eleven-orbital space thus appears with a Pople double-zeta basis for the perturbative energies and a correlation-consistent double-zeta basis for the surface scans, and the two sets of numbers should not be mixed. The agreement between the CASSCF and CC2 photophysical pictures is described by the authors as qualitatively satisfactory rather than quantitative.
reference_short: Chmura, Rode, Sobolewski, Lapinski & Nowak, J. Phys. Chem. A 2008, 112, 13655
notes: Potential energy profiles were computed along a linear synchronous transit path from this tautomer's ground-state minimum to the representative seam point with OH and NH distances of 2.05 Angstrom, at CASSCF(14,11)/cc-pVDZ. At that geometry the pisigma* and S0 energies are nearly the same while at other OH and NH distances they are clearly distinct.
correlation_correction: CASPT2 on the (14,11) CASSCF reference for the vertical excitation energies; CC2 used independently for comparison

compound_name: CO2 radical cation and its quartet states, with the neutral and dication reference points
point_group: Linear D-infinity-h for the doublet ground state and for the vertical excitations; C2v for the bent quartet minima, labelled in Cs where the symmetry is further reduced
geometry_source: Geometry optimization at CCSD/cc-pVTZ in Gaussian 03, with frequency analysis at the same level to confirm genuine minima; MRCI used as a benchmark that provides very similar geometries
method: CASSCF followed by internally contracted multireference configuration interaction (MRCI), used as the benchmark level for the energetics and geometries of the quartet states
software: MOLPRO 2006.1 for the CASSCF and MRCI calculations; Gaussian 03 for the CCSD optimizations and the UB3LYP wave functions used in the bonding analysis
basis_set: cc-pVQZ for the CASSCF and MRCI calculations; cc-pVTZ for the CCSD optimizations; 6-311G* for the UB3LYP calculations underlying the Fermi hole analysis
active_space_orbital_description: The full valence active space, fifteen electrons in twelve orbitals. The core molecular orbitals were constrained to double occupation but fully optimized.
active_space_protocol: A full valence space is used, so no orbital selection judgement enters: every valence orbital is active and the only frozen orbitals are the cores, which are constrained to double occupation while still being optimized. MRCI is then built on that CASSCF reference and serves as the benchmark against which the CCSD results are checked.
multiplicities_studied: singlet for neutral CO2, doublet for the monocation ground state, quartet for the excited states studied, and triplet for the dication
electronic_structure_description: Ground term: X 2Pi_g for the monocation. Table 3 gives energetics and geometries at MRCI/cc-pVQZ, with energies relative to the CO2+ X 2Pi_g ground state at -187.846683 hartree. Neutral CO2 X 1Sigma_g+ is linear with both bond lengths 1.1622 Angstrom at -13.47 eV; the monocation ground state X 2Pi_g is linear at 1.1764 Angstrom, taken as zero. The a 4Sigma_g- state appears as the bent 4B1 (4A'') local minimum at 1.268 Angstrom and 108.6 degrees, 4.19 eV; as a linear global minimum at 1.119 and 2.046 Angstrom, 3.92 eV; as a vertical excitation at the ground state geometry, 10.32 eV; and dissociating to O+(4Su) plus CO(X 1Sigma+) at 5.22 eV. The b 4Pi_u state gives the bent 4B2 (4A') local minimum at 1.308 Angstrom and 120.1 degrees, 5.80 eV; a second local minimum at 1.122 and 2.484 Angstrom and 103.4 degrees, 5.74 eV; a vertical excitation at 8.36 eV; and dissociation to O(3Pg) plus CO+(X 2Sigma+) at 5.64 eV. The c 4Pi_g state gives a bent 2 4B2 local minimum at 1.333 Angstrom and 127.2 degrees, 7.17 eV, with a vertical excitation at 9.48 eV. The dication CO2 2+ X 3Sigma_g- is linear at 1.2140 Angstrom, 23.29 eV, with a vertical ionization at 23.40 eV. At the CCSD level the first excited quartet lies 4.12 eV and the second 5.50 eV above the doublet ground state, shifted by MRCI to 4.19 and 5.80 eV. For both quartet states additional minima corresponding to predissociative complexes of CO with O+ in the 4A'' state and of CO+ with O in the 4A' state lie below the covalent structures, separated from them by barriers of 0.1 eV for the 4A'' state and 1.1 eV for the 4A' state; the 4A' complex stays bent while the 4A'' complex is linear. Mulliken spin densities localize the three unpaired electrons entirely on the oxygen atoms in the 4B1 state, whereas each atom bears one unpaired electron in the 4B2 state. The enormous differences between vertical and adiabatic excitation energies, 6.13 eV for the 4B1 state and 2.56 eV for the 4B2 state, are caused predominantly by the bending of the quartet states.
Other: The multireference treatment here uses the full valence space, fifteen electrons in twelve orbitals, which removes active-space selection as a source of error entirely -- there is nothing to choose, and the only frozen orbitals are cores that remain fully optimized while constrained to double occupation. That matters more than usual for this system because of what is being compared. The quartet states are strongly bent while the doublet ground state is linear, and the resulting gaps between vertical and adiabatic excitation energies are enormous, 6.13 eV for the 4B1 state and 2.56 eV for the 4B2 state. Comparing states of different multiplicity across a 6 eV geometric relaxation is exactly the situation where a truncated or state-tuned space would be suspect, and a full valence space is the clean answer. It also lets the MRCI results serve their stated role as a benchmark: the CCSD excitation energies of 4.12 and 5.50 eV shift only to 4.19 and 5.80 eV at MRCI, and the geometries are very similar, which is the check that validates the cheaper method for the rest of the study. The limitation to note is one of scope rather than of the space. The multireference treatment covers only the CO2 monocation and its dissociation channels; the bonding analysis of the [C2O4]2+ intermediate that gives the paper its title is performed on wave functions calculated at the UB3LYP/6-311G* level, because the authors state that computing the pair densities required for a domain-averaged Fermi hole analysis at the exact level is beyond their possibilities. So the central bonding conclusion, that the intermediate is a complex rather than a covalently bound species, does not rest on the multireference calculation at all, and the eigenvalues tabulated for it -- including the diagnostic broken valence sigma pair at 0.798 and 0.802 for alpha and beta spin -- are density functional quantities. One labelling slip is worth flagging for anyone reading Table 3: the text at one point refers to the vertical excitation energies of the CO2+ dication with the X 2Pi_g term symbol, but a doublet ground state belongs to the monocation, and the table lists the dication separately as X 3Sigma_g-.
reference_short: Feixas, Ponec, Fiser, Roithova, Schroder & Price, J. Phys. Chem. A 2010, 114, 6681
notes: The [C2O4]2+ transient complex formed in the CO2 2+ plus CO2 reaction is analysed by domain-averaged Fermi holes on UB3LYP/6-311G* wave functions, not by the multireference methods, so no separate row is entered for it. Table 2 of that analysis gives alpha and beta eigenvalues for the O(1)C(2)O(3) fragment of the triplet complex, the lowest pair being a broken valence sigma C(4)O(3) contribution at 0.798 and 0.802. The CO2+ cation formed by electron capture in that reaction bears an unpaired electron at the carbon atom.
