compound_name: OClO radical, doublet and quartet electronic states and predissociation of the A 2A2 state
point_group: C2v at equilibrium, reduced to Cs along the oxygen-loss dissociation path, with linear configurations treated in the corresponding linear point groups
geometry_source: Equilibrium geometries and adiabatic relative energies obtained by CASPT2 geometry optimization; potential energy cuts as a function of the bond angle computed with the bond distance fixed at the experimental ground-state value of 1.470 Angstrom; dissociation paths from partial CASPT2 optimizations at fixed bond distances out to 5.0 Angstrom; minimum energy crossing points located at both the reference and perturbatively corrected levels
method: CASSCF reference functions with CASPT2 for the first-order wave function and second-order energy in the full configuration interaction space, together with minimum energy crossing point searches and spin-orbit coupling evaluation
software: Not stated in the extracted text
basis_set: Contracted atomic natural orbital ANO-L basis, Cl [6s5p4d3f] and O [5s4p3d2f]
soc_included: yes, spin-orbit couplings computed at the located crossing points
active_space_orbital_description: Thirteen electrons in thirteen orbitals: the 7a1 through 11a1, 2b1 through 4b1, 4b2 through 7b2 and 1a2 orbitals. Relative to the full valence space the 5a1, 6a1 and 3b2 orbitals, mainly the oxygen 2s and chlorine 3s orbitals, are excluded, and four virtual orbitals, 10a1, 4b1, 11a1 and 7b2, are added. The ground state configuration is (2b1)2 (7a1)2 (4b2)2 (1a2)2 (5b2)2 (8a1)2 (3b1)1 with 9a1, 6b2, 10a1, 4b1, 11a1 and 7b2 unoccupied.
active_space_protocol: The same space as used in earlier multireference configuration interaction studies of this radical, so that the present results can be compared with those directly. Three deep occupied s-type orbitals are traded for four virtual orbitals relative to the full valence space. The thirteen orbitals are re-labelled by irreducible representation as the molecular symmetry changes, in Cs for the oxygen-loss dissociation curves and in the appropriate linear subgroups for linear configurations, so a single space follows the molecule from bent equilibrium through linear geometries to the dissociation asymptote. Full valence active spaces were used instead for the fragment species.
electronic_structure_description: Ground term: X 2B1. Table 1 gives adiabatic relative energies in eV and geometries as bond distance in Angstroms and bond angle in degrees, from the present perturbative calculations alongside earlier configuration interaction and multistate perturbative values and experiment. X 2B1 at 0.0 with 1.476 and 117.7, against 1.476 and 117.9, 1.477 and 116.1, and experimental 1.470 and 117.4. 1 2B2 at 2.10 against 1.98 and 2.20, geometry 1.592 and 89.4. A 2A2 at 2.67 against 2.65, 2.68 and experimental 2.69, geometry 1.630 and 106.4 against experimental 1.627 and 106.2. 1 2A1 at 2.76 against 2.60 and 2.76, geometry 1.605 and 121.5. 1 2Pi_u at 2.15 with 1.582 and 180.0, the global minimum of 1 2A1 lying in the linear configuration. 2 2A1 at 2.86 against 2.78, geometry 1.608 and 136.0. 1 4B1 at 2.39 with 1.615 and 180.0, in the linear configuration. 1 4B2 at 3.08 against 3.08, geometry 1.757 and 155.6. 1 4A2 at 3.11 against 3.22, geometry 1.753 and 163.1. 1 4A1 at 4.02 with 1.780 and 86.4. The computed adiabatic energy of the A 2A2 state, 2.67 eV, is very close to the experimental 2.69 eV. Potential energy cuts as a function of the bond angle from 60 to 180 degrees resemble the previously reported configuration interaction curves. The global minimum of the 1 2A1 state lies in the linear configuration. Computed sum energies for the product groups are 2.74, 4.68, 0.24, 1.23 and 1.90 eV, deviating from experiment by less than 0.20 eV for the oxygen-loss product groups and 0.11 eV for the chlorine-loss group. Two predissociation processes are identified from the crossing point energies and spin-orbit couplings: the first proceeds from the A 2A2 state at 2.67 eV through a crossing with 1 2A1 at 2.79 eV, then a linear transition state at 3.02 eV and an intermediate at 2.64 eV, to atomic oxygen plus ClO at 2.74 eV, the first oxygen-loss limit; the second proceeds through a crossing with 1 2B2 at 2.92 eV. Thirteen electrons occupy thirteen orbitals comprising the 7a1 through 11a1, 2b1 through 4b1, 4b2 through 7b2 and 1a2 sets. Relative to the full valence space three occupied orbitals are removed -- 5a1, 6a1 and 3b2, described as mainly the oxygen 2s and chlorine 3s orbitals -- and four virtual orbitals are added, 10a1, 4b1, 11a1 and 7b2. electronic_structure_description: Ground term: 2B1, taken as the ground state. The valence orbitals of this radical are degenerate, producing a Jahn-Teller split of a few kcal/mol between this state and the 2A2 component in the C2v point group. The starting reference configuration is (9a1)2(6b2)2(1b1)2(2b1)1(1a2)2. The optimized geometry shows a large contribution from a diene-like structure. Tabulated total energies place this state at -193.146897 hartree against -193.146453 for the other component, and the combination with the magnesium cation at -392.510980 against -392.510536 hartree, corresponding to binding energies of 74.0 and 74.3 kcal/mol respectively. Geometries agree with previous theoretical studies to within 3 percent in bond distances and less than 1 percent in bond angles.
Other: The multiconfigurational treatment here is confined to one species for one reason -- orbital degeneracy -- and the paper says so directly: the main problem in the cyclopentadienyl radical is the degeneracy of the valence orbitals, which produces a Jahn-Teller split of a few kcal/mol between the two components. That is precisely the situation a single-determinant method cannot handle, and it is why this fragment alone is treated multiconfigurationally while everything else in the study, including the magnesium complexes that are its subject, is handled by single-reference perturbation and composite methods. The space is specified by symmetry block rather than by total: five valence electrons distributed over four orbitals of b1 symmetry and two of a2 symmetry. Crucially the same space is used for both Jahn-Teller components, each started from its own open-shell reference configuration, which is what makes the small energy difference between them meaningful -- the two states differ by which orbital carries the single electron, and comparing them across differently constructed spaces would confound the splitting with the reference. The validation is a proper enlargement test with a stated criterion. The space was extended by one further virtual orbital of each symmetry, and the resulting optimized geometry came out close to the original; the authors connect the two observations by noting that the added orbitals carry insignificant occupation numbers, less than 0.003. Reporting the occupation numbers rather than just the geometric agreement is what turns this from an assertion into evidence, since an orbital with occupation below 0.003 cannot be contributing to the wave function regardless of what the geometry does. The geometries the space produces are chemically interpretable in a way that supports the assignment: one component shows a large contribution from a diene-like structure while in the other only the carbon-carbon bond perpendicular to the symmetry axis has double-bond character, and both agree with previous theoretical work to within 3 percent in bond lengths and 1 percent in angles. One limitation of scope worth recording: the multiconfigurational energies enter the reaction thermochemistry only through this fragment, so the computed dissociation energies pair a multiconfigurational description of the radical with a single-reference description of everything else, and the two Jahn-Teller components differ by only 0.0004 hartree in the tabulated total energies.

Other: The space is specified by a stated selection rule rather than a fixed count: it should include the necessary amount of occupied and unoccupied ligand orbitals separated by an energy gap from other orbitals. Applying that rule gives different sizes for different complexes -- one highest occupied and one lowest unoccupied orbital from each diketonate ligand together with one occupied and two unoccupied from bipyridine, giving eight electrons in nine orbitals, or two occupied and two unoccupied from phenanthroline, giving ten in ten -- and in the smaller model complexes the space was expanded to include as many ligand pi orbitals as possible, reaching ten in ten for one and twelve in twelve for another. Quasirelativistic pseudopotentials place the lanthanide 4f electrons in the core, so the metal f manifold is absent from the active space entirely and only ligand-localized orbitals are correlated. The justification given is that the 4f orbitals are strongly localized near the nucleus, so the excited levels of the trivalent ion are almost insensitive to the chemical environment; the authors are careful to add that interactions affecting the ligand-localized levels are not neglected, since it is those levels the calculation is actually about. This is a case where the interesting physics has been removed from the space on purpose, and it works because the energy-transfer question concerns the position of the ligand triplet relative to metal levels whose positions are taken as transferable. Gadolinium is used in place of the emitting europium for the same reason -- its own levels lie too high to interfere, so the ligand triplet can be located experimentally and computationally without metal involvement. Two further points bear on the reference. Ground and triplet geometries come from state-specific optimizations while the vertical excitation energies come from state-averaged calculations, averaging over four or five singly excited states of one multiplicity plus the ground state, with singlets and triplets treated in entirely separate calculations. And the perturbative step requires many more states than the reference does: the effective Hamiltonian included the 34 lowest states of each multiplicity for the full complexes and 20 for the models, chosen to ensure convergence of the perturbation estimates. So the space defines what is correlated but the state manifold that stabilises the correction is far larger than the manifold the space was built to describe.

geometry_source: Ground-state isomer and transition-state structures optimized at CASSCF(10,8)/6-31G* and confirmed as minima or a first-order saddle point by harmonic frequencies; the conical intersection determined by state-averaged CASSCF optimization; the surfaces used for dynamics built on a grid based on B3LYP/6-31G* ground-state and CAS(6,4)/6-31G* excited-state optimized structures
method: CASSCF for geometries and conical intersection optimization, CASPT2 single points on a larger three-state-averaged reference for the surfaces, and a semiclassical dynamics simulation performed at a tight-binding density functional level; B3LYP used for comparison on the ground state
software: Gaussian 03 for the CASSCF calculations; Molcas for the CASPT2 calculations
basis_set: 6-31G* throughout, with several basis sets tried for the density functional comparison to estimate basis set effects
active_space_orbital_description: Three spaces are used. Geometry optimizations use ten electrons in eight orbitals, comprising the pi, pi-star and two nonbonding orbitals of the azo group with the remainder taken from pi and pi-star orbitals of the aromatic rings. Energies are recalculated on a fourteen-electron twelve-orbital space. Excited-state grid structures were optimized with a six-electron four-orbital space.
active_space_protocol: The ten-electron eight-orbital space is stated to provide a reasonable account of the isomerization in both electronic states, its azo-group orbitals carrying the reaction coordinate and its ring orbitals connecting to the chromophore. Dynamic correlation is added by single points on a three-state-averaged fourteen-electron twelve-orbital zeroth-order wave function. Because computing a surface as a function of all internal degrees of freedom is practically impossible for this system, the surfaces were built on a selected grid of structures optimized at other levels.
multiplicities_studied: singlet; the S0 and S1 surfaces
nroots_per_mult: three states averaged in the zeroth-order wave function for the perturbative step
electronic_structure_description: Table 1 gives relative energies in kcal/mol for the critical structures at four levels with the same basis: the E isomer at 6.7, 7.9, 7.6 and 10.2; the Z isomer at 0.0 throughout; the ground-state transition state at 34.2, 40.4, 36.7 and 39.2 relative to the Z isomer, or 27.5, 32.5, 29.1 and 29.0 relative to the E isomer; the conical intersection at 43.8, 41.3 and a trajectory-averaged 45.0; the Franck-Condon point of the E isomer at 55.5, 54.0 and 50.7 relative to the E isomer; and the Franck-Condon point of the Z isomer at 67.3, 64.9 and 62.7 relative to the Z isomer. The Z isomer is the more stable of the two, by 6.7 to 7.9 kcal/mol depending on level. Its vertical excitation energy is computed at 64.9 kcal/mol at the reference level and 62.7 with correction, against an experimental absorption at 404 nm corresponding to 70.7 kcal/mol; the gap between its highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbitals is 2.72 eV. Its key bond parameters and the relevant dihedral angle were compared across methods, the angle becoming 94.1 degrees at the reference level. Relaxation dynamics from the excited-state Franck-Condon structure to the conical intersection is found to control the efficiency of the isomerization, while the quantum yields are largely determined by the shape of the ground-state surface.
Other: Three different active spaces appear in this study and each does a different job, which is worth separating because the reported energies mix them. Geometries of the two isomers and the ground-state transition state come from a ten-electron eight-orbital space; its composition is stated as the pi, pi-star and two nonbonding orbitals of the azo group, with the remaining orbitals and electrons taken from pi and pi-star orbitals of the aromatic rings. The azo-group orbitals are the ones that carry the isomerization, and the ring orbitals are what connect it to the chromophore, so the split is chemically motivated rather than a rank cut. Energies are then recalculated on a larger fourteen-electron twelve-orbital space averaged over three states, and the surfaces used for the dynamics are built from that larger space on a grid of structures which were themselves optimized at a density functional level for the ground state and at a still smaller six-electron four-orbital space for the excited state. So a single reported number can involve a six-orbital geometry, a twelve-orbital energy, and no consistent treatment between them; the authors state the reason plainly, that computing a surface as a function of all internal degrees of freedom is practically impossible for this system. The size of the correction is quantifiable from the table because both levels are reported. The ground-state barrier moves from 40.4 kcal/mol at the reference level to 36.7 with correction, and the conical intersection from 41.3 to a trajectory-averaged 45.0, so the barrier falls while the intersection rises, narrowing the gap between them by about seven. Vertical excitations move down by about two to three kcal/mol, from 64.9 to 62.7 and from 54.0 to 50.7, and remain below the experimental band positions of 70.7 and 58.3 kcal/mol at both levels. The isomer energy difference is stable across methods, 6.7, 7.9 and 7.6 kcal/mol at three levels, so it is the barrier and crossing energies rather than the thermodynamics that depend on the treatment. One consequence worth carrying: the dynamics simulations were run at a tight-binding density functional level rather than on the multiconfigurational surfaces, so the trajectory-averaged intersection energy of 45.0 kcal/mol is not directly comparable with the 41.3 and the perturbatively corrected surfaces serve as a static check on a dynamical calculation performed elsewhere.

notes: The bridged azobenzene shows highly efficient photoisomerization; the experimental quantum yield for the cis to trans direction exceeds that for trans to cis, which the study sets out to explain.

geometry_source: Not separately stated for the multiconfigurational calculations; the method tests were performed on a simplified model system with the smallest phosphine ligand because the full calculations are time-consuming
method: CASSCF and CASPT2, alongside broken-symmetry unrestricted perturbation theory from second to fourth order, broken-symmetry coupled cluster with perturbative triples, and broken-symmetry density functional theory; valence bond type wave functions derived from the multiconfigurational solution
software: Not stated in the extracted text
basis_set: Not stated in the extracted text
active_space_orbital_description: Four electrons in four orbitals, comprising two sets of pi and pi-star orbitals of the metal-carbene-vinyl moiety.
active_space_protocol: This smaller space was adopted specifically to characterise the biradical character of the product, after a Hartree-Fock instability was detected in its wave function. It is contained within the larger six-electron six-orbital space used along the reaction coordinate, so the two analyses connect.
electronic_structure_description: A Hartree-Fock instability was detected for this product, and unrestricted treatments lie 5.8 kcal/mol below the restricted Hartree-Fock solution, suggesting the metal-vinylcarbene moiety takes an open-shell singlet biradical-like electronic structure. In the four-orbital space the natural orbitals are essentially the same as the Kohn-Sham orbitals, and the main configuration is a closed-shell singlet with a weight of 90.0 percent, the second and third leading configurations contributing only 0.04 and 0.03 percent; these correspond to two-electron and one-electron excitations between the two central pi orbitals and are what induce the biradical character. Although those weights are small, the occupation number of the upper orbital is considerably larger than zero and that of the lower considerably smaller than 2.0, which the authors take as showing that the biradical character must be properly considered.
Other: Two spaces are used for two different questions and the smaller is contained in the larger, which the authors point out explicitly so that the two analyses connect. A four-electron four-orbital space of two pi and two pi-star orbitals of the metal-vinylcarbene moiety is used to characterise the product, and a six-electron six-orbital space comprising the bonding and antibonding orbitals of the two metal-carbon bonds and the breaking carbon-carbon bond is used along the reaction. The justification for the larger space is spelled out in an endnote and is a model of how to state such a choice: it contains the breaking sigma and sigma-star orbitals and the relevant pi orbitals and metal d orbitals in the reactant, and the corresponding orbitals in the product; the two carbon-carbon sigma bonds that are not broken during the reaction are deliberately excluded, both because they persist and because their bonding and antibonding orbitals lie at very low and very high energy respectively. Two independent checks on that choice are then offered -- valence bond orbitals derived from the same wave function change smoothly from reactant to product, and the perturbatively corrected energies track density functional and coupled cluster values except for one reaction energy. The multiconfigurational treatment was not a stylistic preference: a Hartree-Fock instability was detected in the wave functions of the metal-vinylcarbene products, which is what forced the issue, and the smaller space then quantifies the resulting biradical character. That quantification is careful and worth recording in full, because the two available diagnostics disagree in emphasis. The leading closed-shell configuration carries 90.0 percent weight with the next two contributing only 0.04 and 0.03 percent, which by weight alone would suggest a nearly single-configurational wave function; but the occupation numbers tell a different story, one orbital being considerably larger than zero and its partner considerably smaller than 2.0, which the authors take as showing the biradical character must be properly considered. Configuration weights and occupation numbers are not interchangeable diagnostics, and this is a clean example. Along the reaction coordinate the larger space gives antibonding occupations of 0.08, 0.16 and 0.11 at the transition state, identifying which bonds are actually breaking there. The method comparison is the other useful content. The perturbative activation energy matches coupled cluster and density functional values for the ruthenium system and is moderately smaller for iridium, but the perturbative reaction energy is considerably more negative than both in each system, and the density functional reaction energy deviates from coupled cluster by 5 to 6 kcal/mol. The authors note that coupled cluster is the most accurate where multireference character is small and the perturbative multiconfigurational method the most reliable where it is large, so the disagreement on reaction energies is itself the signal that the products carry that character. A model caveat: these method tests were run on a simplified system with the smallest phosphine ligand because the full calculations are too costly.
reference_short: Ishikawa, Tanimura, Nakao, Sato & Sakaki, Organometallics 2012, 31, 8189
notes: The reaction proceeds more easily in the ruthenium system than in the iridium one, which is the question the electronic analysis addresses. The perturbatively corrected activation energy for this system is almost the same as the coupled cluster and density functional values, while the reaction energy is considerably more negative than both.

ligand_set: A single nitrosyl, with a square planar ligand field represented by point charges placed 1.131 Angstrom from the iron on the x and y axes
geometry_source: Structure optimization of the bent model performed for this system; the surrounding ligand field represented by point charges rather than explicit ligands
method: CASSCF with systematic enlargement of the active space, used to obtain reference spin densities against which density functional results are assessed
software: Not stated in the extracted text
basis_set: Not stated in the extracted text
active_space_orbital_description: The minimal space is seven electrons in seven orbitals: four iron 3d orbitals, both nitrosyl pi-star orbitals, and the iron dx2-y2 orbital. Adding both nitrosyl pi orbitals gives eleven electrons in nine orbitals. Successive enlargements toward a double shell give eleven, twelve, thirteen and finally fifteen orbitals, the largest containing the four iron dxz, dxy, dyz and dz2 double-shell orbitals together with additional empty ligand orbitals.
active_space_protocol: The minimal space was constructed from the orbitals appearing in a qualitative molecular orbital diagram for this system, then systematically enlarged to test convergence of the spin density. Two virtual orbitals with iron dxz and dyz contributions were added first; because the dyz double-shell orbital rotated into an empty ligand orbital, a further virtual had to be admitted to recover it; a virtual with large iron dz2 character was added next, and finally the fourth double-shell orbital together with an additional empty ligand orbital. Identifying the double-shell orbitals is described as not trivial because they mix considerably with antibonding ligand orbitals, requiring additional ligand orbitals to keep the space stable. The fifth iron double-shell orbital could not be included because its destabilization by the point-charge environment would require many further ligand orbitals, and an alternative route adding a ligand sigma and sigma-star pair proved incompatible with including the remaining double-shell orbitals.
electronic_structure_description: For the quartet state the spin density depends only weakly on the size of the active space, and the profiles are similar for all spaces considered. The minimal seven-electron seven-orbital and eleven-electron nine-orbital calculations, which contain no double-shell effect at all, are qualitatively in good agreement with the largest reference, so these minimal spaces already suffice for an accurate spin density distribution. Spaces containing thirteen active electrons also give only small differences. In the natural orbital picture the iron dxy orbital does not interact with the ligand orbitals for any active space considered, while three iron d orbitals, dyz, dxz and dz2, interact strongly and covalently with the nitrosyl sigma and pi-star orbitals to give two bonding, two antibonding and one nonbonding combination.
Other: This is the most thorough active-space convergence study to appear in this collection so far, and its conclusion is state-dependent, which is the finding worth carrying. The space is built up from a qualitative molecular orbital picture: four metal 3d orbitals plus both nitrosyl pi-star orbitals, extended by a fifth metal d orbital, giving a minimal seven electrons in seven orbitals; adding both nitrosyl pi orbitals gives eleven electrons in nine orbitals. It is then systematically enlarged toward a double shell, one metal d orbital at a time, through eleven, twelve, thirteen and fifteen orbitals for the quartet and eleven, twelve and fourteen for the doublet. The obstacles encountered are reported rather than glossed: identifying the double-shell orbitals is described as not trivial because they mix considerably with antibonding ligand orbitals, so additional ligand orbitals had to be admitted to keep the space stable; in one case a double-shell orbital rotated into an empty ligand orbital and a further virtual had to be added to recover it; the fifth metal double-shell orbital could not be included at all because its destabilization by the point-charge environment would require many more ligand orbitals; and an alternative route adding a ligand sigma and sigma-star pair proved incompatible with including the remaining double-shell orbitals. That catalogue of failure modes is more instructive than a bare converged number. The result is that convergence depends on which state is asked about. For the quartet the spin density depends only weakly on the space, and the minimal seven-orbital and nine-orbital calculations without any double-shell effect already agree qualitatively with the largest reference. For the doublet the deviations are larger, the spin density converging gradually toward the reference as the space grows, and the authors state the distinction precisely: the minimal spaces suffice for a qualitative estimate while quantitatively correct spin densities require the metal double-shell orbitals. Consistently, the double-shell contributions to the natural orbitals are noted to be significantly larger for the doublet than for the quartet. So the same molecule, same property, different spin state, and the answer to whether a double shell is needed flips. The bonding picture the space reveals is stable across all of them: one metal d orbital does not interact with the ligand at all, while three others interact strongly and covalently with the nitrosyl orbitals to give two bonding, two antibonding and one nonbonding combination. One structural caveat: the ligand field is modelled by point charges rather than real ligands, and the authors note that the modelled field is not strong enough, so the environment that destabilises the fifth double-shell orbital is itself an approximation.
reference_short: Boguslawski, Jacob & Reiher, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2011, 7, 2740
notes: The study asks whether density functional theory can accurately predict spin densities, using this small model so that a converged multiconfigurational reference is reachable. None of the exchange-correlation functionals investigated proved able to reproduce it. The point charges model a square planar ligand field, but the authors note the modelled field is not strong enough.
correlation_correction: None applied; the multiconfigurational spin densities themselves are the reference quantity

compound_name: ZnCH2, zinc carbene, dissociation to Zn plus methylene
point_group: C2v for the triplet ground state; the singlet shows Cs symmetry and is largely distorted
geometry_source: Structures optimized at the Hartree-Fock level with restricted and unrestricted second-order perturbation theory; the transition state characterized by diagonalization of the force constant matrix and confirmed by following the intrinsic reaction coordinate
method: CASSCF for the dissociation curves and the rearrangement path, alongside Hartree-Fock and second-order Moller-Plesset perturbation theory for structures and energetics
basis_set: An (8s8p6d) basis contracted to [4s4p3d] for the zinc 3s, 3p, 3d and 4s shells; the standard double-zeta plus polarization basis for the other atoms
active_space_orbital_description: Four electrons in six orbitals: the zinc 4s and 4p orbitals together with the methylene sigma and p orbitals.
active_space_protocol: This space was chosen specifically in order to ensure correct dissociation, since the true dissociation limit corresponds to an excited zinc configuration with one electron in 4s and one in 4p rather than to the zinc ground state; a space without the zinc 4p orbitals would dissociate to the wrong asymptote.
electronic_structure_description: The interaction of ground-state zinc with methylene gives two states depending on the methylene spin state; the triplet 3B1 is the ground state in agreement with experiment and earlier calculations, while the 1A' singlet has Cs symmetry and is largely distorted. The dissociation profiles show that interaction between the zinc ground state and triplet methylene would give a repulsive curve, which crosses one arising from the interaction between the excited zinc state and triplet methylene; because under the imposed symmetry constraint both the ground state and the relevant component of the excited multiplet carry the same symmetry, an avoided crossing is observed. The zinc-carbon bond in the ground state is described as a pairing of the methylene sigma electron with the zinc 4s-4p electron, the carbon p and remaining zinc electrons being nonbonding. In the singlet state one molecular orbital is a mix of the methylene p orbital and zinc atomic orbitals, and the bonding electron pair becomes a nonbonding lone pair. Force constants of 2.10 mdyn per Angstrom and bond energies of 28.8 kcal/mol for the triplet and 37.2 kcal/mol for the singlet are reported.
Other: Two different spaces are used and each is chosen for a stated physical requirement rather than by a general recipe. For the dissociation curves the space is four electrons in six orbitals -- the zinc 4s and 4p orbitals together with the methylene sigma and p orbitals -- and the reason given is explicit: the profiles were obtained this way in order to ensure correct dissociation. That matters here because the true dissociation limit is not the zinc ground state but the excited state corresponding to a 4s-4p configuration, so a space lacking the zinc 4p orbitals would dissociate to the wrong asymptote. What the space then reveals is an avoided crossing that a smaller space could not have produced: the interaction of the zinc ground state with triplet methylene gives a repulsive curve which crosses one arising from the excited zinc state, and because under the imposed symmetry both the ground state and the relevant component of the excited multiplet carry the same symmetry label, the crossing becomes avoided. For the rearrangement the space is instead the whole valence space with one deliberate exclusion, eight electrons in nine orbitals comprising the two carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds, the zinc-carbon sigma bond and all their antibonding partners together with the carbon p orbital and two zinc p orbitals. The excluded orbital is the remaining zinc p orbital, left out because it is not expected to be involved in the reaction. Excluding by expected participation rather than by energy is the right criterion for a rearrangement, and the space size is reported concretely as 3696 configuration state functions in the reduced symmetry. The characterisation of the stationary point is done properly: diagonalizing the force constant matrix gave a single imaginary eigenvalue whose normal coordinate corresponds to breaking and forming the zinc-hydrogen and carbon-hydrogen bonds, and the connection to reactant and product was confirmed by following the intrinsic reaction coordinate rather than assumed from the imaginary mode alone. A limitation of scope worth carrying: the multiconfigurational treatment is applied to the dissociation curves and to the rearrangement path, while the structural and energetic characterisation of the various neutral and cationic species rests on Hartree-Fock geometries with second-order perturbation theory for correlation, so most of the reported energetics do not come from a multiconfigurational reference.
reference_short: San Miguel, Marquez & Fernandez Sanz, J. Am. Chem. Soc. 1996, 118, 430
notes: The bonding in these species has been rationalized on the basis of two models, Fischer-type complexes or alternatives. The monopositive and dipositive cations of both carbene and stannylene were also studied, but by single-reference methods.
correlation_correction: None applied to the CASSCF results; second-order perturbation theory used separately on Hartree-Fock references

method: CASSCF for the dissociation curves and the rearrangement path, alongside Hartree-Fock and second-order Moller-Plesset perturbation theory for structures and energetics
basis_set: An (8s8p6d) basis contracted to [4s4p3d] for the zinc 3s, 3p, 3d and 4s shells; the standard double-zeta plus polarization basis for the other atoms
active_space_orbital_description: Four electrons in six orbitals by analogy with the carbene, comprising the zinc 4s and 4p orbitals with the stannylene sigma and p orbitals.
active_space_protocol: Treated in the same way as the carbene, with the space chosen to give the correct dissociation asymptote.
electronic_structure_description: This compound is formed from zinc and stannylene in a manner analogous to the carbene, but because the singlet state of the stannylene fragment lies below its triplet, unlike the methylene case, the ground state of the adduct is expected to be a singlet, and at the perturbation level the triplet indeed falls above it. Molecular orbital diagrams are given for the triplet arising from excited zinc plus triplet stannylene and for the singlet arising from ground-state zinc plus singlet stannylene. In a triplet arrangement of the two heavy-atom p orbitals the fragment gives rise to a 3Sigma- state.
Other: Two different spaces are used and each is chosen for a stated physical requirement rather than by a general recipe. For the dissociation curves the space is four electrons in six orbitals -- the zinc 4s and 4p orbitals together with the methylene sigma and p orbitals -- and the reason given is explicit: the profiles were obtained this way in order to ensure correct dissociation. That matters here because the true dissociation limit is not the zinc ground state but the excited state corresponding to a 4s-4p configuration, so a space lacking the zinc 4p orbitals would dissociate to the wrong asymptote. What the space then reveals is an avoided crossing that a smaller space could not have produced: the interaction of the zinc ground state with triplet methylene gives a repulsive curve which crosses one arising from the excited zinc state, and because under the imposed symmetry both the ground state and the relevant component of the excited multiplet carry the same symmetry label, the crossing becomes avoided. For the rearrangement the space is instead the whole valence space with one deliberate exclusion, eight electrons in nine orbitals comprising the two carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds, the zinc-carbon sigma bond and all their antibonding partners together with the carbon p orbital and two zinc p orbitals. The excluded orbital is the remaining zinc p orbital, left out because it is not expected to be involved in the reaction. Excluding by expected participation rather than by energy is the right criterion for a rearrangement, and the space size is reported concretely as 3696 configuration state functions in the reduced symmetry. The characterisation of the stationary point is done properly: diagonalizing the force constant matrix gave a single imaginary eigenvalue whose normal coordinate corresponds to breaking and forming the zinc-hydrogen and carbon-hydrogen bonds, and the connection to reactant and product was confirmed by following the intrinsic reaction coordinate rather than assumed from the imaginary mode alone. A limitation of scope worth carrying: the multiconfigurational treatment is applied to the dissociation curves and to the rearrangement path, while the structural and energetic characterisation of the various neutral and cationic species rests on Hartree-Fock geometries with second-order perturbation theory for correlation, so most of the reported energetics do not come from a multiconfigurational reference.

notes: The reversal of fragment spin-state ordering relative to methylene is what changes the ground state of the adduct from triplet to singlet, and it is the main point of comparison between the two systems.
correlation_correction: None applied to the CASSCF results; second-order perturbation theory used separately on Hartree-Fock references

software: ORCA for the density functional calculations; Gaussian 09 for the coupled cluster calculations, performed without the frozen core approximation

active_space_orbital_description: A ladder of spaces sharing the same orbital-class construction: nine electrons in eight orbitals covering the boron and oxygen 2s and 2p shells; nine in sixteen adding 3s and 3p; nine in twenty-eight adding 4s and 3d; and thirteen in thirty adding the 1s core orbitals.
active_space_protocol: The space is enlarged in identifiable stages, first by successive polarization shells and finally by admitting the core orbitals, so that the effect of core correlation on the computed property can be separated from that of the polarization shells.
electronic_structure_description: The Fermi contact term of the hyperfine coupling is the property tracked, together with the spin-dipolar term. The spin density is decomposed into the contribution from the singly occupied natural orbital and the summation of all other natural orbital contributions, and these are found to move in opposite directions as the space is enlarged. For this radical and its isoelectronic cation the core correlation increases the summation of the other natural orbital contributions, in contrast to the cyanide radical where it reduces them.
Other: A density matrix renormalization group solver removes the combinatorial limit on space size, so this study can do what most cannot: enlarge the space systematically until a property converges, and identify which orbital classes are responsible. The spaces are tabulated by orbital content rather than by count alone, running from a full valence eight-orbital space up to thirty-six orbitals, and the enlargement proceeds in identifiable stages -- adding a second and third shell of polarization functions, then the core orbitals. The property tracked is the Fermi contact term of the hyperfine coupling, which depends on spin density at the nucleus and is notoriously sensitive to core-shell spin polarization. Two findings are transferable well beyond this method. First, the two enlargement directions are not interchangeable and their importance differs by centre and by molecule. For the aluminium centre the term is too low without core correlation but too high with core correlation and without the metal 4d polarization shell, and good agreement, a 3.43 percent error, comes only when both are present; the authors go further and separate the two effects by comparing spin density distributions, concluding that the singly occupied natural orbital spin density is more significantly affected by the polarization shell than by the core correlation. For the carbon centre of the cyanide radical, relaxing the orbitals with the 1s orbitals in the space brings the error down to 4.43 percent and the result converges onto coupled cluster with perturbative triples, indicating the space has captured the high-order correlation the property requires. Second, and more cautionary, the decomposition shows that a converged total can hide compensating errors. The spin density is analysed as the singly occupied natural orbital contribution plus the sum of all others, and these move in opposite directions as the space grows -- in one radical the singly occupied contribution falls rapidly while the sum of the others rises slowly, in another the core correlation reduces the sum of the others rather than changing the singly occupied part. Without core orbitals the totals come out too low through largely negative contributions from the remaining natural orbitals; with core orbitals but no polarization shell they come out too high through an inflated singly occupied contribution. Two failures are recorded honestly rather than buried. The nitrogen centre of the cyanide radical comes out completely wrong at the configuration interaction level, wrong even in sign, and that does not change with the space; orbital relaxation recovers the correct sign but not the magnitude. And for one oxygen centre the only method agreeing with the matrix value is attributed by the authors to fortuitous error cancellation rather than to accuracy. Taken together this is the clearest available demonstration that convergence of a spin-dependent property with active space size is centre-specific, direction-specific, and not diagnosable from the total alone.
reference_short: Lan, Kurashige & Yanai, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2014, 10, 1953
notes: One of three isoelectronic diatomics sharing the same ladder of active spaces, which allows the effect of the space to be separated from the effect of the particular molecule.
correlation_correction: The density matrix renormalization group solver itself supplies near-full configuration interaction correlation within the chosen space; no external perturbative correction

compound_name: 7-Azaindole complexed with one methanol, excited-state double proton transfer
geometry_source: Stationary points fully optimized at the CASSCF and time-dependent density functional levels with 6-31G(d,p), 6-311G(d,p) and 6-311+G(d,p) basis sets in the gas phase; vibrational frequencies computed at the same levels and used for zero-point corrections
method: CASSCF geometry optimization and frequencies with second-order multireference perturbation theory single points at the stationary points; time-dependent density functional theory with five functionals for comparison
software: Gaussian 09 for the CASSCF and density functional calculations; GAMESS for the multireference perturbation theory single points
active_space_orbital_description: Ten electrons in nine orbitals: four pi bonding orbitals, the four corresponding antibonding orbitals, and one nitrogen lone pair.
active_space_protocol: The space is described as an essential component of the calculation and is built from the chromophore's pi system plus the nitrogen lone pair, the latter being required because the reaction transfers a proton onto and away from that nitrogen. The identical space is used for both the one-methanol and two-methanol complexes, so the additional solvent molecule contributes no active orbitals.
electronic_structure_description: Table 4 gives barrier heights, tautomerization energies and dipole moments in the excited state, with zero-point-corrected values in parentheses and energies in kcal/mol. For the single-methanol complex: CASSCF/6-31G(d,p) gives a barrier of 17.1 (13.7) and a tautomerization energy of -31.9 (-31.3); CASSCF/6-311G(d,p) gives 16.4 (13.5) and -32.3 (-31.5); with perturbative correction these become 8.71 (5.31) and -19.22 (-18.6) in the smaller basis and 7.90 (4.97) and -18.6 (-17.9) in the larger. For the two-methanol complex: CASSCF/6-31G(d,p) gives 13.5 (10.6) for the first transition state and 14.4 (10.2) for the second, with a tautomerization energy of -32.3 (-31.9); CASSCF/6-311G(d,p) gives 13.7 (11.5) and 15.7 (12.1) with -31.8 (-31.4); with perturbative correction the barriers become 4.95 (2.06) and 7.37 (3.14) in the smaller basis and 3.98 (1.81) and 10.2 (6.55) in the larger, with tautomerization energies of -19.6 (-19.2) and -18.9 (-18.5). Density functional barriers for the same processes range from 4.67 to 9.20 kcal/mol for the single-methanol complex and from 1.99 to 7.29 for the two-methanol complex depending on functional and basis, several giving negative zero-point-corrected barriers for the latter. The excited-state double proton transfer in this complex proceeds through a single transition state. Its barrier falls from 16.4 kcal/mol at the reference level to 7.90 with perturbative correction in the larger basis, and from 13.5 to 4.97 once zero-point energy is included, so the correction roughly halves it. The tautomerization energy moves from -32.3 to -18.6 kcal/mol. The tautomerization energies of this complex and its two-methanol analogue agree within 1 kcal/mol, which suggests that the relative formation energies of the cyclic hydrogen bonds with the parent and with the tautomer are approximately the same for the one and two methanol complexes.
Other: The space is described by the authors as an essential component of the calculation and is specified by chemical role: four pi bonds, the four corresponding antibonding orbitals, and one nitrogen lone pair, giving ten electrons in nine orbitals. The lone pair is the load-bearing inclusion, since the reaction is a proton transfer onto and away from nitrogen, and a purely pi space would describe the chromophore's excitation while missing the site where the chemistry happens. Notably the same space is used for both the one-methanol and the two-methanol complex, so the additional solvent molecule contributes no active orbitals of its own; the space follows the chromophore rather than the hydrogen-bonded bridge that carries the transferred protons. What makes this record valuable is that the paper reports both the reference and the corrected barriers for every structure, and the correction is enormous relative to the quantity. For the single-methanol complex the barrier falls from 16.4 kcal/mol at the reference level to 7.90 with correction in one basis, and from 13.5 to 4.97 once zero-point energy is included -- roughly halved. The tautomerization energy likewise moves from -32.3 to -18.6 kcal/mol, a shift of nearly 14. The authors state the general finding directly: tautomerization energies and barrier heights are highly dependent on the dynamic electron correlation. So no number from the reference wave function alone should be quoted here. More consequentially, the correction changes a mechanistic conclusion rather than merely shifting numbers. For the two-methanol complex two transition states were located, and at the reference level the paper states that no obvious difference was found between their barriers. After correction they separate to 3.98 and 10.2 kcal/mol, a gap of 6.2, and the authors conclude on that basis that the triple proton transfer occurs preferably through the lower one. The mechanism is therefore invisible at the level that produced the geometries and only appears once dynamic correlation is added -- and since the geometries and the zero-point corrections both come from the uncorrected level, the two transition states being compared were located on a surface that does not distinguish them. A practical note on scope: the zero-point corrections applied to the corrected barriers come from frequencies computed at the reference level, and the density functional comparison in the same table shows barriers varying by several kcal/mol between functionals and basis sets, with some functionals giving negative zero-point-corrected barriers for the two-methanol complex, so the multiconfigurational route is the only one that gives a consistent positive barrier there.
reference_short: Fang & Kim, J. Phys. Chem. A 2011, 115, 13743
notes: The density functional barriers for this complex agree with the corrected multiconfigurational value within about 1.2 kcal/mol in the larger basis, but the same functionals deviate by up to 4.6 kcal/mol for the two-methanol complex.
correlation_correction: Second-order multireference perturbation theory single points at the CASSCF stationary points

For the two-methanol complex: CASSCF/6-31G(d,p) gives 13.5 (10.6) for the first transition state and 14.4 (10.2) for the second, with a tautomerization energy of -32.3 (-31.9); CASSCF/6-311G(d,p) gives 13.7 (11.5) and 15.7 (12.1) with -31.8 (-31.4); with perturbative correction the barriers become 4.95 (2.06) and 7.37 (3.14) in the smaller basis and 3.98 (1.81) and 10.2 (6.55) in the larger, with tautomerization energies of -19.6 (-19.2) and -18.9 (-18.5). Density functional barriers for the same processes range from 4.67 to 9.20 kcal/mol for the single-methanol complex and from 1.99 to 7.29 for the two-methanol complex depending on functional and basis, several giving negative zero-point-corrected barriers for the latter. Two transition states were located for the excited-state triple proton transfer in this complex. At the reference level no obvious difference was found between their barriers, 13.7 and 15.7 kcal/mol in the larger basis. After perturbative correction they separate to 3.98 and 10.2 kcal/mol, the second being 6.2 kcal/mol higher, on which basis the transfer is concluded to occur preferably through the first. Two concerted but asynchronous processes are anticipated, with a stepwise mechanism and a possible intermediate also considered. The tautomerization energy is -18.5 kcal/mol including zero-point energy, within 1 kcal/mol of the single-methanol value.
Other: The space is described by the authors as an essential component of the calculation and is specified by chemical role: four pi bonds, the four corresponding antibonding orbitals, and one nitrogen lone pair, giving ten electrons in nine orbitals. The lone pair is the load-bearing inclusion, since the reaction is a proton transfer onto and away from nitrogen, and a purely pi space would describe the chromophore's excitation while missing the site where the chemistry happens. Notably the same space is used for both the one-methanol and the two-methanol complex, so the additional solvent molecule contributes no active orbitals of its own; the space follows the chromophore rather than the hydrogen-bonded bridge that carries the transferred protons. What makes this record valuable is that the paper reports both the reference and the corrected barriers for every structure, and the correction is enormous relative to the quantity. For the single-methanol complex the barrier falls from 16.4 kcal/mol at the reference level to 7.90 with correction in one basis, and from 13.5 to 4.97 once zero-point energy is included -- roughly halved. The tautomerization energy likewise moves from -32.3 to -18.6 kcal/mol, a shift of nearly 14. The authors state the general finding directly: tautomerization energies and barrier heights are highly dependent on the dynamic electron correlation. So no number from the reference wave function alone should be quoted here. More consequentially, the correction changes a mechanistic conclusion rather than merely shifting numbers. For the two-methanol complex two transition states were located, and at the reference level the paper states that no obvious difference was found between their barriers. After correction they separate to 3.98 and 10.2 kcal/mol, a gap of 6.2, and the authors conclude on that basis that the triple proton transfer occurs preferably through the lower one. The mechanism is therefore invisible at the level that produced the geometries and only appears once dynamic correlation is added -- and since the geometries and the zero-point corrections both come from the uncorrected level, the two transition states being compared were located on a surface that does not distinguish them. electronic_structure_description: Table 1 gives vertical excitation energies corrected at the multireference perturbation level with oscillator strengths. The pi-pi-star states lie at 4.840 eV with oscillator strength 0.097, 5.277 eV with 0.055 and 5.536 eV with 0.030, the first two being assignable as the 1La and 1Lb states with leading single-excitation contributions of 62 and 33 percent. The n-pi-star states lie at 5.080, 5.348 and 5.814 eV. The two families interleave across the range. For the nucleoside in aqueous solution the first absorption maximum is at 251 nm, 4.94 eV, and the maximum for the free base is quoted at 256 nm, 4.84 eV, alongside 234 nm, 5.28 eV.
Other: Two spaces are used and, unusually, the smaller one is validated against the larger by an explicit test rather than by assertion. The larger space is eighteen electrons in thirteen orbitals, built from three lone pair orbitals -- one on the oxygen and two on the nitrogens -- together with ten pi orbitals, and used with four-state averaging for the vertical excitation energies. The smaller is twelve electrons in nine orbitals with six-state averaging, used for the conical intersection search, and the authors state their justification directly: it was considered adequate to describe the low-lying pi-pi-star and n-pi-star energies from comparisons with larger active spaces at the ground state minimum, which produced nearly the same energies and the same state ordering. Testing both the energies and the state ordering is the right pair of criteria, since a space that reproduces energies while reordering states would be useless for a decay-path study where which state is reached determines the outcome. Including the lone pairs alongside the pi manifold is what makes the n-pi-star states representable at all, and those states interleave with the pi-pi-star states in this molecule -- the computed manifold alternates between the two types across the range from 4.84 to 5.81 eV -- so a pi-only space would have produced a spectrum with the wrong composition even if individual pi-pi-star energies came out reasonably. geometry_source: Structures from single-crystal X-ray determination of the synthesized salts
method: CASSCF and CASSCF with n-electron valence-state second-order perturbation theory for the singlet-triplet splittings, and CASSCF with a spin-orbit state-interaction and magnetic anisotropy treatment for the g tensor and excited states; broken-symmetry density functional theory attempted for comparison

active_space_orbital_description: Nine electrons in nine orbitals: the five chromium 3d atomic orbitals together with two pi-bonding and two pi-antibonding molecular orbitals of the toluene ligands, which are mixed with the metal d orbitals in a 3d5 configuration.
active_space_protocol: The space admits the ligand pi orbitals that mix with the metal d set rather than the metal d orbitals alone, which is what makes the description of the formally 3d5 sandwich centre meaningful. One sextet, twenty-four quartet and seventy-five doublet spin states obtained from the multiconfigurational calculation were mixed by spin-orbit coupling, giving two hundred fifty-two spin-orbit states, from which the g tensor of the lowest Kramers doublet was computed.

electronic_structure_description: The ground-state g tensor and the energies of a series of electronically excited doublet and quartet states were computed for this cation. The g tensor of the lowest Kramers doublet was obtained from the spin-orbit mixed states. For comparison the g tensors of all the paramagnetic species in the study were also computed by a density functional method with the same relativistic Hamiltonian.
Other: The multiconfigurational treatment is used here because the cheaper alternative demonstrably failed, and the paper says so plainly. For the anion-cation pairs the authors were unable to obtain the correct broken-symmetry solutions at all, and for a related salt studied earlier the exchange couplings from that approach came out nonrealistically large; the multiconfigurational route was adopted in its place. That is the clearest kind of justification for a multireference calculation -- not that it might be better, but that the single-determinant description does not exist for the states in question. Two quite different spaces then serve two quite different purposes. For the exchange couplings between radical pairs the space is minimal, two electrons in two orbitals, one singly occupied orbital per radical, which is exactly the space that can represent the singlet and triplet combinations whose splitting is the quantity wanted and nothing more. For the metal cation the space is nine electrons in nine orbitals built by chemical composition: the five metal d orbitals together with two pi bonding and two pi antibonding orbitals of the arene ligands, chosen because those ligand orbitals mix with the metal d orbitals. Admitting the mixed ligand orbitals rather than the metal d set alone is what makes the description of a formally 3d5 centre in a sandwich environment meaningful. The consequence of the small pair space is visible in the tables and worth flagging. For the radical-radical pairs the three methods disagree by more than a factor of two on the largest coupling -- minus 8.25, minus 3.70 and minus 7.45 per cm from density functional, multiconfigurational and perturbatively corrected treatments respectively -- and the multiconfigurational value without correction is the outlier, closer to zero than either of the others. At longer contact distances the uncorrected values collapse to exactly zero while the corrected ones retain small residual couplings. For the anion-cation pairs, where only the multiconfigurational route was available, the correction changes the sign of the largest coupling, from plus 1.00 to minus 1.55 per cm, so whether that interaction is ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic depends entirely on the dynamic correlation added after the space. Given that these couplings are then used to interpret magnetic susceptibility data, that sign change is the whole result. A note on the spin-orbit treatment for the metal cation: one sextet, twenty-four quartet and seventy-five doublet states from the multiconfigurational calculation were mixed to give two hundred fifty-two spin-orbit states, so the state manifold entering the property calculation is far larger than the space itself suggests.

active_space_protocol: Full valence wave functions were constructed specifically to understand the sensitivity of geometries and physical properties to the level of correlation effects, at the coupled-cluster optimized geometries. The space is diagnostic rather than productive: no energies used in the paper's conclusions come from it.
electronic_structure_description: The multiconfigurational occupation numbers reveal a departure from the mean-field description that resolves a charge puzzle. The germanium lone-pair orbital lying parallel to the symmetry axis has an occupation of 1.939 and the perpendicular nonbonding orbital 0.054, against exactly 2.0 and 0.0 respectively at the mean-field level. This corresponds to a double excitation shifting electrons from the lone pair on germanium to the nonbonding orbital perpendicular to the axis. The negative partial charge found on germanium, contrary to the electronegativity ordering, is associated with that lone-pair orbital acting as an electron reservoir. This molecule is one of five stationary points on the singlet surface of the germavinylidene-germyne system, which also includes two isomerization transition states.
Other: The multiconfigurational calculation is not the workhorse of this study but a diagnostic, and its role is stated exactly: full valence wave functions of ten electrons in ten molecular orbitals were constructed to understand the sensitivity of geometries and physical properties to the level of correlation effects. Everything quantitative -- the geometries, the relative energies, the rovibrational analysis -- comes from coupled cluster with basis set extrapolation, and the multiconfigurational wave functions are built at those coupled-cluster geometries rather than at their own. Using the full valence space removes any orbital-selection judgement, which is the right choice when the space exists to answer whether a single-determinant description suffices rather than to compute a number. What it delivers is a specific, quantitative departure from the single-determinant picture that resolves a chemical puzzle. The occupation number of the germanium lone-pair orbital lying along the symmetry axis falls to 1.939 while the perpendicular nonbonding orbital rises to 0.054, against exactly 2.0 and 0.0 at the mean-field level. Those deviations are small in absolute terms but they correspond to a specific double excitation transferring density between the two orbitals, and the authors use them to explain a negative partial charge on germanium that runs contrary to the electronegativity ordering -- the lone-pair orbital acting as an electron reservoir. This is a good illustration of occupation numbers being informative at the third decimal place: a 0.06-electron shift is far too small to matter energetically yet is exactly what identifies which orbital is polarizable. The corresponding configuration interaction expansion coefficients and the full set of valence occupation numbers are relegated to supplementary material, so only the two values quoted in the running text are recoverable here. electronic_structure_description: Four lowest excited electronic states were computed in solvent at the perturbatively corrected level. The two lowest transitions, assigned as the pi-pi-star Lb and La states, come at 4.16 eV (298 nm) and 4.70 eV (264 nm); the first is compared with an experimental absorption maximum at 4.09 eV (303 nm) used in the fluorescence work, and the second agrees well with an experimental band at 5.00 eV (248 nm). A fourth transition at 5.44 eV (228 nm) corresponds to an experimental feature near 5.85 eV (211 nm). The n-pi-star state lies at 4.14 eV (300 nm). In the gas phase the n-pi-star state is the lowest excited state, but on interaction with water it shifts to the blue while the pi-pi-star Lb state is considerably stabilised, so the latter becomes lowest in both the equilibrium and nonequilibrium solvation conditions. In water the emission energy from the pi-pi-star Lb state is 3.24 eV (383 nm) under electrostatic nonequilibrium, giving a Stokes shift of 0.92 eV (85 nm); allowing the excited state lifetime to reach solute-solvent electrostatic equilibrium gives 2.85 eV (435 nm), in very good agreement with an experimental emission maximum at 2.67 eV (464 nm), and a Stokes shift of 1.31 eV (137 nm) against an experimental 1.40 eV. Dipole moments range from 11.1 to 19.8 D across the states considered. Spin-orbit coupling elements between the n-pi-star state and the triplet manifold indicate favourable conditions for intersystem crossing, consistent with the observed nonfluorescent decay.
Other: The space is built by chemical role and, unusually, its contents were selected by an explicit prior calculation rather than by inspection. Twelve electrons occupy twelve orbitals: five pi and six pi-star orbitals chosen as those that best describe the three lowest pi-pi-star excited states, plus one oxygen lone-pair orbital added specifically to describe the lowest n-pi-star state. The authors state how the selection was made -- by analyzing the contribution to the low-lying excited states in a previous multiconfigurational calculation with a larger active space restricted to single through quadruple excitations. The single lone-pair orbital is the load-bearing addition here. The n-pi-star state it enables is not a spectroscopic curiosity but the centre of the paper's mechanism: that state is the lowest in the gas phase, is pushed to the blue by water while the bright pi-pi-star state is strongly stabilised, and the spin-orbit couplings computed between it and the triplet manifold are what indicate favourable conditions for intersystem crossing. A space of pi orbitals alone would have reproduced the absorption spectrum and missed the nonradiative channel entirely, and would also have missed the solvent-induced reordering of the two lowest excited states, since the two move in opposite directions on solvation. One set of orbitals is state-averaged over the five lowest roots, so the same reference serves both the bright and dark states whose relative position is the mechanistic question. Two limitations attach to the numbers. The multiconfigurational treatment supplies energies at geometries obtained elsewhere, the ground state from second-order perturbation theory with a Pople basis and the solvent environment from a sequential classical simulation and quantum mechanical embedding, so the space never determines a structure except for the excited-state optimization used for the intersystem crossing analysis. And the core electrons of carbon and oxygen are frozen in the perturbative step, which is standard but means the correction does not describe core relaxation on excitation. The agreement obtained is good where testable: an emission energy of 2.85 eV against an experimental 2.67, and a Stokes shift of 1.31 eV against 1.40, both in water.

active_space_orbital_description: The largest space is the full pi valence, eight electrons in eight orbitals. Spaces were varied from the minimal two-electron two-orbital diradical description up to that full valence space.
active_space_protocol: Spaces were varied systematically from the minimal two-electron two-orbital description to the full pi valence eight-electron eight-orbital space, with orbitals taken alternately from the triplet and from the singlet state to test the dependence of the results on the orbital source. The full pi valence space proved too large to serve as a reference for variational single and double excitation configuration interaction or even for the reduced difference-dedicated expansion, so a selection procedure based on the weight of configurations in the reference wave function was applied at that level. The difference-dedicated method omits the two-hole two-particle excitations involving orbitals outside the space, which at second order contribute equally to both states provided the same orbital set is used.
electronic_structure_description: The adiabatic triplet-singlet gap is the key quantity, with an experimental value of 9.6 plus or minus 0.2 kcal/mol. Earlier work predicted 11.7 kcal/mol, reduced to 11.0 kcal/mol or 3850 per cm after correcting for frequencies, and vertical and adiabatic values of 11.3 kcal/mol or 3952 per cm are quoted. Restricting to the minimal two-orbital reference gives 12.4 kcal/mol or 4355 per cm, comparable to an earlier perturbatively corrected value of 10.8 kcal/mol or 3790 per cm obtained from spin-flip coupled cluster structures. With orbitals taken from the full pi valence calculation the minimal space shows an onset of stability but still a 66 percent error against experiment. Adding single excitations to the minimal reference, or using the reduced difference-dedicated expansion at that level, gives results stable with respect to the orbital source and the space dimension but no improvement over the plain full valence calculation, so neither captures the differential correlation. Difference-dedicated calculations from state-specific orbitals give the worst results, which is expected since the method's conditions hold rigorously only when both expansions use the same orbital set; those from singlet-state orbitals are stable, independent of the space used to obtain the orbitals, and very close to experiment, but the authors state this agreement is purely fortuitous. Broken-symmetry density functional results using the triplet and broken-symmetry solutions at the corresponding optimized geometries, especially from the M06-2X functional, give the closest agreement with experiment for both the gap and the electron affinity, improving further when the full pi valence optimized geometry is used to correct for spin contamination effects on the broken-symmetry geometry. The multiconfigurational, perturbative and configuration interaction treatments all systematically overestimate the experimental value even with the full pi valence reference and a relatively large basis set.
Other: This paper is an extended argument that the physically obvious minimal space is inadequate, and it is unusually careful about distinguishing a right answer from a right reason. The natural description of a diradical is two electrons in two orbitals, and the paper tests spaces from that minimum up to the full pi valence eight electrons in eight orbitals, adding dynamical correlation by second-order multireference perturbation theory, by variational single and double excitation configuration interaction, and by a difference-dedicated variant that omits the two-hole two-particle excitations which contribute equally to both states at second order. The conclusion is stated flatly: the minimal reference space is inadequate. Several distinct pieces of evidence support it. Restricting to the minimal space gives an adiabatic gap of 12.4 kcal/mol against an experimental 9.6, and even with orbitals taken from the full pi valence calculation the minimal space shows only an onset of stability while retaining a 66 percent error, which the authors read as showing that dynamical correlation plays an essential role. Adding singles to the minimal reference, or using the reduced difference-dedicated expansion at that level, gives results stable with respect to which state supplied the orbitals and to the space dimension but no better than the plain full-valence calculation, so those methods are simply not capturing the differential correlation. The most instructive result is one the authors decline to claim credit for. Difference-dedicated calculations using orbitals from the singlet state come out stable, independent of the space used to generate the orbitals, and very close to experiment -- and the paper states that the agreement is purely fortuitous, because that method should approximate the full single and double excitation treatment, which with the same reference does not reproduce experiment. They then consider and reject the obvious excuse, that truncated configuration interaction lacks size consistency, noting that size-consistency effects are almost negligible for electronic excitations even though they matter for bond breaking. Reporting a near-perfect number and then explaining why it should not be trusted is the kind of thing worth preserving. The practical constraint that shapes the study is that the full pi valence space is too large to serve as a reference for variational single and double excitation configuration interaction or even for the reduced variant, so at that level a configuration selection based on the weight of configurations in the reference wave function had to be applied. The overall verdict is that the perturbative, configuration interaction and complete active space treatments all systematically overestimate the experimental gap even with the full pi valence reference and a relatively large basis, from which the authors conclude either that an accurate description must go beyond this level -- including sigma electrons and higher polarization functions -- or that the measured value is affected by the experimental conditions. Geometry matters too: using the full pi valence optimized geometry improves agreement by correcting for spin contamination in the broken-symmetry structure, and those geometries are essentially insensitive to basis set.

electronic_structure_description: The calculated ground state is not a triplet but consists of three open-shell singlets lying 0.44, 0.06 and 0.02 eV below the triplet. These are multiconfigurational singlets with different contributions from the trivalent and divalent metal configurations: the three states are described as 0.92 and 0.08, 0.34 and 0.66, and 0.63 and 0.37 respectively. Their contributions from the two ligand pi-star orbitals are 0.89 and 0.11 for the most stable, 0.35 and 0.65 for the second, and 0.68 and 0.32 for the third. The most stable state is dominated by the trivalent metal and first ligand orbital configurations, while the two nearly degenerate higher states have those configurations less dominant. The f-occupancy of the most stable state is 0.92, identified as the square of the coefficient of the trivalent configuration in a two-configuration wave function that also contains a divalent metal with a neutral ligand. Selected crystallographic distances at 173 K are metal-carbon in the range 2.630 to 2.653 Angstrom with a mean ring distance of 2.642, a mean metal to ring centroid distance of 2.35 Angstrom, and a centroid-metal-centroid angle of 139.5 degrees.
Other: The space is specified by composition rather than by count: the electrons are distributed over four 4f orbitals of the metal and the two pi-star orbitals of the diimine ligand, and the authors state that only one active space and one set of inactive orbitals were used throughout. Restricting the metal contribution to four of the seven f orbitals is a deliberate truncation -- the f shell of this lanthanide is nearly full, so most of it is inert, and only the subset that can exchange an electron with the ligand needs to be correlated. The two ligand pi-star orbitals are the essential partners, because the entire question is whether an electron has transferred from metal to ligand and, if so, which ligand orbital receives it. What the space produces is a quantitative decomposition that no single-determinant description could give. The three lowest open-shell singlet states are reported as mixtures of the two metal configurations in the proportions 0.92 and 0.08, 0.34 and 0.66, and 0.63 and 0.37, with corresponding ligand contributions of 0.89 and 0.11, 0.35 and 0.65, and 0.68 and 0.32 for the two pi-star orbitals. The leading coefficient of the most stable state is identified explicitly with a physical observable, the f-occupancy, defined as the square of the coefficient of the trivalent metal configuration in a two-configuration wave function; that quantity is measurable by X-ray absorption and is what connects the calculation to experiment. So the space is not merely producing energies but a number that can be checked spectroscopically. The substantive finding is a reordering that depends on ligand substitution. For the unsubstituted ligand and for one methylated isomer the ground state is a pair of nearly degenerate triplets with the open-shell singlet well above -- 2.1 eV in one case and only 0.08 and 0.09 eV in another -- while for the 4,7-dimethyl adduct the ordering inverts and three open-shell singlets lie 0.44, 0.06 and 0.02 eV below the triplet. Since these gaps are of order a few hundredths of an electronvolt and the same fixed space is used for every adduct, the comparison across the series is meaningful in a way it would not be had the space been re-tuned per molecule; but by the same token gaps of 0.02 eV are far below any reasonable accuracy claim for the method, so the identification of a specific ordering among the three singlets should be treated as qualitative. A limitation of scope: the calculations use a small-core relativistic pseudopotential on the metal and a modest double-zeta basis on the ligand, no dynamic correlation is added on top of the multiconfigurational reference, and the orbital energy diagram used to rationalise the singlet-triplet ordering is described by the authors as only qualitative though reflecting the computed energies.

active_space_protocol: A single fixed space of four metal 4f orbitals and two ligand pi-star orbitals applied to every adduct in the series, so that the small energy differences between adducts reflect the substitution rather than a re-tuned reference. Restricting the metal contribution to four of the seven f orbitals reflects that the f shell is nearly full and only the subset able to exchange an electron with the ligand needs to be correlated.
