electronic_structure_description: This adduct was characterized crystallographically at 173 K alongside the 4,7-dimethyl compound and treated with the same fixed active space. Its metal-carbon distances range from 2.699 to 2.781 Angstrom with a mean ring distance of 2.74, a mean metal to ring centroid distance of 2.46 Angstrom, and a centroid-metal-centroid angle of 140.0 degrees, so its coordination sphere is appreciably more expanded than that of the 4,7-dimethyl adduct whose corresponding values are 2.642, 2.35 and 139.5.
Other: The space is specified by composition rather than by count: the electrons are distributed over four 4f orbitals of the metal and the two pi-star orbitals of the diimine ligand, and the authors state that only one active space and one set of inactive orbitals were used throughout. Restricting the metal contribution to four of the seven f orbitals is a deliberate truncation -- the f shell of this lanthanide is nearly full, so most of it is inert, and only the subset that can exchange an electron with the ligand needs to be correlated. The two ligand pi-star orbitals are the essential partners, because the entire question is whether an electron has transferred from metal to ligand and, if so, which ligand orbital receives it. What the space produces is a quantitative decomposition that no single-determinant description could give. The three lowest open-shell singlet states are reported as mixtures of the two metal configurations in the proportions 0.92 and 0.08, 0.34 and 0.66, and 0.63 and 0.37, with corresponding ligand contributions of 0.89 and 0.11, 0.35 and 0.65, and 0.68 and 0.32 for the two pi-star orbitals. The leading coefficient of the most stable state is identified explicitly with a physical observable, the f-occupancy, defined as the square of the coefficient of the trivalent metal configuration in a two-configuration wave function; that quantity is measurable by X-ray absorption and is what connects the calculation to experiment. So the space is not merely producing energies but a number that can be checked spectroscopically. The substantive finding is a reordering that depends on ligand substitution. For the unsubstituted ligand and for one methylated isomer the ground state is a pair of nearly degenerate triplets with the open-shell singlet well above -- 2.1 eV in one case and only 0.08 and 0.09 eV in another -- while for the 4,7-dimethyl adduct the ordering inverts and three open-shell singlets lie 0.44, 0.06 and 0.02 eV below the triplet. Since these gaps are of order a few hundredths of an electronvolt and the same fixed space is used for every adduct, the comparison across the series is meaningful in a way it would not be had the space been re-tuned per molecule; but by the same token gaps of 0.02 eV are far below any reasonable accuracy claim for the method, so the identification of a specific ordering among the three singlets should be treated as qualitative. A limitation of scope: the calculations use a small-core relativistic pseudopotential on the metal and a modest double-zeta basis on the ligand, no dynamic correlation is added on top of the multiconfigurational reference, and the orbital energy diagram used to rationalise the singlet-triplet ordering is described by the authors as only qualitative though reflecting the computed energies.

active_space_protocol: The multiconfigurational model was applied to this smaller molecule specifically to calibrate a cheaper density functional model, which was then used for the larger target molecule. Crossing points between the singlet and triplet surfaces were located with a conical intersection algorithm, and higher-level single-point energies were computed at the resulting geometries.
electronic_structure_description: The multiconfigurational model produces a minimum energy path on the singlet surface proceeding through a first transition state, a shallow local minimum associated with a singlet nitrene-dinitrogen intermediate, and a second transition state before giving singlet methyleneimine and dinitrogen. However, when the relative energies of those points are recomputed with coupled cluster and quadratic configuration interaction models, the second transition state falls 1 to 2 kcal/mol below the intermediate it should follow, so the shallow intermediate does not survive the higher-level treatment. Both the multiconfigurational and the density functional models find that the triplet azide dissociates without barrier to triplet nitrene and dinitrogen, and for a given high-level single-point model all triplet relative energies from density functional geometries lie within 2 kcal/mol of those from multiconfigurational geometries, with singlet values agreeing within 1 kcal/mol. The triplet nitrene-dinitrogen complex lies 35.3 kcal/mol below its singlet counterpart, close to the singlet-triplet splitting of 31.2 kcal/mol derived from photoelectron spectroscopy on the corresponding anion. The first crossing point lies 38.8 kcal/mol above the singlet azide, close to an independent multireference averaged quadratic coupled cluster value of 39.6 kcal/mol; the second crossing lies 31.0 kcal/mol above the triplet nitrene with that reaction 51.9 kcal/mol exothermic. The barrier to triplet methyleneimine from the triplet nitrene-dinitrogen complex is 44.5 kcal/mol from density functional geometries, 2 kcal/mol lower than from multiconfigurational ones. Tabulated relative energies for the fragment species computed with the reduced space include 28.1 to 41.5 kcal/mol for singlet nitrene plus dinitrogen and 26.5 to 31.6 kcal/mol for the second transition state plus dinitrogen across the several single-point models.
Other: The multiconfigurational calculation is used here as a calibration standard rather than as the production method, and the logic is stated explicitly: geometries for the smaller azide were obtained both with a density functional model and with a ten-electron eight-orbital multiconfigurational model, found to be in reasonable agreement, and on that basis the cheap model was applied to the larger molecule that is the paper's actual subject. The multiconfigurational treatment is what licenses everything downstream, and the agreement is quantified rather than asserted -- for a given high-level single-point treatment, relative energies from density functional geometries fall within 1 kcal/mol of those from multiconfigurational geometries on the singlet surface and within 2 kcal/mol for triplet structures. Two spaces appear, ten electrons in eight orbitals and a smaller four electrons in three orbitals, both with the same augmented double-zeta basis, and the reduced space is used for some fragment species where the larger one is unnecessary. What the multiconfigurational geometries are specifically needed for is the crossing points between singlet and triplet surfaces, located with a conical intersection algorithm, since the decomposition proceeds by intersystem crossing from a singlet azide to a triplet nitrene and no single-reference method describes both surfaces on a common footing. The validation against experiment runs through a quantity the space is well suited to: the computed separation between the triplet and singlet nitrene-dinitrogen complexes is 35.3 kcal/mol, close to the singlet-triplet splitting of 31.2 kcal/mol derived from photoelectron spectroscopy on the corresponding anion. The most instructive result is a disagreement between levels that changes the shape of the path. The multiconfigurational model produces a minimum energy path on the singlet surface passing through a shallow local minimum associated with a nitrene-dinitrogen intermediate before a second transition state, but when relative energies at those geometries are recomputed with coupled cluster and quadratic configuration interaction methods, that second transition state falls 1 to 2 kcal/mol below the intermediate it supposedly follows. The stationary point structure produced by the reference is therefore not consistent with the energies of the higher-level treatment applied at those same geometries -- a shallow intermediate that survives at one level and vanishes at another. The authors note that similar results had been reported previously. For the crossing points the agreement with an independent multireference treatment is good, 38.8 kcal/mol against 39.6 from a multireference averaged quadratic coupled cluster calculation.
reference_short: Chen & McQuaid, J. Phys. Chem. A 2012, 116, 3561
notes: This molecule serves as the calibration system whose agreement between the multiconfigurational and density functional geometries justified applying the cheaper model to the larger target. electronic_structure_description: Relative energies of all possible vertical and adiabatic transitions were computed at the perturbatively corrected level with this space. The lowest excited singlet is a charge-transfer transition from the aminophenyl electron-donor moiety to the cationic quinolizinium acceptor ring. Two singly occupied orbitals lie in different spatial domains, which suppresses exchange in the triplet and closes the singlet-triplet gap, providing a favourable intersystem crossing channel; the analysis rests on inspecting the confinement of the active orbitals to the donor or acceptor ring. Configuration state function weights and natural orbital occupation numbers are reported alongside the orbitals. Experimentally the emission of similar derivatives is quenched, and rotation of the aminophenyl ring relative to the quinolizinium ring is implicated in the deactivation.
Other: The orbital selection here uses one method's orbitals to build another's space: the active spaces were chosen from the highest-lying pi and pi-star orbitals obtained as eigenvectors of Kohn-Sham density functional calculations. That is a practical and increasingly common route, and the authors add the check that makes it defensible -- natural orbitals and their occupation numbers were monitored to assure the desired active space convergence, since a space seeded from another method's orbitals can converge onto a different set than intended. A second practical detail is recorded that rarely appears in print: a smaller eight-electron seven-orbital space was sometimes used to provide an initial guess for the twelve-electron ten-orbital calculations when convergence problems were encountered. Two sizes serve two roles. The full systems use twelve electrons in ten orbitals, while a set of truncated model compounds uses six electrons in six orbitals, so the trends computed across the models are internally consistent but not directly comparable in magnitude with the full-system numbers. The quantity the space is asked to deliver is a small energy difference between states of different multiplicity, and the physical argument the paper makes depends on orbital localisation rather than on energy alone: when the two singly occupied orbitals occupy different spatial domains -- one on the electron-donor ring, one on the acceptor -- exchange is small and the singlet-triplet gap collapses, opening an intersystem crossing channel. The computed gaps bear this out, falling from 0.58, 0.62 and 0.81 eV at the ground-state geometry to 0.04, 0.11 and 0.13 eV when the two rings are rotated to orthogonality, and rising to 0.74 through 1.37 eV on protonation because the triplet then experiences more exchange. So the space must be able to represent orbitals localised on either ring, and the whole analysis rests on inspecting where the active orbitals sit rather than on the numbers alone. The authors are careful about how far that inspection can be pushed, stating that examining the confinement of orbitals to the donor or acceptor ring is instructive for envisioning the fate of the excited state but should not be treated conclusively, since no full exploration of the excited-state surfaces was performed for the models. Gaps of 0.04 eV are also well below any accuracy claim for the method, so the ordering within the rotated series is qualitative. Configuration state function weights and occupation numbers are reported alongside the orbitals rather than energies alone, which is the right pairing for an argument about which configurations carry a state.
reference_short: Yalcin, Thomas, Tian, Seferoglu, Ihmels & Dede, J. Org. Chem. 2014, 79, 3799
notes: Protonation of the amino group switches off the charge transfer and closes the intersystem crossing channel, which is the pH-responsive fluorescence switching the study explains.

electronic_structure_description: The computed T1 diagnostic is 0.017, comfortably below the 0.05 upper limit proposed for single-reference transition metal complexes, and the weight of the leading configuration in the multiconfigurational wave function exceeds 0.9, so the ground state has negligible multireference character. Spin contamination in broken-symmetry density functional calculations did not appear for this species. Fifteen quintet, thirty-six triplet and thirty-six singlet states spanned by the full valence space were coupled in the spin-orbit calculation.
Other: The multiconfigurational calculations here exist to settle a question raised by a cheaper diagnostic, and the paper works through three independent measures of multireference character rather than trusting one. The starting concern is that the computed T1 diagnostics -- 0.017 for the bare metal and 0.054, 0.040, 0.034 and 0.035 for the successive oxides -- approach or exceed the upper limit of 0.05 proposed for single-reference transition metal complexes, which would call the coupled cluster thermochemistry into question. Two further diagnostics are then applied. Spin contamination in broken-symmetry density functional calculations appears only for the dioxide, at 40 percent. And the weight of the leading configuration in the multiconfigurational wave function is computed directly, coming out above 0.9 for every species examined, from which the authors conclude that despite the relatively large T1 values the ground state wave functions have negligible multireference character. Reporting three diagnostics that partly disagree, and letting the configuration weight arbitrate, is a more careful procedure than the common practice of quoting T1 alone. The space itself is full valence -- the oxygen 2s and 2p together with the metal 5s and 4d -- so no orbital selection judgement enters, which is the right choice when the space exists to test whether a single determinant suffices rather than to compute a production number. That choice also sets the scope: full valence calculations were computationally feasible only for the metal atom, the monoxide and the dioxide, so the two higher oxides that dominate the gas phase chemically were never treated multiconfigurationally at all. The same space then supports the spin-orbit treatment, and the state manifolds are large: fifteen quintet, thirty-six triplet and thirty-six singlet states for the atom, the seven lowest states of each multiplicity for the monoxide, and the first twenty states of each multiplicity within a two electronvolt window for the dioxide. Three different dynamical correlation treatments were applied on the same reference -- variational configuration interaction with a size-consistency correction, perturbation theory with the ionization-potential electron-affinity corrected zeroth-order Hamiltonian, and a quasi-degenerate partially contracted valence perturbation scheme -- with all of them extrapolated to the complete basis set limit from triple through quintuple zeta, the reference and correlation energy components extrapolated separately. Having several correlation treatments on one common space is what allows method spread to be separated from space adequacy.

electronic_structure_description: This species has the largest T1 diagnostic of the set at 0.054, exceeding the 0.05 upper limit proposed for single-reference transition metal complexes, which is what prompted the multiconfigurational investigation. Nevertheless the weight of the leading configuration exceeds 0.9 and no spin contamination appeared in broken-symmetry density functional calculations, so the ground state wave function is judged to have negligible multireference character despite the diagnostic. The three post-CASSCF correlation treatments were all applied to this species and extrapolated to the complete basis set limit.
Other: The multiconfigurational calculations here exist to settle a question raised by a cheaper diagnostic, and the paper works through three independent measures of multireference character rather than trusting one. The starting concern is that the computed T1 diagnostics -- 0.017 for the bare metal and 0.054, 0.040, 0.034 and 0.035 for the successive oxides -- approach or exceed the upper limit of 0.05 proposed for single-reference transition metal complexes, which would call the coupled cluster thermochemistry into question. Two further diagnostics are then applied. Spin contamination in broken-symmetry density functional calculations appears only for the dioxide, at 40 percent. The space itself is full valence -- the oxygen 2s and 2p together with the metal 5s and 4d -- so no orbital selection judgement enters, which is the right choice when the space exists to test whether a single determinant suffices rather than to compute a production number. That choice also sets the scope: full valence calculations were computationally feasible only for the metal atom, the monoxide and the dioxide, so the two higher oxides that dominate the gas phase chemically were never treated multiconfigurationally at all. active_space_orbital_description: The twelve remaining valence electrons in twelve valence orbitals: the eighth through tenth sigma, the third and fourth pi and the delta, corresponding to the iron 3d and 4s and the oxygen 2p, plus an additional eleventh sigma and fifth pi. A nine orbital variant omits the last two. The first six sigma and first two pi orbitals are doubly occupied and inactive, as is the seventh sigma because of its almost pure oxygen 2s character.
active_space_protocol: Two nested spaces on a common inactive core, giving 270 and 49285 configurations respectively; the smaller was run with the second-order Douglas-Kroll-Hess Hamiltonian and the larger without, at both the CASSCF and the multireference configuration interaction level.
electronic_structure_description: The leading configuration of the twelve-in-twelve multireference wave function for S = 2 is core 8sigma2 3pi4 9sigma1 delta3 4pi2, corresponding to the 5Delta state, with weight 82, 78, 75 and 71 percent at bond lengths of 1.5, 1.62, 1.7 and 1.8 Angstrom. The unrestricted Hartree-Fock spin expectation value is about 6.7 against an expected 6, and the coupled cluster T1 diagnostic is about 0.1, above the 0.05 threshold. Experimental bond lengths of 1.616 and 1.57 Angstrom and vibrational frequencies of 880, 965 and 882 wavenumbers are tabulated, with heats of formation of 60.0 plus or minus 5.0, 61.9 plus or minus 4.8, 65.5 plus or minus 3.0 and 64.8 plus or minus 3.0 kcal/mol.
Other: The multireference calculations here are a control experiment on a single molecule rather than the production method, and the sensitivity they expose is about what a space does when the correlation treatment on top of it is removed. Two spaces were built on the same inactive core: the sigma one through six and pi one through two orbitals were frozen, and the seventh sigma orbital was frozen too on the explicit ground that it is of almost pure oxygen 2s character -- a composition argument, not an energetic one, and the kind of justification for a freezing choice that most papers omit. The remaining twelve valence electrons then went either into nine orbitals, the eighth through tenth sigma, third and fourth pi and delta, corresponding to the metal 3d and 4s and the oxygen 2p, or into twelve orbitals adding the eleventh sigma and fifth pi. The two spaces differ by a factor of about 180 in configuration count, 270 against 49285. The decisive comparison is not between the two spaces but between CASSCF and MRCI on the same twelve orbital space: the bond lengths from CASSCF, which lacks dynamic electron correlation, are noticeably longer than those from MRCI, which has both static and dynamic correlation. The authors draw the general lesson that dynamic correlation is important for reliable geometry optimization -- in other words, enlarging or perfecting the active space does not rescue a geometry if the dynamic correlation outside it is missing. The multireference wave function also settles what the cheaper diagnostics only hint at. The unrestricted Hartree-Fock spin expectation value is about 6.7 against an expected 6, and the coupled cluster T1 diagnostic is about 0.1, twice the 0.05 threshold, which would suggest serious multireference character. The MRCI(12,12) wave function instead shows a single leading configuration, core 8sigma2 3pi4 9sigma1 delta3 4pi2, carrying 82 percent weight at 1.5 Angstrom. That weight is not constant: it falls monotonically to 78, 75 and 71 percent at 1.62, 1.7 and 1.8 Angstrom, so the multiconfigurational character grows steadily as the bond stretches even over this narrow range around the minimum. A space validated at equilibrium is therefore being validated at its most favourable point. The relativistic treatment is entangled with the space comparison in a way worth flagging: only the smaller nine orbital space was run with the second-order Douglas-Kroll-Hess Hamiltonian, so the curve that differs in space size also differs in Hamiltonian and the two effects are not separated. Separately, the DKH2 Hamiltonian shifts all energies down by about 2.1 kcal/mol while adding 3s3p correlation raises them by about 1.6, effects of the same size as the chemical accuracy the study is aiming for. The multireference character of the reaction itself is never probed with these methods: the transition state TS2 has a spin expectation value of about 6.9 and T1 below 0.12, which the authors acknowledge indicates some multireference character, yet no CASSCF or MRCI calculation was performed on it, on the stated ground that the accuracy of that particular energy is not crucial for the kinetics and thermodynamics sought. The one stationary point most likely to need a multiconfigurational treatment is thus the one that did not get one.

electronic_structure_description: The global minimum of the system, 116.0 kcal/mol below the S(3P) + c-C3H(2B2) reactants, in a 2A' state. The vertical gap to the lowest 2A'' state is only 7.0 kcal/mol, while the lowest quartets lie far above at 77.4 (4A') and 77.0 (4A'') kcal/mol. Mulliken analysis gives C-C and S-C overlap populations of 0.406 e (C3-C4), -0.126 e (C2-C3) and 0.953 e (S-C2); most of the spin density sits on C2 (0.579 e) with a non-negligible 0.242 e on sulfur and 0.417 e on C4, the last partly from spin polarization of the C3-C4 bond (C3 carries -0.223 e).
Other: Two entirely different active spaces are used for two different jobs in this paper, and neither is the space one would guess from the other. The vertical excitation gaps at the doublet minima come from multireference configuration interaction with a Davidson correction on a state-averaged CASSCF reference in a space of only four orbitals; the entrance-channel energy profiles come from CASSCF alone in a space of eleven orbitals. The small space is defined purely by orbital rank within symmetry blocks -- [14a'15a'3a''4a''] for the planar minima and [17a-20a] for the nonplanar ones -- with no statement of what those orbitals are chemically. Because the labels are positional, the same nominal four orbitals hold five electrons in the planar case and only three in the nonplanar one, so the two halves of the same table rest on spaces that differ in electron count as well as in symmetry labelling, and a gap for a planar isomer is not strictly comparable to one for a nonplanar isomer. The state averaging is equally weighted across 2A'-2A''-4A'-4A'' for the planar set and 2A-2A-4A for the nonplanar set: averaging doublets and quartets together in a single set of orbitals is what makes the doublet-quartet gaps computable at all, but it forces one orbital set onto states separated by as much as 139 kcal/mol, which is a severe constraint on a four-orbital space. The entrance-channel spaces are larger but are not held fixed across the comparison the paper's conclusions rest on. For the linear reactant, [12a'-18a', 2a''-5a''] holds eleven electrons in eleven orbitals, and the same space is used for both doublets and quartets. For the cyclic reactant, the doublets use [11a'-17a', 3a''-5a''], eleven electrons in ten orbitals, while the quartets use [11a'-17a', 3a''-4a''], one orbital smaller, with the electron count not restated. The doublet and quartet profiles for the cyclic reactant are therefore not computed in a common space, yet the central conclusion -- that the doublet surfaces are attractive while the quartet surfaces are repulsive with low barriers -- is drawn from comparing exactly those two sets of curves. The number of averaged states swings as well, from three of each symmetry for the linear doublets to nine 2A' plus eight 2A'' for the cyclic doublets and two 4A' plus four 4A'' for the cyclic quartets, so the orbital compromise being imposed differs from figure to figure. The authors are candid about the central limitation: the shallow barriers seen in the profiles 'might well disappear if a true reaction coordinate were used or even if the dynamical correlation effects not captured by the CASSCF wave functions were included'. That is an explicit admission that a CASSCF-only surface, however large the space, cannot settle whether a small barrier is real -- and both the barrier on the B 2A' profile and the avoided crossing that causes it are load bearing for the reaction mechanism proposed. There is also a place where the space is acknowledged to be too small and no larger one was attempted: the two highest minima show doublet instability and symmetry breaking, with the lowest 2A' and 2A'' states interacting strongly enough at nonsymmetric geometries to give two equivalent nonsymmetric minima, and the authors state that deciding whether these species are truly symmetric 'would require, for instance, large-scale MRCI-type computations' which they declined to perform because those minima lie too high to matter dynamically. Finally the two spaces come with different basis sets, 6-311G** for the multireference gaps and cc-pVDZ for the profiles, so nothing in the paper puts the small and large spaces on a common footing where they could be compared against each other.

electronic_structure_description: The highest-lying minimum, 2A, only 26.8 kcal/mol below reactants. Vertical gaps are 17.4 kcal/mol to the second doublet and 46.4 kcal/mol to the quartet. It shows a low 207 cm-1 asymmetric stretching mode but then a relatively high 525 cm-1 wagging mode. The unpaired electron is localized mainly on C4 (0.808 e). The density functional method gives a symmetric Cs structure while the quadratic configuration interaction method gives a nonsymmetric one, a doublet instability arising because the lowest 2A' and 2A'' states interact strongly at nonsymmetric geometries to give two equivalent nonsymmetric minima; a Cs-constrained 2A'' minimum lies only 1.1 kcal/mol above the nonsymmetric one.
Other: Two entirely different active spaces are used for two different jobs in this paper, and neither is the space one would guess from the other. The vertical excitation gaps at the doublet minima come from multireference configuration interaction with a Davidson correction on a state-averaged CASSCF reference in a space of only four orbitals; the entrance-channel energy profiles come from CASSCF alone in a space of eleven orbitals. The small space is defined purely by orbital rank within symmetry blocks -- [14a'15a'3a''4a''] for the planar minima and [17a-20a] for the nonplanar ones -- with no statement of what those orbitals are chemically. Because the labels are positional, the same nominal four orbitals hold five electrons in the planar case and only three in the nonplanar one, so the two halves of the same table rest on spaces that differ in electron count as well as in symmetry labelling, and a gap for a planar isomer is not strictly comparable to one for a nonplanar isomer. The state averaging is equally weighted across 2A'-2A''-4A'-4A'' for the planar set and 2A-2A-4A for the nonplanar set: averaging doublets and quartets together in a single set of orbitals is what makes the doublet-quartet gaps computable at all, but it forces one orbital set onto states separated by as much as 139 kcal/mol, which is a severe constraint on a four-orbital space. The entrance-channel spaces are larger but are not held fixed across the comparison the paper's conclusions rest on. For the linear reactant, [12a'-18a', 2a''-5a''] holds eleven electrons in eleven orbitals, and the same space is used for both doublets and quartets. For the cyclic reactant, the doublets use [11a'-17a', 3a''-5a''], eleven electrons in ten orbitals, while the quartets use [11a'-17a', 3a''-4a''], one orbital smaller, with the electron count not restated. The doublet and quartet profiles for the cyclic reactant are therefore not computed in a common space, yet the central conclusion -- that the doublet surfaces are attractive while the quartet surfaces are repulsive with low barriers -- is drawn from comparing exactly those two sets of curves. The number of averaged states swings as well, from three of each symmetry for the linear doublets to nine 2A' plus eight 2A'' for the cyclic doublets and two 4A' plus four 4A'' for the cyclic quartets, so the orbital compromise being imposed differs from figure to figure. The authors are candid about the central limitation: the shallow barriers seen in the profiles 'might well disappear if a true reaction coordinate were used or even if the dynamical correlation effects not captured by the CASSCF wave functions were included'. That is an explicit admission that a CASSCF-only surface, however large the space, cannot settle whether a small barrier is real -- and both the barrier on the B 2A' profile and the avoided crossing that causes it are load bearing for the reaction mechanism proposed. There is also a place where the space is acknowledged to be too small and no larger one was attempted: the two highest minima show doublet instability and symmetry breaking, with the lowest 2A' and 2A'' states interacting strongly enough at nonsymmetric geometries to give two equivalent nonsymmetric minima, and the authors state that deciding whether these species are truly symmetric 'would require, for instance, large-scale MRCI-type computations' which they declined to perform because those minima lie too high to matter dynamically. Finally the two spaces come with different basis sets, 6-311G** for the multireference gaps and cc-pVDZ for the profiles, so nothing in the paper puts the small and large spaces on a common footing where they could be compared against each other.

electronic_structure_description: A very low lying 2A1 excited state of the cyclic reactant must be taken into account: it drops below the 2B2 ground state on a change of the HCC angle of about 5 degrees, and the energies involved are comparable to the S(3P)-S(1D) gap. Both states correlate with 2A' states in planar geometry, so S(3P) + c-C3H(2B2, 2A1) gives rise to two 2A' and four 2A'' states. Both 2A' profiles are attractive while only the lowest 2A'' is; the other 2A'' correlating with ground-state reactants rises steeply below an S-C distance of about 2.2 Angstrom, peaking there because of repulsion from a sulfur p-electron pair along the bond axis. ligand_set: Corrin macrocycle, an axial imidazole and an axial methyl group
geometry_source: Selected points along a one-dimensional cut of the potential energy surface obtained from constrained density functional optimizations with a split-valence polarized basis; the multiconfigurational calculations are single points at those geometries
method: CASSCF and CASPT2, run as a comparison against benchmark completely renormalized coupled cluster calculations with non-iterative triples in a multilevel local correlation framework, and against a range of density functionals
basis_set: ANO-S, contracted 6s5p3d1f on cobalt, 3s2p1d on nitrogen and carbon and 2s on hydrogen, chosen to match the 6-31G* basis used in the coupled cluster and density functional work (505 against 496 functions); larger bases were not affordable
relativistic_treatment: Estimated only, by perturbative one-electron Darwin contact and mass-velocity terms, and found essentially negligible at about 1.5 kcal/mol
active_space_orbital_description: Ten electrons in eleven orbitals in three subgroups: the doubly occupied 3dx2-y2, 3dyz and 3dxz orbitals on cobalt together with their 4d correlating counterparts; the bonding Co-C sigma(dz2) orbital and its sigma*(dz2) counterpart augmented by a correlating orbital of 4dz2 character to improve the axial binding region; and the occupied 3dxy plus n and unoccupied 3dxy minus n orbitals formed from the bonding and antibonding combinations of cobalt 3dxy with the lone pairs on the four surrounding nitrogens.
active_space_protocol: The largest space affordable. The orbitals had to be largely centred on the axial cobalt-methyl fragment, restricting information about the interaction of cobalt and methyl with the corrin conjugation to a minimum; the 4d correlating counterparts were included for the double shell effect, described as standard procedure for transition metal complexes. The ideal space -- the valence shells of cobalt, the methyl group and the surrounding nitrogens, or better all atoms of the corrin conjugation -- would have been unmanageable.
multiplicities_studied: The closed-shell parent and the doublet fragments produced on homolysis
electronic_structure_description: The cobalt-methyl bond breaking is formally a multireference problem. Bond dissociation energies for this model: 20.1 kcal/mol purely electronic at CASSCF and 58.8 at CASPT2 on the same space, becoming 15.1 and 53.8 with zero-point corrections and 10.2 and 35.9 once counterpoise corrections of 6.7 and 19.7 kcal/mol are applied. The benchmark coupled cluster value is about 38 kcal/mol and the experimental values are 37 plus or minus 3 and 36 plus or minus 4. The dissociation products are Im-[Co(II)corrin]+ and a methyl radical. Coupled cluster analysis shows large single excitations of sigma(dz2) to sigma*(dz2) type alongside equally important double excitations of the same type, and rapidly growing single and double excitations into unoccupied orbitals that mix the antibonding sigma*(dz2) character with the delocalized corrin conjugation as the bond stretches.
Other: This is a paper whose central negative result is about active space adequacy, so the sensitivity finding is the conclusion rather than a side remark. The authors state plainly that CASSCF and CASPT2 have difficulties with the cobalt-methyl bond breaking because using adequate active spaces is prohibitively expensive, while the smaller and affordable spaces are insufficient. The numbers make the point sharply. On the same space, the purely electronic bond dissociation energy is 20.1 kcal/mol at CASSCF and 58.8 at CASPT2, a 38.7 kcal/mol spread for one reference wave function, against a benchmark coupled cluster value of about 38 and experimental values of 37 plus or minus 3 and 36 plus or minus 4. Neither multiconfigurational number is in harmony with either. The authors read that enormous perturbative correction not as dynamical correlation being recovered but as an excessive second-order term trying to compensate for deficiencies of the reference and failing to eliminate them -- a diagnostic worth borrowing: when the perturbative correction is comparable in size to the quantity being computed, the reference is the problem, not the perturbation. What is missing from the space is identified concretely rather than gestured at. The ideal space would correlate the valence shells of cobalt and the methyl group together with those of the nitrogens around cobalt, or better still all the atoms of the corrin conjugation, but that is unmanageable, so the orbitals actually chosen had to be largely centred on the axial cobalt-methyl fragment with the interactions with the corrin conjugation restricted to a minimum. The coupled cluster wave functions then show exactly what that omission costs: as the bond is stretched, single and double excitations grow rapidly into unoccupied orbitals that mix the antibonding sigma*(dz2) character with the delocalized corrin network, and those excitations simply do not appear in the multiconfigurational wave function in the 4.0 to 4.5 Angstrom region where the reference curve has already levelled off. So the failure is not diffuse; a specific class of excitation, absent by construction from the chosen space, is what would be needed to bring the dissociation curve into the experimental range. The space itself is otherwise carefully built -- each of the three doubly occupied 3d orbitals carries its 4d correlating counterpart for the double shell effect, the sigma and sigma* pair carries a 4dz2 correlating orbital, and the bonding and antibonding combinations of 3dxy with the four nitrogen lone pairs are included -- which is precisely the point: a well-designed space built on the standard prescriptions still fails, because the prescriptions address the metal centre while the physics that matters lives on the ligand conjugation. There is a further, purely practical warning: the energies from the largest calculations affordable do not stabilize at 4.0 to 4.5 Angstrom, so the cobalt-methyl distance had to be pushed out to 8.5 Angstrom to reach the asymptote, whereas the coupled cluster curve has already levelled off by 4.5. An inadequate space thus also shifts where the dissociation limit apparently lies, which would silently corrupt a bond energy computed on a shorter scan. Having exhausted the space, the authors tested what else might rescue the result. Scalar relativistic effects, from perturbative one-electron Darwin and mass-velocity terms, are essentially negligible at about 1.5 kcal/mol. Basis set superposition error is not: the counterpoise corrections are 6.7 kcal/mol at CASSCF and 19.7 at CASPT2, bringing the values to 10.2 and 35.9. The perturbative number now lands inside the experimental range, and the authors refuse to claim it, calling a counterpoise correction of about 20 kcal/mol too large to be an accurate estimate of the superposition error and the resulting agreement a probable fortuitous cancellation of errors. They also raise the size inextensivity of the diagonalize-then-perturb formulation as a possible contributor at this system size, while noting it is hard to prove. The stated remedy is not a bigger basis but a different formalism, an incomplete model-space multireference perturbation theory that would admit more active orbitals; and they add the caution that a space appropriate for the smaller pentaammine model may not transfer to the 58-atom corrin system at all.
reference_short: Kozlowski, Piecuch et al., J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2012, 8, 1870
notes: The paper writes the space as (11,10) throughout while stating in the methods that it contains 10 electrons and 11 orbitals, so the label is orbitals-first rather than the usual electrons-first; the orbital-by-orbital breakdown in the text confirms 10 electrons in 11 orbitals. The multiconfigurational curve does not reach its asymptote until 8.5 Angstrom, against 4.0-4.5 Angstrom for the coupled cluster reference curve.
correlation_correction: Second-order perturbation theory on the CASSCF reference; the correction is 38.7 kcal/mol, comparable to the bond energy itself, which the authors read as evidence that the reference is inadequate rather than that the correction is working

geometry_source: All structures optimized independently at the CASSCF, multireference configuration interaction and CCSD(T) levels, with harmonic frequencies computed to confirm the nature of each stationary point and reaction paths followed by a quadratic steepest descent procedure
method: Full valence complete active space SCF used as the reference for internally contracted multireference configuration interaction with the Davidson size-consistency correction, alongside CCSD(T) and explicitly correlated CCSD(T)-F12 calculations for comparison; complete basis set limits obtained by extrapolating the active-space and correlation contributions separately
basis_set: aug-cc-pVXZ with X = D, T, Q and 5, plus aug-cc-pwCVXZ core-valence sets for the core correlation estimates; complete basis set limits obtained from (T,Q) pairs for the multireference calculations and (Q,5) pairs for coupled cluster
active_space_orbital_description: Full valence complete active space. The paper never states the space as an electron or orbital count, giving it only as the full valence reference wave function.
active_space_protocol: Full valence throughout, with no space-size testing; the sensitivity explored instead is the effect of the correlation treatment applied on top of that fixed reference, and of the basis set and core correlation.
electronic_structure_description: The global minimum and the zero of the relative energy scale. Optimized C-C and C-H distances are 1.2146 and 1.0738 Angstrom at CASSCF with the quadruple zeta basis, 1.2075 and 1.0633 at the multireference configuration interaction level and 1.2069 and 1.0636 at CCSD(T), against experimental and semi-experimental values clustered near 1.203 and 1.062. The CASSCF bond lengths are the outliers, the C-H distance being about 0.010 Angstrom too long. Harmonic frequencies for the CH asymmetric stretch, CH symmetric stretch and CC stretch are 3400, 3311 and 1969 wavenumbers at CASSCF against 3499, 3409 and 1999 at the multireference level and 3497-3501, 3415-3418 and 2011-2013 experimentally.
Other: The space here is full valence, so no orbital selection judgement enters, and what the paper exposes instead is how much of the answer lives outside that space and where the CASSCF reference alone silently fails. The isomerization energy is 53.66 kcal/mol at CASSCF with the quadruple zeta basis, 46.06 once configuration interaction is built on the same reference, and 44.76 at coupled cluster with the same basis: a full valence space with no dynamical correlation on top overestimates the reaction energy by about nine kcal/mol, more than twenty percent, and the same pattern holds for the barrier, 57.21 against 49.14. A full valence space is as complete a static-correlation treatment as this molecule admits, so this is a clean measure of what such a space cannot do by itself. The sharpest failure is topological rather than energetic. In the flat region of the isomerization path the secondary minimum M1 and the secondary transition state TS1 are, at the CASSCF level, indistinguishable: their total energies differ by seven microhartree and their relative energies come out as 52.71 and 52.72 kcal/mol, an ordering resolved to four thousandths of a kcal/mol. Adding the configuration interaction on the identical reference separates them to 46.96 and 48.06, and the geometries separate too -- the Jacobi angle goes from 100.43 and 102.95 degrees at CASSCF, barely two degrees apart, to 99.71 and 109.20 at MRCI. So on this surface it is the dynamical correlation, not the active space, that decides whether a stationary point is a minimum or a saddle, and a study that stopped at the CASSCF surface would have found a single feature where there are two. The reverse lesson appears in the dissociation regions. There the single-reference coupled cluster curve declines artificially beyond about 3.5 Angstrom and yields a wrong dissociation limit, and it collapses at separations only slightly beyond equilibrium in several other channels, while the multireference treatment on the full valence reference gives the correct limit for every arrangement. Yet at the stationary points themselves the coupled cluster description is good. The two methods are therefore each reliable on the complement of where the other is, and the paper is explicit that a global surface needs the multireference route for that reason alone rather than because the stationary points demand it. The extrapolation machinery treats the two pieces as physically distinct: the complete basis set limit is taken by splitting the total energy into the CAS contribution, extrapolated with a Karton-Martin form in the inverse 5.34 power of the cardinal number, and the correlation contribution, extrapolated by the uniform singlet- and triplet-pair scheme. Extrapolating the active-space energy and the correlation energy with different functional forms is the right acknowledgement that they converge differently with basis size, and it is a detail most papers using a full valence reference do not bother with. Two cautionary numbers close the account. The Davidson size-consistency correction lowers the multireference reaction energy by 1.51 kcal/mol, from 46.06 to 44.55, which is comparable to the entire spread among careful literature estimates. And the extrapolated multireference values drift away from, rather than toward, the best available estimate of 43.4 plus or minus 0.6: the complete basis set limits are 46.53 from the multireference calculations against 45.23 from coupled cluster, and with the core-valence basis 48.28 against 45.94. Core correlation, estimated by correlating all electrons, shortens bonds toward experiment by about 0.0027 and 0.0013 Angstrom on average and raises the CC stretch by about 8 wavenumbers across all five stationary points -- an effect entirely outside the valence space.

active_space_protocol: One space used unchanged for all three states, giving 588, 616 and 588 configuration state functions for the ground, first and second excited states. The first excited state A 2A1 has a doubly occupied 2b1 and singly occupied 5a1, giving a much more obtuse bond angle; the second excited state B 2B2 arises from excitation out of the predominantly P-H bonding 2b2 orbital into the nonbonding 2b1 and has an extremely acute bond angle. Relative energies with the largest basis, as T0 values: the ground to first excited splitting is 53.9 (SCF), 53.7 (CASSCF), 52.9 (configuration interaction), 53.0 (CASSCF-SOCI), 52.6 (CCSD) and 52.2 kcal/mol (CCSD(T)), against experimental values of 52.26 and 52.08. The ground to second excited splitting, never measured, is 74.1, 72.0, 72.7, 71.9, 72.0 and 71.3 kcal/mol across the same sequence. Stability analysis of the SCF wave functions gives an instability index of zero for the ground state and one for each excited state, the negative eigenvalues corresponding to 5a1 to 2b1 and 2b2 to 2b1 orbital rotations respectively.
Other: One fixed seven-electron eight-orbital space serves all three electronic states, and the paper is a clean measurement of how little that space buys on a system whose states are individually well described by a single determinant. So on this splitting the active space contributes almost nothing while dynamical correlation contributes the entire correction; adding an active space to SCF and stopping there would have left the answer no better. For the second excited state the same space does more: 74.1 at SCF falls to 72.0 with the active space, a two kcal/mol shift, because that state is reached by exciting out of the P-H bonding 2b2 orbital into the nonbonding 2b1, and the resulting bonding rearrangement is what a static-correlation treatment can capture. The instructive accident is that this bare CASSCF value, 72.0, sits closer to the best estimate of 71.3 than the single-reference configuration interaction value of 72.7 does, while the configuration interaction built on the CASSCF orbitals gives 71.9 -- so ranking methods by the agreement of one number would put the cheapest multiconfigurational treatment above a more complete single-reference one, for the wrong reason. The space is held constant across states but the configuration count is not, being 588, 616 and 588 state functions for the ground, first and second excited states respectively; the ground and second excited states, of different spatial symmetry, happen to yield identical counts while the first excited state gets 28 more. The most interesting methodological point is that the multireference character is diagnosed without a multiconfigurational wave function at all, by stability analysis of the open-shell SCF solutions. The ground state has an instability index of zero, so correlated methods built on it are reliable. Both excited states have an index of one, and the eigenvector of the negative eigenvalue names the offending rotation in each case -- 5a1 into 2b1 for the first excited state, 2b2 into 2b1 for the second -- which identifies precisely one lower-lying state at that geometry, namely the ground state. The sign of the second eigenvalue then fixes the state ordering, showing that the second excited state lies above the first at the first excited state's geometry. That is a great deal of information about the reference wave function extracted before any correlated calculation, and it is what licenses the single-reference treatments used for the production numbers. The practical consequence is also spelled out: despite the instability, no variational collapse occurs in asymmetrically distorted geometries, because the geometrical differences between ground and excited states are large enough that only one lower state exists, and the orthogonality of the first two states in Cs symmetry lets even the asymmetric stretching frequency be computed safely. A final scoping detail worth noting is that the multiconfigurational work is confined to relative energies at geometries optimized elsewhere: the CASSCF wave functions were built at the single-reference configuration interaction geometries, and the corresponding zero-point energies were borrowed from that method for the CASSCF and CASSCF-SOCI energy separations, so no geometry or frequency in this paper comes from the active space.

geometry_source: Stationary points and minimum energy paths optimized with the BMK density functional and the MG3S basis; the multiconfigurational calculations are single-point corrections at those geometries
method: CASSCF with second-order perturbation theory (CASMP2), used as a single-point correction to a density functional minimum energy path within dual-level direct dynamics
software: Gaussian 09 for the electronic structure; POLYRATE for the rate calculations
active_space_orbital_description: Eight electrons in eight orbitals, specified by rank as the range from the third occupied orbital below the frontier to the third virtual above it (HOMO minus 3 to LUMO plus 3), with no chemical characterisation.
active_space_protocol: A single fixed rank-defined space applied as a single-point correction at each stationary point of the two-step mechanism; no space-size testing was performed for this reaction.
electronic_structure_description: A two-step decomposition in which dissociation of the chlorine atom gives a diradical intermediate, followed by elimination of methyl chloride and ring closing to tetrahydrothiophene. On the density functional surface the first barrier is 62.0 kcal/mol, the intermediate lies at 18.8 and the second barrier at 64.1, all relative to the reactant; the perturbative multiconfigurational correction moves these to 74.5, 12.6 and 79.8. The rate constant was computed from the minimum energy path of the second step only, neglecting the influence of the first step and the intermediate.
Other: This paper contains one of the more direct measurements of active-space sensitivity available anywhere, because the quantity that changes is a rate constant and the comparison is against experiment. For the carbon-phosphorus dissociation, enlarging the space from four electrons in four orbitals to ten in ten is found to significantly decrease the CASSCF and CASMP2 energy difference between reactant and transition state -- by about 9 kcal/mol at a separation of 4.0 Angstrom. The consequence is not subtle: the computed rate constant, which was too small by seven orders of magnitude with the small space at the perturbative level, comes within about three and a half orders of magnitude with the larger one, an improvement of roughly three and a half decades from an active space change alone. The small space is not carelessly chosen either -- it is the chemically obvious one, the sigma and sigma* orbitals of the bond being broken, which is exactly what a practitioner would select for a homolysis -- and it is still badly insufficient, which is the lesson worth carrying. The paper stops there for cost reasons, stating that calculations with an even larger space were not pursued, so the sequence is truncated before convergence and the ten-orbital number should not be read as converged. The location of the variational transition state moves with the space and the correlation treatment too: at 700 K the generalized transition state sits at a phosphorus-carbon separation of about 5.2 Angstrom on the density functional surface, 3.6 with the small-space CASSCF and 4.0 with the small-space CASMP2, a spread of 1.6 Angstrom in where the bottleneck is judged to be. Since variational transition state theory locates the bottleneck by maximizing a free energy along the path, an active space that tilts the potential also relocates the dividing surface, and both errors feed the rate. The multiconfigurational treatment was reached for here only because the single-reference route failed outright: no saddle point could be found on the density functional surface, and the composite method built on coupled cluster with perturbative triples gave an unphysical result, a barrier lower than the reaction energy, which the authors attribute to the known failure of that base energy at large internuclear separation from omitted higher-order clusters or divergence of the triples expansion. With the multiconfigurational correction, no saddle point and no unphysical result appears. So the space is being used to fix a qualitative pathology, and the residual quantitative error is then traced to the space being too small. The other multiconfigurational calculation in the paper uses a rank-defined space, eight electrons in eight orbitals running from the third occupied below the frontier to the third virtual above it, applied to a diradical intermediate in a chlorine dissociation. Defining a space by orbital rank rather than by chemical character is convenient but means its composition is whatever the reference happens to place in those slots at each stationary point, and here the correction it produces is large and of inconsistent sign: the first barrier rises from 62.0 to 74.5 kcal/mol, the intermediate falls from 18.8 to 12.6, and the second barrier rises from 64.1 to 79.8. Raising both barriers while lowering the intermediate deepens the well by 24 kcal/mol in total, and the resulting rate constants come out five and ten orders of magnitude too small at the two dynamical levels, with the activation energies greatly overestimating experiment. Given that the single uncorrected functional does better on this reaction, the perturbative correction on a rank-defined space is making the kinetics worse, not better -- the mirror image of the dissociation case, and a caution that a multiconfigurational correction is only an improvement when the space is chosen for the chemistry rather than for its position in the orbital list.

The paper stops there for cost reasons, stating that calculations with an even larger space were not pursued, so the sequence is truncated before convergence and the ten-orbital number should not be read as converged. The location of the variational transition state moves with the space and the correlation treatment too: at 700 K the generalized transition state sits at a phosphorus-carbon separation of about 5.2 Angstrom on the density functional surface, 3.6 with the small-space CASSCF and 4.0 with the small-space CASMP2, a spread of 1.6 Angstrom in where the bottleneck is judged to be. electronic_structure_description: The strong-acceptor representative. Measured S and B band wavelengths are 489 and 373 nm with oscillator strengths of 0.01 and 0.89; the perturbatively corrected calculation gives S at 451 and 453 nm with strengths 0.010 and 0.008 and B at 342 and 343 nm with strengths 1.369 and 1.353, while time-dependent density functional theory gives 450, 449, 353 and 352 nm. The space is four electrons in four orbitals -- the two highest occupied and two lowest unoccupied orbitals -- described as the minimum necessary to reach the ground state and the four lowest singlet excited states that carry the observed bands, and it is the multiconfigurational realization of the Gouterman four-orbital model for porphyrinoids. For excitation energies this works: the perturbatively corrected wavelengths track experiment and reproduce the red shift on going from the acceptor to the donor derivative. The failure appears in the properties that the paper actually needs, the angular momentum matrix elements that set the sign of the magnetic circular dichroism, and it is a failure of orbital shape rather than of space size. Recomputing with orbitals averaged over all five states instead of separate sets for ground and excited states halves the computed angular momenta, which the authors take as direct evidence of high sensitivity to the orbital shapes. They connect this to a documented precedent, the calculation of EPR g factors for copper complexes, where different orbital averaging schemes greatly changed the angular momenta and the cause was traced to how much metal character the singly occupied antibonding orbital carried; there the fix was to average over the two states with the bonding and antibonding combinations singly occupied. Here that fix is unavailable, because the angular momentum cannot be attributed to the covalency of one bond and the states involved are not tied to a single singly occupied orbital. The decisive sentence is the one most papers would omit: more elaborate multiconfigurational calculations employing larger active spaces revealed highly fluctuating values for the angular momentum. Enlarging the space did not converge the property, it destabilized it, so the authors abandoned orbital-optimized CASSCF in favour of configuration interaction within the same four orbitals held fixed at either Hartree-Fock or Kohn-Sham shapes. The choice between those two fixed orbital sets then decides the answer outright. With Kohn-Sham orbitals the angular momenta come out with the correct signs, negative for the acceptor and positive for the donor, matching the observed sign anomaly; with Hartree-Fock orbitals both come out positive, and the anomaly the paper set out to explain simply disappears. The oscillator strengths tell the same story from the other side. The orbital-optimized calculation predicts lower absorption intensity for the donor compound, contrary to experiment, where the acceptor compound is the weak one, and time-dependent density functional theory scores better; among the fixed-orbital variants the Hartree-Fock one repeats the wrong ordering while the Kohn-Sham one matches. compound_name: Bis(cyclopentadienyl)ytterbium with a methyl-substituted alpha-diimine, Cp2Yb(Me2-DAB)
ligand_set: Two cyclopentadienyl rings and a chelating alpha-diimine
geometry_source: Fixed at the density functional (BP86) optimized geometry of the triplet state, chosen because those geometries better reflect the experimental structures
method: Multi-state CASPT2 on CASSCF reference wave functions, with a non-standard zero value of the shift in the zeroth-order Hamiltonian and an imaginary level shift of 0.2 hartree; state-averaged CASSCF over the two lowest states was used where strongly interacting states were near-degenerate
software: MOLCAS 7.6 for the multiconfigurational calculations, with Cholesky decomposition and density fitting; ADF for the density functional geometry optimizations
basis_set: An ab initio model potential and basis for ytterbium with 24 electrons in the valence shells, primitives (14s10p9d8f3g) contracted to [6s5p5d4f1g]; atomic natural orbital sets elsewhere, two s and one p on hydrogen and three s, two p and one d on carbon and nitrogen

active_space_orbital_description: Sixteen electrons in thirteen orbitals: three orbitals each of a1, a2 and b2 symmetry and four of b1, made up of eight occupied orbitals (two per symmetry) and five virtual ones, chosen so that the cyclopentadienyl pi system, the diimine pi system and the ytterbium 4f orbitals are correlated in a balanced and computationally feasible way. Two smaller spaces were also used: fourteen electrons in eight orbitals, comprising the fourteen 4f electrons localized mainly on the metal plus the lowest diimine pi* orbital, and twenty-four electrons in thirteen orbitals, obtained by adding three filled orbitals in each symmetry from the two ligand pi systems.
active_space_protocol: A deliberate two-stage series: first the number of active electrons was increased with the virtual space constrained to the single accepting pi* orbital, then the virtual space was enlarged to allow electronic relaxation. The smaller spaces were run to obtain a correct single-determinant description of each low-lying singlet and triplet and thereby validate the largest one.

electronic_structure_description: Ground term: a 1A1. The ground state is a diradical with eigenfunctions delocalized over the ytterbium 4f and diimine pi* orbitals, written on localized orbitals as the two-configuration singlet (4f)2(pi*)0 minus (4f)0(pi*)2 and equivalent to an open-shell (4f)1(pi*)1 configuration on delocalized orbitals; the corresponding triplet lies only about 310 wavenumbers above, consistent with the observed magnetic coupling constants of a few hundred wavenumbers. Relative energies in eV across the three spaces (14e/8a, 24e/13a, 16e/13a): a3A1 0.04, 0.001, 0.04; a1A2 0.164, 0.082, 0.451; b1A2 0.115, 0.033, 0.140; a1B1 0.144, 0.09, 0.433; b1B1 0.176, 0.121, 0.219; a1B2 0.195, 0.162, 0.384. The low-lying states correspond to excitations from 4f orbitals of b1, b2, a1 and a2 character into the diimine pi* orbital of b1 symmetry. The purely ionic configuration is only the eleventh root of A1 symmetry in the smallest space, so valence tautomerism is discarded.
Other: Three active spaces were built deliberately as a two-stage test -- first increasing the number of active electrons while holding the virtual space to a single accepting orbital, then enlarging the virtual space to allow electronic relaxation -- and the outcome splits sharply by which quantity is being asked for. The singlet-triplet gap that the whole paper turns on is essentially space-independent: 310 wavenumbers with 14 electrons in 8 orbitals, 260 with 24 in 13, and 310 again with 16 in 13. The authors state the stronger form of this result explicitly, that quasi-degeneracy of the low-lying singlet and triplet states is retrieved within 50 wavenumbers in every symmetry whatever the space, whether constrained to one virtual orbital or extended to include relaxation, and they treat that invariance as the evidence for the diradical picture. That is the right use of a space-size series: not to converge a number but to show a qualitative conclusion does not depend on the choice. The higher states behave completely differently, and anyone reusing these numbers should notice. The lowest A2 state sits at 0.164 eV in the smallest space, drops to 0.082 when electrons are added at fixed virtual space, and jumps to 0.451 when the virtual space is opened -- a factor of five and a half across three reasonable choices. The lowest B1 state does the same thing, 0.144 then 0.09 then 0.433, and the B2 state roughly doubles. So enlarging the occupied part of the space and enlarging the virtual part move these excitation energies in opposite directions, and neither the trend nor the magnitude is converged at 13 orbitals. A single number quoted from any one of these spaces would be meaningless without the series. The construction logic of the 16-electron 13-orbital space is worth recording because it is stated in unusual detail: eight occupied orbitals, two in each of the four symmetries, plus five virtual ones, chosen so that the fragments -- the cyclopentadienyl pi system, the diimine pi system and the metal 4f shell -- are correlated in a balanced and computationally feasible way. The smaller 14-electron 8-orbital space is the physically motivated minimum, the fourteen 4f electrons plus the single lowest ligand pi* acceptor, and the 24-electron space adds three filled orbitals in each symmetry from the two ligand pi systems. Balance across fragments rather than orbital rank or energy window is the selection criterion throughout. The multiconfigurational treatment also settles a chemical question that no amount of density functional work could: whether the ground state is a valence tautomer. The purely ionic configuration turns out to be the eleventh root of A1 symmetry in the smallest space, far above the ground state, so the valence tautomerism hypothesis is discarded. The diradical singlet, written on localized orbitals as a two-configuration mixture and equivalent to a single open-shell configuration on delocalized orbitals, is exactly the object a single determinant cannot represent, and the authors say plainly that replacing indenyl by cyclopentadienyl or bipyridine by the diimine moves the system from a regime where density functional theory suffices to one that requires multiconfigurational methods. Two technical choices are non-default and matter for reproducibility: the shift parameter in the zeroth-order Hamiltonian was set to zero rather than its usual value, and an imaginary level shift of 0.2 hartree was applied, alongside strong damping in the orbital optimization. Setting that shift to zero with a lanthanide 4f space is a significant departure that will move relative energies, and it is reported without justification.

electronic_structure_description: Ground term: 1Sigma, dominated by the closed-shell configuration one would write for a single determinant. The excited triplet has two degenerate configurations and a significantly different geometry from the ground state; the transition is dominated by the 4pi to 5pi excitation and requires promotion to a higher orbital in addition to a spin flip. The vertical transition energy to the lowest triplet state is 3.58 eV, in the 2 to 4 eV range characteristic of this series.
Other: The active spaces here are unusually small -- two electrons in five orbitals for the odd-carbon series and four in six for the even one -- and the paper is explicit that this is the result of a convergence test rather than an economy: extensive calculations involving 8 or 12 electrons were run on selected species as a check on the inclusion of all relevant configurations and on the convergence of the transition energies, and the added computational cost of the more extensive space was not justified by the minimal change in transition energies. The justification is then made structural rather than numerical, which is the more useful form. The excited states arise purely from pi to pi transitions out of the ground state, so a space spanning the relevant pi manifold is argued to be sufficient by construction, and the resulting wave functions are analysed to confirm it: the small space produces 10 configurations for the triplets and 15 for the singlets in the odd-carbon series, of which three dominate the singlet -- about 65 percent for the configuration with the partially occupied orbitals and about 15 percent each for the other two -- while the triplet is over 96 percent a single configuration. Configurations involving the remaining virtual levels contribute less than 5 percent in total. Crucially the authors report that these composition observations remain valid even when as many as 12 electrons and 12 orbitals are put into the space, so the enlargement is shown not to redistribute weight rather than merely not to move the energy. Reporting the configuration weights before and after enlargement, not just the energies, is what makes the small-space claim checkable. The two series need different spaces for a physical reason worth carrying: in the odd-carbon clusters the excitation is a spin flip within a pi orbital or into a degenerate partner, so two active electrons suffice and the transition energies all land within about 0.5 eV of each other; in the even-carbon clusters the electron must also be promoted to a higher orbital, four electrons are needed, the configuration count rises to 105 for both states, and the transition energies jump to the 2 to 4 eV range with a substantially different excited-state geometry. So the required space size tracks whether the excitation changes the orbital occupied or only the spin coupling, which is a better predictor than molecular size. A limitation of the design should be noted alongside the result. Every multiconfigurational energy here is a vertical excitation computed at a density functional ground-state geometry, and the paper says plainly that these differ from the adiabatic values obtained from separately optimized structures. For the even-carbon series, where the triplet geometry is significantly different from the ground state, that gap matters, and no geometry in this study comes from the active space. A separate caution against conflating two convergence tests: the finding that additional diffuse functions had no effect at all on bond lengths or relative state energies concerns the basis set, tested on two of the odd-carbon species, and is a distinct claim from the active-space test.

compound_name: Dinitrogen, N2, along the dissociation coordinate
point_group: D2h was used computationally; the active orbitals correspond to the sigma-g, sigma-u, pi-u and pi-g orbitals of the full D(infinity)h group

method: CASSCF in which the active space is described by a variational two-electron reduced density matrix rather than by configuration interaction, with density fitting or Cholesky decomposition of the electron repulsion integrals permitting simultaneous optimization of large numbers of external orbitals
software: A free and open-source variational two-electron reduced density matrix plugin to PSI4; NWChem for the dinitrene geometry optimizations; Q-Chem for the single-reference comparisons
basis_set: cc-pVQZ, with a cc-pVQZ-JKFIT auxiliary basis for density fitting

active_space_protocol: A small standard space used as a validation case, to establish that the errors introduced by density fitting and Cholesky decomposition of the integrals are negligible relative to the errors from incomplete N-representability conditions.
nroots_per_mult: one
electronic_structure_description: The natural orbital occupation numbers show the onset of degeneracy of the pi-u with pi-g orbitals and of sigma-g with sigma-u as the bond is stretched. The qualitative features of the configuration-interaction-driven curve are reproduced well by the density-matrix-driven approach.
Other: This paper exists to remove the size limit on the active space, so the sensitivity it documents is what happens once that limit is gone -- and the answer is that both the space and the orbital optimization turn out to matter qualitatively, not just quantitatively. Replacing the configuration interaction description of the active space with a variational two-electron reduced density matrix makes the cost polynomial rather than exponential, and the demonstration reaches 50 electrons in 50 orbitals with all 1892 orbitals -- inactive, active and external -- optimized simultaneously. The decisive result is a natural orbital occupation crossing: the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied natural orbital occupations become nearly equal at 10-acene but do not stay that way, and the au/b3g and b1u/b2g occupations cross at 11-acene. Earlier calculations in minimal basis sets, both by this density matrix route and by density matrix renormalization group in configuration interaction mode, found no such crossing even at 12-acene. The authors attribute the difference to the larger basis and to the orbital optimization, and state that both are necessary to predict the qualitative behaviour of the occupation numbers correctly. That is a rare case of an active space calculation changing a qualitative conclusion about electronic structure rather than a number, and it locates the cause in orbital relaxation rather than in space size -- the comparison calculation had the same pi orbitals and three times as many antibonding partners, but no orbital rotations. The trade being made is visible too. The accuracy of a density matrix approach is set by which N-representability conditions are enforced, and that turns out to be system-dependent in a way space size is not. For the acenes the two-electron conditions alone suffice for good agreement with density matrix renormalization group results. For the dinitrene biradicals they do not: enforcing only those conditions overstabilizes the singlet and inflates the gaps to 4.528 and 3.848 kcal/mol, against configuration interaction driven values of 0.919 and 0.395, while adding the partial three-electron conditions brings agreement to within a third of a kcal/mol. So a practitioner gains access to a space fifty orbitals wide but acquires a new convergence parameter that must itself be checked per system. Even the loose variant remains far better than any single-reference alternative: neither perturbation theory, coupled cluster with or without triples, nor the hybrid functional predicts the correct spin state at all, the magnitude varies wildly with method, and the only single-reference approach with the right sign overshoots by two orders of magnitude. The space construction rules are stated explicitly enough to be reused. For a linear polyacene with k fused rings the space is (4k+2, 4k+2) built from pz atomic orbitals, comprising 2k+1 bonding pi orbitals and 2k+1 antibonding pi*, distributed as k orbitals each of b2g and au symmetry and k+1 each of b3g and b1u. For a dinitrene with k rings it is the 3k+1 occupied pi orbitals, the 3k+1 antibonding pi*, plus the singly occupied in-plane sigma orbitals on the nitrogens. Two caveats worth carrying: the singlet-triplet gaps are essentially unchanged between double and triple zeta bases, with the largest difference 0.7 kcal/mol for naphthalene, so basis convergence is not what limits these numbers; and the acene geometries come from restricted and unrestricted density functional optimizations rather than from the active space, which the authors themselves invoke to explain the one non-monotonic point in the series at 11-acene.

point_group: Linear; computed in the C2v subgroup
geometry_source: Potential energy curves scanned over internuclear distances from 1.80 to 3.63 Angstrom, with spectroscopic constants extracted from them
method: State-averaged CASSCF followed by multireference configuration interaction with single and double excitations and the Davidson correction; spin-orbit coupling from the spin-orbit pseudopotential
basis_set: An ECP28MWB pseudopotential and basis for lutetium, including its spin-orbit pseudopotential; an all-electron (17s,12p,5d,4f) set contracted to [6s,5p,3d,2f] for chlorine
relativistic_treatment: A 28-electron relativistic effective core potential on lutetium, with the associated spin-orbit pseudopotential
soc_included: yes, computed only in the 22-electron correlation treatment because the f orbital plays an important role in the spin-orbit interaction
active_space_orbital_description: Nine active orbitals: three sigma from the metal 6s, 6p-zero and 5d-zero, four pi from the metal 6p and 5d components with unit angular momentum, and two delta from the 5d components with angular momentum two, distributed as 4a1, 2b1, 2b2 and 1a2 and written [4221] in the C2v irreducible representations. The chlorine valence occupied orbitals are treated as inactive at the CASSCF level. The number of active electrons is not stated.
active_space_protocol: A single fixed space, with the sensitivity test carried out instead on the number of electrons correlated in the subsequent configuration interaction: 16 valence electrons with 44 frozen including the metal f shell, against 22 with the fourteen f electrons freed. The larger treatment was adopted because the f shell appears as the highest valence shell of the metal cation in the active natural orbitals.
nroots_per_mult: twenty states in total below 43000 wavenumbers, with thirty-three spin-orbit components computed for the first fifteen; the five highest were excluded from the spin-orbit treatment because they correlate with higher states not included
electronic_structure_description: Ground term: X 1Sigma+. Around the equilibrium distance the molecule is treated as ionic, Lu+Cl-, with the molecular states correlating to the lowest levels of the cation plus chloride; the ionization potential of the metal is 5.43 eV and the electron affinity of chlorine 3.6135 eV, and the measured dissociation energy is 31800 wavenumbers. With 22 electrons correlated the ground state has an equilibrium distance of 2.38 Angstrom, a harmonic frequency of 348 wavenumbers and an anharmonicity of 1.07, against measured values of 2.37 and 337 and a density functional prediction of 2.38 and 329. The twenty states comprise (1-3)1Sigma+, (1-3)1Pi, (1-4)3Pi, (1)3Sigma+, (1,2)1Delta, (1,2)3Delta, (1,2)3Sigma-, (1)1Phi, (1)3Phi and (1)1Gamma. Selected excitation energies with 22 against 16 electrons correlated, in wavenumbers: (1)3Delta 13223 against 13792, (1)3Pi 14573 against 14922, (1)3Sigma+ 15831 against 16005, (1)1Delta 17491 against 17895, (1)1Pi 19803 against 20322 with an observed 20844, (2)1Sigma+ 22210 against 22314 with an observed 21828, (1)3Sigma- 33777 against 34747, (3)3Pi 33876 against 34769 and (2)1Pi 34491 against 34734.
