Two complete sets of spectroscopic constants are reported for the same twenty states, one correlating 16 valence electrons with 44 frozen including the metal f shell, the other correlating 22 by unfreezing the fourteen f electrons. The reason given for preferring the larger treatment is structural rather than energetic: in the active natural orbitals the f shell comes out as the highest valence shell of the metal cation, so freezing it means freezing orbitals that the calculation itself places in the valence region. That is a good diagnostic to borrow -- let the natural orbitals, not the formal shell labels, decide what counts as core. The difference is modest for the lower states and grows with excitation energy: the ground state bond length shifts by 0.008 Angstrom and its harmonic frequency by about 10 wavenumbers, the first excited triplet moves 569 wavenumbers, and the higher states move 900 to 1000. More consequential than any single shift is that the state ordering changes. Three states near 34000 wavenumbers -- the first 3Sigma-minus, the third 3Pi and the second 1Pi -- are spread over 714 wavenumbers in that order with 22 electrons correlated, but with 16 they collapse into a 35-wavenumber cluster with the 1Pi state lowest instead of highest. Freezing the f shell therefore does not merely shift a dense manifold, it inverts it and makes three well-separated states look near-degenerate, which would change any assignment of an observed band in that region. The f shell matters even more for the relativistic part, and the authors act on this: spin-orbit coupling was computed only in the 22-electron treatment, on the explicit ground that the f orbital plays an important role in the spin-orbit interaction, so the 16-electron results exist only as a correlation-space comparison and were never carried through to the thirty-three spin-orbit components. The active space itself is specified by composition rather than by counts: three sigma orbitals from the metal 6s, 6p-zero and 5d-zero, four pi from 6p and 5d with unit angular momentum, and two delta from 5d with angular momentum two, distributed as 4a1, 2b1, 2b2 and 1a2 in the reduced symmetry group. The chlorine valence occupied orbitals are deliberately left inactive at the CASSCF stage and only enter through the subsequent configuration interaction, which is a defensible split for a molecule the authors treat as ionic, but it means the ligand contribution to any state with charge-transfer character is described at a lower level than the metal contribution. The number of active electrons is never stated. A separate validation worth noting is that the atomic ion levels were computed first with the same pseudopotential and compared against measured levels before any molecular work, so the basis and core choice are checked against a known spectrum rather than assumed.

electronic_structure_description: The ground state is 91 percent a single determinant with a dipole moment of 14.9 debye and all six active orbital occupations within 0.09 of integer values (1.96, 1.93, 1.91, 0.09, 0.03, 0.07). The first excited state, 1A', is 81 percent one determinant describing transfer of a pi electron from the naphthyl 9a'' orbital into the antibonding 15a'' on the pyridinium, with a second determinant at 8 percent, a dipole moment of 3.4 debye and occupations of 1.94, 1.40, 1.90, 0.10, 0.60, 0.06. The second excited state, 2A', has a leading determinant of only 64 percent plus a 23 percent contribution describing a pi to pi* excitation between the naphthyl 9a'' and 16a'' orbitals that localizes positive charge on the amino nitrogen; its dipole moment is 3.9 debye and two of its occupations are 1.04 and 0.98, close to half filled. Perturbatively corrected excitation energies in eV are 2.67 vertical, 2.60 for the 0-0 transition and 2.56 in emission for the first state, and 3.63, 3.41 and 3.14 for the second; a range-separated functional gives 2.87, 2.80, 2.74 and 3.59, 3.42, 3.13.
Other: The space is chosen by a documented procedure rather than by inspection, which is the part worth reusing. A restricted active space calculation was run first over the entire pi system -- twenty electrons in nineteen orbitals -- using only the first and third subspaces and allowing single and double excitations from the occupied into the virtual orbitals, and the six-electron six-orbital space used for all subsequent work was read off from that. So the full pi manifold is surveyed cheaply once, and the expensive complete treatment is then confined to the six orbitals the survey identifies as carrying the transitions. The resulting space is specified orbital by orbital, as the 8a'', 9a'', 10a'', 12a'', 15a'' and 16a'' orbitals, and it spans both ends of the chromophore, which matters because both excitations of interest are charge transfers between them. Whether six orbitals suffice is then answered from the wave functions rather than asserted. The ground state is 91 percent a single determinant, so the paper concludes a single-reference description is adequate for it. The first excited state is 81 percent one determinant, a clean transfer of a pi electron from the naphthyl 9a'' orbital into the antibonding 15a'' localized on the pyridinium, with a second determinant at 8 percent. The second excited state is the one that justifies the multiconfigurational treatment: its leading determinant carries only 64 percent, and a second at 23 percent describes a separate pi to pi* excitation within the naphthyl unit that moves positive charge from the ring onto the amino nitrogen. A 23 percent secondary determinant is well outside what a single-reference method represents, and it is a physically different charge rearrangement, not a correction to the first. The occupation numbers tell the same story in a form independent of the determinant basis: in the second excited state two active orbitals sit at 1.04 and 0.98 electrons, almost exactly half-filled, whereas in the first excited state the corresponding pair is 1.40 and 0.60 and in the ground state all six are within 0.09 of integer occupancy. Reporting both the configuration weights and the occupation numbers, which are not interchangeable diagnostics, is what makes the adequacy claim checkable here. The active space also predicts structural consequences that are then verified: the bond length changes between ground and excited states follow the pattern the determinants imply, with the N-H bond lengthening on population of the pyridinium antibonding orbital and the naphthyl bonds lengthening as density leaves the bonding pi orbitals. Finally the multiconfigurational result is used as the reference against which a much cheaper method is validated for the production work: a range-separated functional agrees with the perturbatively corrected excitation energies to an average of 0.11 eV and at worst 0.20, while the plain functional is wrong by more than 1 eV for each state because it cannot describe charge transfer. That is the correct division of labour -- the small correlated calculation certifies the method that is then applied across a hundred configurational snapshots -- but it also means every environment-dependent number in the paper rests on the cheaper method, with the active space entering only through this one gas-phase calibration on a truncated model.

electronic_structure_description: A closed-shell planar molecule of A-prime symmetry, the reference point for all relative energies. Its pyrolysis begins by breaking the ring nitrogen-oxygen bond to give a carbonylvinylnitrene. Because the lowest singlet of that nitrene is of A-double-prime symmetry, having one electron in a sigma and one in a pi orbital, the reaction cannot proceed adiabatically in planar symmetry and a conical intersection must be circumvented by out-of-plane distortion. The transition state for this step is accordingly slightly nonplanar with a wave function mixing closed- and open-shell configurations, and the barrier is just under 50 kcal/mol.
Other: This is one of the clearest published treatments of active space consistency along a reaction path, and the selection criterion is stated as a principle: in studies of chemical reactions it is very important to choose a space containing all the orbitals and electrons that change along the considered pathways, both to avoid discontinuities in the potential surfaces and to make energies comparable. Eight electrons in seven orbitals proved sufficient -- provided it contained the right orbitals, which is where the interest lies, because the composition of that fixed-size space changes identity three times along the path. In the heterocyclic reactant it is the five pi and pi* orbitals holding the six pi electrons plus the sigma and sigma* of the ring N-O bond. In the vinylnitrenes those N-O orbitals are replaced by the singly occupied in-plane p orbital on nitrogen and the in-plane p lone pair on oxygen. In the azirine one of the pi/pi* pairs turns into the sigma and sigma* of the newly formed C-N bond. Same seven slots throughout, three different sets of orbitals, chosen so that what enters and leaves the space is exactly what the chemistry changes. Because the reactions pass between open- and closed-shell singlet states, state-averaged orbitals were used throughout; a space optimized for either state alone would not permit a smooth passage. The honesty about where the scheme fails is what makes this worth recording in full. No compatible space could be found for four of the primary products, so the vinylnitrene space was used for their transition states instead, justified by those transition states being very early since the reactions are exothermic by 55 to 70 kcal/mol, and adopted explicitly because a consistent space was needed for comparability. The cost is stated: that space does not contain the sigma and sigma* orbitals of the reactive X-H bonds being broken, because those could not be included in the vinylnitrenes. Separately, the transition states leading out of the azirine to the nitrile ylide and to another product required the sigma and sigma* of the ring C-C bond rather than of the C-N bond, a genuinely incompatible space, and the authors' response was to recompute the azirine geometry and energy in that second space as well so that all the relative energies remain comparable. Recomputing a common reference in each of two incompatible spaces is the correct fix and is almost never done. The multiconfigurational treatment also overturns two single-reference results. A transition state found at the density functional level for a direct concerted rearrangement, with a stable wave function, could not be located at all with the active space -- attempts either failed or collapsed onto the open-shell transition state leading elsewhere -- from which the authors conclude that the lower-lying concerted path is an artifact of constraining the system to the closed-shell surface. At another transition state the closed-shell reference is outright unstable, and the multiconfigurational wave function confirms significant open-shell character. Conversely the space corrects a prior multiconfigurational result too: on an earlier four-electron four-orbital surface the parent vinylnitrene was reported as a transition state for azirine interconversion, whereas with the larger consistent space three of the four planar structures are shallow minima. A symmetry argument constrains everything: the closed-shell species are of A-prime symmetry while the lowest singlet nitrene has one electron in a sigma and one in a pi orbital and is therefore A-double-prime, so the reaction cannot proceed adiabatically in planar symmetry and a conical intersection must be circumvented by out-of-plane distortion. The computed transition state is indeed slightly nonplanar with a wave function mixing closed- and open-shell configurations, while the transition state for the lowest hydrogen shift is almost planar and solidly closed shell, meaning the surface crossing has already happened before it is reached. One caution for anyone reusing the numbers: the authors note that relative energies of closed-shell and open-shell transition states are affected to surprisingly different extents by the Davidson correction for quadruple excitations, defer the analysis of why to a separate paper, and state that their chemical conclusions do not depend on which set is used.

ligand_set: A tert-butyl substituted bipyridine-phosphine ligand and two carbonyls
geometry_source: Optimized with the M06 functional and a Stuttgart-Dresden effective core potential on the metal with a double-zeta plus polarization basis on main group elements; geometries of the later complexes were taken from previous studies
method: CASSCF followed by n-electron valence state perturbation theory, computed at density functional geometries and used as the reference against which a large set of density functionals is assessed; the resolution of identity chain of spheres approximation was used for efficiency
software: ORCA 2.9.0 for the multiconfigurational and double-hybrid calculations; GAUSSIAN09 revisions C.01 and D.01 for the hybrid density functional work
relativistic_treatment: An effective core potential on second and third row transition metals, included in the def2 basis sets
active_space_orbital_description: Twelve electrons in twelve orbitals, obtained by the occupancy-pruning procedure from an initial space of metal d natural orbitals.
active_space_protocol: Second-order perturbation theory natural orbitals were generated as the CASSCF guess, the natural orbitals containing transition metal d functions were selected as the initial active space, and after preliminary CASSCF calculations the space was reduced by removing orbitals with occupancies very close to 2 or 0, on the grounds that excitations to or from such orbitals do not contribute to the wave function and their presence can cause convergence problems. Singlet, triplet and quintet states, or doublet, quartet and sextet where appropriate, were considered.
electronic_structure_description: The closed-shell configuration dominates the singlet at nearly 80 percent weight, with the second most important configuration also closed shell, so the complex is best described as a closed-shell singlet with a zerovalent iron centre and a neutral bipyridine-type ligand. The highest occupied orbital holds close to two electrons and is a bonding metal-ligand combination, that is, metal-to-ligand backbonding of the kind familiar from transition metal carbonyls. The shortening of the inter-ring carbon-carbon bond, sometimes read as evidence for electron transfer, is attributed here to partial occupation of an orbital with bonding character across that bond. A biradical description is also argued to be chemically implausible, since it would require an iron(I) centre alongside a radical anion that would rather lose its extra electron.
Other: The active space here is not chosen by chemical intuition but produced by a stated, repeatable procedure, and that procedure is the paper's most transferable content. Second-order perturbation theory natural orbitals are generated first as the CASSCF guess; the natural orbitals carrying transition metal d character are taken as the initial space; preliminary CASSCF calculations are run; and the space is then pruned by removing orbitals whose CASSCF occupancies come out very close to 2 or 0. The justification given is twofold and worth separating: occupancies at the integer limits mean excitation to or from those orbitals does not contribute to the wave function, so they are useless, and keeping them can cause convergence problems, so they are worse than useless. Starting large and shrinking on an occupancy criterion is the opposite of the usual practice of starting from a chemically chosen minimum and enlarging, and it leaves an audit trail -- the final spaces, from eight to twelve orbitals across ten complexes, are reported as outputs of the procedure rather than as choices. The spaces then answer a question that formal electron counting cannot: whether a bipyridine ligand is innocent or is present as a radical anion. The verdict differs across the series and is read off the configuration state function weights and orbital occupancies rather than from geometry. Where one closed-shell configuration dominates at nearly 80 percent, with the frontier orbital holding close to two electrons, the ligand is neutral and the shortening of the inter-ring bond comes from metal-to-ligand backbonding. Where two closed-shell configurations share the wave function at 55 to 65 and 25 to 35 percent, two orbitals emerge at occupancy near one and the ground state is an open-shell singlet with a genuine radical anion. Where three configurations contribute comparably, including one with five unpaired electrons, the description is a radical anion on a metal centre one oxidation state above the closed-shell alternative. A pair of orbitals at occupancy one, one bonding and one antibonding, is explicitly interpreted as equivalent to breaking the mixing between them, which is a compact way of stating what a biradical is in orbital terms. This also supplies a warning about a widely used structural diagnostic. The inter-ring bond shortens on coordination, and that shortening has been read as evidence of electron transfer to the ligand; the active orbitals show it can equally arise from partial occupation of an orbital with bonding character across that bond, so the same geometric signature is produced by backbonding without any electron transfer. The authors note prior work reaching the same conclusion for ruthenium complexes, and their own comparison shows the bond length is not a reliable oxidation state indicator. A chemical plausibility argument is used alongside the wave function analysis: for the iron carbonyl complexes a biradical description would require a metal in an unfavourable oxidation state alongside a radical anion that would rather give up its extra electron, so both fragments are better off reverting to a neutral ligand on a zerovalent metal. Two practical caveats attach to the numbers. The perturbative correction can reverse the qualitative assignment relative to bare CASSCF for at least one complex in this set, so the ligand innocence verdict is not a property of the space alone. And the two largest complexes were run in a double-zeta rather than triple-zeta basis purely because of size, so their spaces are compared against the others at unequal basis quality.

electronic_structure_description: The isolated chromophore, used as the reference case in which only the pi-pi* radiative pathway is available and no charge-transfer quenching channel exists. Its oscillator strength for the pi-pi* absorption is three to fifteen times smaller than that of the zinc complex.
Other: Three different active spaces are used across one series of closely related molecules -- twelve electrons in nine orbitals for the free ligand, twelve in ten for the closed-shell metal complexes, and eleven in nine for the copper complex -- and the pattern of change is itself informative. Adding a closed-shell metal ion adds one orbital while leaving the electron count alone, consistent with a metal acceptor orbital entering the space without contributing electrons; the copper complex has one fewer electron and one fewer orbital, reflecting its open-shell doublet manifold. No space-size test is reported and the orbital compositions are never enumerated, so the reader has counts but not contents. The consequence is that the comparison the paper rests on -- why the fluorescence turns on for one metal and stays off for another -- is drawn across calculations in spaces of different size, and nothing establishes that a common space would give the same relative ordering. The most interesting methodological move is that a failure to converge is read as a chemical result rather than as a technical problem. For the zinc complex, several attempts to optimize the charge-transfer state were unsuccessful, and the authors interpret this as evidence that promoting an electron from the nitrogen lone pair into the pi* manifold becomes extremely difficult once the metal-nitrogen coordination bond is strong enough, concluding that the competing nonradiative channel is completely closed. That inference is chemically reasonable and matches the twelve-fold experimental increase in emission intensity, but it is worth flagging as a distinct class of evidence: an optimization that will not converge in a particular active space is not the same as a state that does not exist, and the argument would be stronger with a space in which the state could be located and shown to lie high. The spaces do deliver the things multiconfigurational treatment is needed for. Conical intersections are located rather than inferred, including one at a nitrogen-carbon distance of 2.258 Angstrom lying 3.04 eV above the ground state zero point, from which the authors compute that about 63 percent of the photon energy has gone into bond fission. The character of the wave function is tracked along the path and changes qualitatively: the Franck-Condon region of the charge-transfer state is a zwitterionic radical configuration, while at the intersection one unpaired electron sits in the nitrogen-carbon sigma* orbital and the structure is a typical diradical, with roughly 0.65 electron transferring back between the two molecular fragments along the way. A diradical intersection reached from a zwitterionic Franck-Condon point is exactly the situation where a single-reference excited-state method would fail, and the changing configurational character along one coordinate is also a reminder that a space adequate at the vertical geometry need not remain so. Dynamical correlation is added by second-order perturbation theory on a five-root state-averaged reference, so all five states share one set of orbitals; for the copper complex, where four states including metal d-d and ligand pi-pi* excitations spanning 1.12 to 4.93 eV must be described together, that is a demanding compromise for a nine-orbital space.

electronic_structure_description: Ground term: quintet 5A. Relative energies in kcal/mol at third order, second order and CASSCF: the lowest singlet at 43.88, 54.41 and 60.34, the lowest triplet at 27.56, 35.66 and 41.83. Leading determinant coefficients in the natural orbital basis are 0.95 for the singlet, 0.95 for the triplet and 1.00 for the quintet. Both excited spin states are close to single-determinantal.
Other: A single four-electron four-orbital metal d space serves five of the six complexes in this isovalent series, and the sixth breaks it -- which is the finding worth carrying, because the six differ only in metal and formal charge and nothing about the ligand changes. For the most positively charged complex the metal d orbital energies fall relative to two three-centre two-electron pi orbitals of the ligand backbone, so those orbitals stop being doubly occupied and must enter the space, giving eight electrons in six orbitals. In every other complex those same ligand orbitals remain closed and can be left out. So the required space is set by where the metal d manifold sits relative to specific ligand orbitals, which moves with formal oxidation state, and a space validated on five members of a series can fail on the sixth for a reason invisible in the connectivity. The space selection itself is documented and repeatable: configuration interaction natural orbitals in a minimal basis provide starting orbitals, large configuration interaction calculations within a candidate space are run, and the final active spaces are chosen by examining which orbitals are most important in that vector. State averaging over two singlets and two triplets was used because the low-lying singlet and triplet states are nearly degenerate; optimizing either alone would bias the comparison the paper exists to make. The wave function analysis then does something the energies alone cannot. Every quintet ground state except one is a pure single determinant, coefficient 1.00, from which the authors conclude single-reference methods should describe those ground states properly. The singlets and triplets are not: leading coefficients run from 0.54 to 0.97, and for the chromium complex the lowest singlet needs four determinants with coefficients 0.56, -0.54, -0.38 and 0.25 before the open-shell terms even begin. A leading coefficient of 0.56 against a second at -0.54 is a two-configuration state in all but name. The exception is the ruthenium complex, whose quintet leading coefficient is only 0.894 and whose singlet is 0.47, so the authors explicitly question whether single-reference methods can characterize its ground state at all. That flag matters because it is the one complex where the ground state is not the quintet. The correlation treatment moves the numbers far more than the state ordering does, and unevenly. For the iron complex the singlet lies 71.84 kcal/mol above the quintet at CASSCF, 58.52 at second order and 28.17 at third order -- a 44 kcal/mol collapse, meaning the CASSCF gap on this space is wrong by more than a factor of two. For chromium the third-order triplet gap of 51.41 sits well below the second-order 78.02, while the singlet gaps at the two orders agree to 1.3 kcal/mol; so the perturbation series is not uniformly converged even within one complex. Anyone quoting one of these numbers needs the order it came from. Two technical caveats attach to the reference values. Different numbers of orbitals were frozen at the two perturbation orders, 18 against 27, and the full third-order energies are estimates formed by adding the difference between the two orders at the more restrictive freezing to the less restricted second-order energy. And the whole study uses a model complex with the axial ligand sites left empty, deliberately, to isolate the metal-salen interaction -- so these spaces describe a four-coordinate fragment rather than the catalyst.
reference_short: Takatani, Sears & Sherrill, J. Phys. Chem. A 2010, 114, 11714
notes: Along with the iron complex, one of the cases where high leading coefficients coexist with large corrections from the perturbation treatment.

electronic_structure_description: Ground term: X 1Ag. The lowest excited state is a bright B2u state, the short-axis-polarized 1La, at 2.31 eV, well described by a single configuration involving one electron transfer between two natural orbitals. The second is dark, of Ag symmetry, at 2.88 eV, and is multiconfigurational with dominant configuration state functions involving double excitations. The third is bright, 1B3u, the long-axis-polarized 1Lb, at 3.13 eV, described by two single-excitation configurations. The bright state agrees closely with the measured gas-phase 0-0 transition at 2.31 eV and with absorption maxima in neon (2.28), argon (2.21) and krypton (2.19) matrices, and with values of 2.37 and 3.12 eV derived from solution 0-0 transitions.
Other: The active space question is confronted directly rather than assumed away, and the answer is qualified by which states you want. The authors state the ideal -- the full pi system in the CASSCF -- concede it is computationally intractable, and note the opposite failure mode explicitly, that too small a space may lead to numerical and sometimes qualitative inaccuracies. The compromise is four pi orbitals per pentacene unit, described as the minimum set needed to describe the states involved in singlet fission, giving eight electrons in eight orbitals for dimers and twelve in twelve for trimers. That minimum is then calibrated against a much larger reference on the monomer, fourteen electrons in fourteen pi-like orbitals with a triple-zeta atomic natural orbital basis, and separately stress-tested by varying the space size on the herringbone dimer. The verdict is stated with a scope limit that is the most useful sentence in the paper: affordable active spaces describe the lowest-lying excited states within the typical accuracy of the method, about 0.2 eV, while higher lying states and scans of their potential energy surfaces may in some cases require significantly larger spaces. So the same space is adequate for a vertical excitation and potentially inadequate for the surface that excitation moves on -- exactly the distinction a singlet fission study needs, since its mechanism turns on geometry reorganization. The authors also warn that monomer results do not necessarily extrapolate to oligomers, particularly for intermolecular charge-transfer states, and rather than assume otherwise they bring in an independent many-body Green's function method to cross-check the eight-orbital dimer results. That cross-check reveals precisely where each method fails, and the failures are complementary. The Green's function approach misassigns the monomer's second excited state, giving a state of different symmetry, because the reference state is dominated by doubly excited configurations that lie beyond its scope; the multiexciton state central to singlet fission is likewise simply absent from it in the dimer. Conversely it captures the delocalization of charge-transfer states that a small-space treatment on a finite cluster handles less well, and the two methods disagree by about 0.3 eV on those states and on which pairs are near-degenerate. A state built from double excitations is the one thing the cheaper method cannot see, and it is the state the whole phenomenon depends on -- the clearest possible argument for why a multiconfigurational space is required here and not merely preferred. The wave function composition is tracked quantitatively across structures rather than just labelled: the leading multiexciton configuration carries 61 percent weight in the herringbone dimer against 77 percent in the parallel dimer, so the same nominal state is substantially more mixed in one packing than the other. And the energetic conclusion depends on cluster size in a way the space does not: bright states are stabilized as the system grows while the multiexciton state is far less sensitive, so the gap between them widens from about 0.1 eV in dimers to 0.3 to 0.7 eV in trimers. A mechanism judged nearly barrierless on a dimer therefore requires significant geometry reorganization on a trimer, which means the cluster model, not the active space, is the limiting approximation for that conclusion. Two technical settings are stated and worth carrying: the zeroth-order Hamiltonian uses the standard 0.25 atomic unit shift and an imaginary level shift of 0.1 atomic units guards against intruder states; oscillator strengths combine CASSCF transition dipole moments with perturbatively corrected energy differences.
reference_short: Coto, Sharifzadeh, Neaton & Thoss, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2015, 11, 147
notes: The Green's function method assigns a B1g state as the second excited state instead of the Ag state found here, a difference traced to its known inability to describe doubly excited configurations. The computed third state differs by about 0.5 eV from an earlier matrix assignment, which the authors tentatively reassign to a higher B3u state. Coupled cluster values of 2.35 and 3.27 eV for the two bright states are quoted for comparison.

geometry_source: Singlet equilibrium structures optimized with multireference configuration interaction and a core-valence quadruple-zeta basis; triplet structures at all-electron CCSD(T) with the same basis
method: CASSCF with CASPT2 and multireference configuration interaction with single and double excitations plus the Davidson correction for the singlet states; unrestricted Hartree-Fock, perturbation theory and coupled cluster up to full quadruple excitations for the triplets, with relative energies obtained by focal point analysis extrapolated to the complete basis set limit
software: MOLPRO and CFOUR, with the MRCC program interfaced to MOLPRO for the highest coupled cluster excitations
basis_set: Correlation-consistent polarized core-valence sets cc-pCVXZ with X = D, T, Q and 5, extrapolated to the complete basis set limit; equilibrium structures at the cc-pCVQZ level
active_space_orbital_description: Twelve electrons in twelve orbitals, comprising the core 1s and valence 2s and 2p shells of beryllium and carbon together with the 1s shells of the hydrogen atoms; the core shells are therefore inside the active space rather than frozen. Canonical orbitals obtained by diagonalizing the effective Fock operator.
active_space_protocol: A single space applied to all singlet states of both isomers and the connecting transition state, with no size variation. Triplet states were treated by single-reference methods, justified by agreement to within 0.6 kcal/mol between multireference configuration interaction and coupled cluster with perturbative triples across them; all electrons were correlated in all computations.
electronic_structure_description: Ground term: 3B1, the global minimum of the system and experimentally unknown. Its bonding is described by a correlation diagram from singlet beryllium and triplet methylene fragments, with the HCH angle contracting from 132 degrees in free triplet methylene to 111 degrees here. The beryllium-carbon bond dissociation energy is 62.1 kcal/mol from focal point analysis at the complete basis set limit, built from an unrestricted Hartree-Fock value of 56.98 with increments of +15.17 at second order, -10.06 at coupled cluster singles and doubles, +2.18 for perturbative triples and negligible contributions beyond, then corrected by -3.17 for zero-point energy, +0.86 for core correlation and -0.01 for the diagonal Born-Oppenheimer correction. The lowest excited state is the open-shell 1B1 singlet, an antisymmetric combination of two equally important determinants, at 5.0, 4.6 and 4.9 kcal/mol at the CASSCF, second-order and configuration-interaction levels. The 1A1 state follows with a dominant closed-shell configuration, at 20.8, 18.5 and 16.8 kcal/mol, giving an 11.9 kcal/mol separation between the two singlets.
Other: One twelve-electron twelve-orbital space serves every state in this study, and because five levels of theory are tabulated on a common basis the error of the bare space can be read off state by state -- with the striking result that it ranges from essentially zero to more than 20 kcal/mol on the same orbitals. The space is unusual in composition: it includes the 1s core shells of beryllium and carbon alongside the 2s and 2p valence shells and the hydrogen 1s orbitals, so core correlation is treated variationally inside the space rather than left to the perturbative or coupled cluster treatment. For a system this small that is affordable, and it matters, since the separate core correction computed elsewhere in the paper runs to about 0.9 kcal/mol on bond energies. Now the state dependence. For the lowest excited singlet of the carbene, CASSCF gives 5.0 kcal/mol against 4.6 at second order and 4.9 with configuration interaction and the Davidson correction -- agreement to within a tenth of a kcal/mol, and one would conclude the space is complete. For the second singlet the same space gives 20.8 against 16.8, an error of 4. For the ground state of the linear isomer it gives 21.3 against 7.3, and coupled cluster values of 5.8 and 6.7 corroborate the corrected number: the bare space overestimates a key isomerization energy by a factor of three, roughly 14 kcal/mol. Worst of all is the highest singlet of the linear isomer, 51.0 against 30.0, a 21 kcal/mol error. The transition state, by contrast, is off by only 3.7. So on one fixed space the error is not a roughly constant offset that would cancel in relative energies -- it varies by more than 20 kcal/mol between states, which means no amount of error cancellation rescues a CASSCF-only energy ordering here. The qualitative consequence is visible in the same table. The two lowest excited states of the linear isomer are essentially degenerate once dynamical correlation is included, 30.4 and 30.6 at second order and 30.0 for both with configuration interaction, as their two-determinant pi squared origin would suggest. At the CASSCF level they are split by 13 kcal/mol, 37.9 against 51.0. A space that describes the static correlation of both states correctly, and produces the right two-determinant wave functions, still gets their relative energies badly wrong; the near-degeneracy is restored entirely by correlation outside the space. That is a useful counterexample to the intuition that degeneracies are the province of the active space and quantitative shifts the province of dynamical correlation. The wave function analysis is what makes the multireference treatment necessary rather than merely available. The lowest excited singlet is written explicitly as an antisymmetric combination of two equally important determinants, and the two excited states of the linear isomer likewise arise as two-determinant functions from a pi squared configuration -- objects no single reference can represent. The triplets, by contrast, are well behaved: configuration interaction with the Davidson correction and coupled cluster with perturbative triples differ by at most 0.6 kcal/mol across them, which is why the triplet surface is handled entirely by single-reference methods and a focal point analysis extrapolated to the basis set limit, while the multiconfigurational machinery is reserved for the singlets. Splitting the work by spin state according to which states actually need a multiconfigurational reference, and demonstrating rather than assuming that the triplets do not, is cleaner practice than applying one method throughout. One consequence worth carrying: without the zero-point correction the lowest excited singlet of the carbene falls below the experimentally observed ground state of the linear isomer, so which species is the relevant low-lying one depends on a correction outside the electronic structure entirely.

geometry_source: Initial geometries and velocities sampled from a harmonic Wigner distribution over all 30 degrees of freedom (500 phase space points) about the neutral equilibrium structure, itself optimized at B3LYP/6-31G*; an additional unsampled trajectory starts at that structure with no kinetic energy
method: State-averaged CASSCF providing forces for an Ehrenfest mean-field treatment in which the nuclei move classically by Newton's equations and the electrons are propagated by the time-dependent Schroedinger equation, using a Hessian-based predictor-corrector algorithm with a mass-weighted step of 0.0025 amu^(1/2) bohr, about 0.04 femtoseconds
software: A development version of Gaussian, revision H.10; the Newton-X package for the Wigner sampling
active_space_orbital_description: The six pi orbitals of the aromatic ring, holding the five electrons remaining after ionization.
active_space_protocol: State averaged over the two lowest cationic states, which are degenerate at the conical intersection and whose coherent superposition is the initial condition being varied. The restriction to two states is justified by the 0.2 eV gap between them at the neutral equilibrium geometry against more than 2 eV to the second excited state.
nroots_per_mult: the two lowest cationic states
electronic_structure_description: At the equilibrium geometry of the neutral molecule the two cationic adiabatic states coincide with the quasi-diabatic states: the ground state has quinoid character and the first excited state antiquinoid character, separated by 0.2 eV, with more than 2 eV to the next state. Around the conical intersection the quinoid structure is a minimum on the cationic ground state while the antiquinoid structure is a transition state. electronic_structure_description: One of only two stationary points in the study requiring a multiconfigurational treatment, with a spin expectation value of 0.98 against 0.50 or below for all other transition states. Its relative energy of 84.5 kcal/mol is high compared with the rest of the surface, so formation of the trans isomer is not expected except at very high temperatures. Coupled cluster with perturbative triples gives -0.6450, -0.3627, 12.5544 and -0.7126, -0.3797, 12.6968 with the valence bases and -0.6435, -0.2162, 12.3522 and -0.7191, -0.3011, 12.4477 with the core-valence ones. The best multireference values are 5 percent below and 37 percent above the measured gas-phase couplings for the terminal and central nitrogens; the corresponding coupled cluster values are 7.4 percent below and 11.8 percent above and agree most closely with experiment. Both multireference methods correctly place the terminal nitrogen coupling above the central one, as observed. An oxygen coupling of 12.4 plus or minus 1.2 MHz was estimated from relaxation data assuming a terminal nitrogen value of 0.774 MHz, against 12.92 MHz derived another way.
Other: The property computed here -- the electric field gradient at each nucleus -- is a one-electron expectation value close to the nucleus rather than an energy difference, and that changes what the active space is good for. The space is essentially full valence, sixteen electrons in twelve orbitals with the three core 1s orbitals excluded, so there is no orbital selection judgement to question; what the tables expose instead is how far such a space gets on its own, and the answer depends sharply on which nucleus is asked about. For the oxygen the CASSCF and configuration interaction values agree to within about 1 percent across every basis, 12.39 against 12.37 for one pairing and 12.27 against 12.40 for another, so the bare space is adequate there. For the central nitrogen it is not: adding configuration interaction on the same reference moves the value from -0.6449 to -0.4221 with one basis, a 35 percent change, and from -0.5680 to -0.3689 with another, again about 35 percent. Basis set effects are of the same size as the correlation effects and do not converge monotonically, which compounds the problem. For the central nitrogen the CASSCF value runs -0.6449, -0.6453, -0.3882 and -0.5680 across the four bases, so switching from a valence to a core-valence set at triple zeta changes it by 40 percent and going to quadruple zeta moves it back most of the way. This matters because the core 1s orbitals are frozen in every one of these calculations: the field gradient is a nuclear-region property, the core is where the density is largest, and it is being described entirely by the basis rather than by the correlated wave function. A space that excludes the core is not obviously the right space for a core-sensitive observable, and the erratic basis dependence is the symptom. Against experiment the multireference route wins at one site and loses badly at the other -- the best configuration interaction values are 5 percent low for the terminal nitrogen and 37 percent high for the central one -- while the single-reference coupled cluster treatment with perturbative triples, correlating all electrons, comes out 7.4 percent low and 11.8 percent high and is judged the closest overall. electronic_structure_description: The measured axial zero-field splitting parameter is +9.9(1) wavenumbers with a vanishing rhombic parameter, g values of 2.18 and 1.91, and no observed slow relaxation without a field. The model calculation gives +12.3 wavenumbers, in good agreement. This is one of the three complexes where the admixture of excited determinants into the lowest spin-orbit eigenvector stays below 20 percent and the lowest transition lies above 1000 wavenumbers.
Other: The space is the minimal one for magnetic anisotropy -- the five metal 3d orbitals holding the six or seven d electrons -- and the value of this paper is that it supplies a working criterion for when that minimum suffices, tested across six complexes with measured anisotropy parameters. Agreement between computed and experimental axial parameters is good for three of the six and poor for the other three, and the split tracks two diagnostics that come out of the same calculation. Where the admixture of excited determinants into the lowest spin-orbit eigenvector stays below 20 percent and the lowest transition lies above 1000 wavenumbers, the computed parameters match: +12.3 against a measured +9.9, and magnitudes of 77.1 and 71.8 against measured 72 and 82. Where the admixture exceeds 20 percent and the lowest transition falls below 500 wavenumbers, the discrepancies are pronounced. Both diagnostics are byproducts of the calculation rather than external quantities, so a practitioner can tell in advance whether a d-only space will do. The reasoning behind them is worth stating: a five-orbital space treats ligand contributions only through the orbital optimization, so when low-lying states mix strongly into the ground state, the physics being omitted from the space is exactly what is now determining the answer. The authors add a caution independent of the space, that when excited states mix in appreciably the computed anisotropy parameters lose their original physical meaning, and a second that when the rhombicity approaches its limiting value of one third -- as it does for all three cobalt complexes -- the sign of the computed axial parameter is vague. A number quoted from such a calculation may be right in magnitude and meaningless in sign, which is why the cobalt values are reported here with plus-or-minus signs. The reason for going multiconfigurational at all is quantified rather than assumed: density functional calculations give nearly identical parameters for every complex of a given metal, from -3.7 to -2.7 wavenumbers across the three iron compounds and +10.6 to +11.3 across the three cobalt ones, which is flatly inconsistent with measured values spanning +9.9 to -33 and -57 to -82 respectively. A method that returns the same answer for chemically distinct complexes is not resolving the chemistry, and the authors cite a systematic study concluding that multireference wave function methods are superior once the parameter leaves the range of plus or minus 10 wavenumbers. Two further design choices are recorded. The orbitals are averaged over the ten and five high-spin roots rather than optimized for a single state, which is what allows one orbital set to serve the whole spin-orbit manifold. And the spin-orbit coupling matrix is built and diagonalized within the active space itself using effective Hamiltonian theory, so the space limits not only the ligand-field description but also the relativistic treatment layered on it. Spin-spin contributions were checked and found below 1 wavenumber. Finally the models are heavily truncated -- bulky silyl and cyclohexyl groups replaced by hydrogens with only the hydrogen positions reoptimized -- so steric influences on the ligand field present in the real compounds are absent from every one of these calculations.

electronic_structure_description: The global minimum conformer, with a carbon-phosphorus bond length of 1.84 Angstrom. Vertical excitation energies for the three lowest singlets are 5.96, 6.19 and 7.49 eV at the CASSCF level, 5.24, 5.34 and 6.36 after the multistate perturbative correction, and 5.11, 5.17 and 5.68 eV by coupled cluster. The first two states lie only 0.1 to 0.2 eV apart depending on the method, while the third is separated by about 1 eV. Along the bond cleavage coordinate the first state is stabilized by 0.41 eV and the second by 0.34 eV before reaching their minima; the two then become nearly degenerate, with a CASSCF gap of 0.004 eV, and a conical intersection between them was located close to the second state's minimum. Charge back transfer through the sigma* orbital drives configuration exchanges that appear as avoided crossings, introducing barriers of 0.303 eV at 2.25 Angstrom in the second state and 0.113 eV at 2.10 Angstrom in the first; optimized within the excited states these become 0.168 and 0.155 eV at 2.05 Angstrom, and net of the excess energy available from vertical excitation they fall to 0.026 and 0.017 eV.
Other: This paper documents the whole chain of compromises that turns an intractable problem into a running calculation, and every link is stated with its cost. The complete precursor would require six pi orbitals from each of five phenyl rings plus the sigma and sigma* of the breaking bond -- thirty-two electrons in thirty-two orbitals, some ten to the eighteen configurations, explicitly out of reach. Two separate reductions follow. First the molecule is cut: three of the five phenyl rings are replaced by hydrogens, chosen so the model still contains one ring on each moiety and therefore preserves the interplay between local excitations and charge transfer between them that the mechanism depends on. That truncation is defended with experimental evidence, namely that replacing a ring on the benzhydryl moiety does not change the observed photochemistry, and its effect on vertical energies is then quantified by stepwise enlargement rather than assumed. Second the space within the model is cut: four of the six pi orbitals per remaining ring are kept, together with the sigma and sigma* of the bond being broken, giving ten electrons in ten orbitals. The two orbitals dropped from each ring are the fully bonding and fully antibonding ones, omitted to keep the space manageable, and the authors say plainly that their influence on relative energies is mostly taken into account by the perturbative correction rather than by the reference. That is an honest statement of where a piece of the physics has been moved to. The remaining orbitals are not arbitrary either: the eight pi orbitals are described as essential for the excitation and the initial charge exchange, while the bond cleavage can only be described with the sigma and sigma* pair, so the space is assembled from what each part of the mechanism requires. Two independent validations are then run, and both address failure modes a single check would miss. The stability of the space is examined along the whole dissociation coordinate, not only at the equilibrium geometry -- necessary because the wave function character changes repeatedly along that coordinate, with configuration exchanges showing up as avoided crossings and the orbital occupations in the dissociation limit differing entirely from those at the Franck-Condon point. And the composition of the space at the Franck-Condon geometry is checked against an independent coupled cluster calculation, confirming that all major contributing configurations to the four lowest excited singlets are inside the chosen space. Verifying which configurations matter with a method that has no active space is the right way to test a space, since it cannot be biased by the choice being tested. The sensitivity of the resulting numbers is large and asymmetric. Vertical excitation energies for the three lowest singlets are 5.96, 6.19 and 7.49 eV at the reference level, 5.24, 5.34 and 6.36 after the perturbative correction, and 5.11, 5.17 and 5.68 by coupled cluster: the correction is about 0.7 eV for the two lowest states but 1.1 eV for the third, and even then the third state remains 0.7 eV above the independent value while the first two land within 0.2. So the space plus correction is balanced for the states that matter and unbalanced for the one above them. The barrier heights that carry the mechanistic conclusion are smaller than any of these discrepancies -- 0.113 and 0.303 eV along the ground state path, 0.155 and 0.168 when optimized in the excited states, and 0.017 and 0.026 eV net once the excess energy from vertical excitation is counted -- which means the conclusion rests on differences an order of magnitude below the absolute accuracy, and is defensible only because the two states being compared share one space and one correction.

electronic_structure_description: The ground state wave function is multireference with three major configuration state functions. The unpaired electron is distributed between a cobalt dyz orbital at 49 percent weight and a corrin pi orbital at 26 percent, so the one-electron oxidation is neither purely metal-centred nor purely ligand-centred. A further 10 percent contribution comes from a quartet configuration corresponding to electron transfer from the sigma(Co-C) bonding orbital to its antibonding counterpart; this partial depopulation of the bonding orbital is offered as the reason for the lowered dissociation energy found in the density functional calculations. The first excited state lies only 0.22 eV higher and has the same multireference character, with the unpaired electron localized mainly on the cobalt dxz orbital and the corrin pi orbital instead. Removal of an electron changes the key geometrical parameters, including the axial bond lengths, only slightly relative to the parent complex.
Other: The paper opens its multiconfigurational section by naming active space selection as one of the most challenging steps, especially for large molecules combining a transition metal with a tetrapyrrolic ligand, and its answer is transferability: the orbitals were chosen following spaces previously established for other cobalamin derivatives, where they had been found appropriate both for excited state benchmarks and for describing cleavage of the metal-carbon bond. Reusing a space validated on related systems for a different question is a reasonable strategy, and here it is backed by a statement that several other spaces were tested before settling on this one -- though the alternatives and what they gave are not reported, so the reader has the conclusion without the evidence. The composition is fully enumerated and follows a recognizable recipe: three cobalt 3d orbitals, the sigma orbital of the axial metal-carbon bond, two corrin pi orbitals, and then a matching set of six correlating orbitals -- cobalt 4d and the lowest corrin pi* -- included specifically for the double shell effect. Four occupied metal d orbitals plus two occupied corrin pi orbitals plus six virtual correlating partners gives eleven electrons in twelve orbitals. Pairing every occupied orbital with a correlating partner is what distinguishes a space built for a transition metal from one built by frontier orbital rank, and it is half the space here. The space earns its keep by producing a result no single determinant could. The ground state is genuinely multireference, with three major configuration state functions: the unpaired electron sits on a cobalt d orbital with 49 percent weight and on a corrin pi orbital with 26 percent, so the oxidation is neither cleanly metal-centred nor cleanly ligand-centred but distributed between them -- exactly the question the paper set out to settle. A further 10 percent comes from a quartet configuration corresponding to transfer from the metal-carbon sigma orbital to its antibonding partner, and the authors connect that partial depopulation directly to the reduced bond strength seen in density functional calculations. A 10 percent contribution of different spin multiplicity is invisible to a single-reference treatment yet is offered as the mechanistic explanation for a measurable weakening, which is a good illustration of what the space buys. The first excited state lies only 0.22 eV above the ground state and has the same multireference character with the unpaired electron on a different d orbital and the corrin pi -- a near-degeneracy of two states differing by which orbital carries the hole, which is the pseudo Jahn-Teller situation the title refers to and which no single-determinant method can represent. State averaging is used for exactly this reason, since orbitals optimized for either state alone would break the near-degeneracy being studied. The main caveat is scope rather than space size. Every multiconfigurational calculation here is a single point on a density functional geometry of a truncated model in which the nucleotide loop and side chains are removed and the lower axial ligand is replaced by imidazole, with a modest split-valence polarized basis. The geometry choice is defended by agreement of the computed axial bond lengths with crystallography for the parent complex, and the truncation by extensive prior use, but neither the geometry nor the basis is at the level of the wave function analysis built on them.

electronic_structure_description: The reference compound of the series, with an experimental band maximum near 236 nm in acetonitrile and absorption beginning at 400 nm. The perturbatively corrected transitions run from a very weak metal-to-carbene charge transfer at 355 nm through a series of carbonyl and carbene charge-transfer states -- 318 nm with oscillator strength 0.160, 313, 310, 289, 285 and 279 nm -- to an intense mixed intraligand and carbonyl charge-transfer band at 250 nm with strength 0.602, then further transitions at 243 and 222 nm. Its lowest allowed excitations have predominantly carbonyl charge-transfer character with a weak carbene admixture, unlike the 2-substituted heterocyclic complexes. Its measured reduction potential is -1.995 V, the most negative of the series, and its computed lowest unoccupied orbital energy of -0.042 eV is the least stable.
Other: One space of twelve electrons in fourteen orbitals is held fixed across a series of seven complexes that differ in carbene substituent and in metal, which makes the comparison across the series clean -- but the number of states averaged is not held fixed, and the paper records what that costs. Fifteen electronic states were computed for every system except one, for which eighteen were needed, and the authors attribute a blue shift in that compound's calculated spectrum directly to the higher number of states: the shift is 'probably due to the higher number of excited states calculated'. That is an explicit admission that the state-averaging manifold, not just the orbital space, sets the answer, and it is the kind of caveat most papers leave unstated. Anyone comparing that compound's spectrum with the others in the series is comparing calculations that share a space but not a state manifold. point_group: C2v, imposed during the constrained optimizations; removing the constraint was tested repeatedly and never gave a different structure
geometry_source: Constrained optimizations in which the distance between the radical centres is frozen and all other degrees of freedom relaxed, scanned from 130 to 240 pm; single-point energies at higher levels computed for many structures along that coordinate
method: CASSCF potential energy curves compared against four density functionals and single-reference methods, with single-point multireference configuration interaction including single and double excitations plus a size-consistency correction, CASPT2, and CCSD(T)
active_space_orbital_description: The bonding and antibonding combination of the two radical lobes, plus the six ring pi orbitals. A smaller space containing only the two radical-lobe combinations was also used throughout for comparison.

electronic_structure_description: A singlet biradical whose two radical centres are separated by a distance that the various methods disagree about. Optimized separations with the triple-zeta basis are 217.4 pm for the eight-orbital space and 218.0 pm for the two-orbital space, falling to 219.7 and 220.0 pm with the double-zeta basis; the associated ring carbon-carbon distances agree between the two spaces to about one picometre. Along the sequence of correlation treatments on the eight-orbital reference the minimum moves to 215 plus or minus 4, then 210 plus or minus 1, then 207 plus or minus 1 pm, while the perturbative treatment places it at 210 pm. Restricted Hartree-Fock gives a qualitatively wrong surface and strongly overemphasizes bonding between the radical centres; even the two-configuration treatment moves the separation 70 pm outward from it. Second-order perturbation theory on a restricted reference gives a reasonable 208.3 pm but too steep a descent, and its reference wave function is externally unstable at larger separations, where the stability matrix acquires one or sometimes two negative eigenvalues.
Other: This is a rare direct test of whether enlarging an active space helps, run on a structural parameter rather than an energy, and the verdict is blunt: enlargement of the active space from two electrons in two orbitals to eight in eight 'does not result in any improvements', while inclusion of dynamic electron correlation is called indispensable. The two-orbital space is the minimum that captures the physics -- the bonding and antibonding combination of the two radical lobes -- and the eight-orbital space adds the six ring pi orbitals on top. The numbers bear the claim out: the equilibrium separation of the radical centres comes out at 218.0 pm with the small space and 217.4 pm with the large one at the same basis, a difference of half a picometre, and the two spaces give bond lengths agreeing to about one picometre throughout. Six extra orbitals for six-tenths of a picometre is as clean a null result as this kind of comparison produces, and it is worth recording because the pi system is exactly what intuition would say to add. What does move the answer is correlation outside the space, and it moves it monotonically: the lowest-energy separation is 215 plus or minus 4 pm at the reference level, 210 plus or minus 1 after configuration interaction on that reference, and 207 plus or minus 1 once the size-consistency correction is applied. Eight picometres of structural change from correlation treatment against half a picometre from doubling the space three times over. The error bars shrink along the same sequence, from 4 pm to 1 pm, so the surface is not merely shifting but becoming better defined -- the authors note the potential energy curve becomes successively flatter with higher excitations, which is why the bare reference locates its minimum so loosely. One further diagnostic deserves carrying. The size-consistency correction lowers the energy by about 85 kcal/mol on average, from which the authors conclude that even the configuration interaction calculation, containing nearly eighteen million contracted configurations, does not cover all important terms. A correction of that magnitude on a variational calculation of that size is a warning that convergence with respect to excitation level is far from reached, and it is stated rather than glossed. The perturbative alternative is flagged for a specific known bias: it suffers systematic errors proportional to the number of unpaired electrons and artificially favours separation of electrons, so its energy rises too steeply as the radical centres approach and it places the minimum at 210 pm. For a biradical, that is exactly the wrong direction of bias for the question being asked. The authors' final position is that the close similarity of curves from three different correlation treatments confirms the conclusions do not depend on the choice, while the basis set remains the open question -- they note that very large bases may be needed given how slowly the electron-electron cusp converges and how strongly dynamic correlation shapes this particular curve.

geometry_source: Optimized directly at the CASSCF level under a Cs symmetry constraint
method: CASSCF potential energy surface scans and geometry optimizations, with second-order multireference Moller-Plesset perturbation corrections computed at several conformations including all valence and virtual orbitals; the conical intersection was optimized in a reduced space and verified in the larger one
software: GAMESS for most calculations; Gaussian 03 for the conical intersection optimization
basis_set: Huzinaga-Dunning double-zeta with polarization functions added on the skeletal carbons (exponent 0.75) and on nitrogen (exponent 0.80), a double-zeta plus polarization quality set; the polarization functions on the skeletal carbons are stated to be necessary to obtain a reasonable intersection
active_space_orbital_description: Ten electrons in the highest five occupied and lowest five unoccupied pi orbitals. These were selected from all seven occupied and lowest seven unoccupied pi orbitals by a configuration interaction calculation including up to triple excitations, discarding the two lowest occupied orbitals whose occupations exceeded 1.98 and the two highest unoccupied whose occupations fell below 0.02, a criterion verified for all sampled conformations.
active_space_protocol: Reduced in two stages from the fourteen-electron fourteen-orbital full pi space, declared desirable but unrealistic for surface scanning. The ten-orbital space serves the scans and the minima; an eight-orbital space, justified by the same preliminary calculation, was used for the conical intersection search and then checked by a ten-orbital calculation at the located geometry confirming the state gap remained small enough. All work is confined to Cs symmetry, so a planar structure has C2v symmetry and nonplanar distortion is allowed only within the mirror plane.
nroots_per_mult: the ground and first excited singlet states
electronic_structure_description: The stable ground state structure is planar with two-fold symmetry and an aromatic bond-equalized skeleton in which all peripheral carbon-carbon distances resemble an aromatic bond length. Its bicyclic skeleton closely resembles that of the parent hydrocarbon, so the nitrile substituent perturbs the ring system only modestly. The molecule carries fourteen pi electrons in total, ten from the bicyclic skeleton and four from the nitrile group.
Other: The space here is arrived at by a two-stage reduction from a stated ideal, with each stage justified numerically rather than by assertion, and the criterion is occupation numbers taken from an independent calculation. The desirable space is named first: fourteen electrons in fourteen orbitals, since the molecule has fourteen pi electrons, ten from the bicyclic skeleton and four from the nitrile group. That is declared unrealistic for scanning potential energy surfaces, so a configuration interaction calculation including up to triple excitations was run over all seven occupied and the lowest seven unoccupied pi orbitals, and the resulting occupation numbers used to prune. The lowest two occupied orbitals came out above 1.98 and the highest two unoccupied below 0.02, so those four were dropped, leaving ten electrons in ten orbitals. The crucial detail is that the occupation criterion was checked for all sampled conformations, not just at equilibrium -- a space pruned on occupation numbers at one geometry can easily fail elsewhere on a surface that runs to a conical intersection, and the authors closed that gap explicitly. Using triple excitations rather than a cheaper diagnostic to generate the occupations is also worth noting, since the orbitals being judged are the ones whose importance a lower-level method would be least able to assess. A second reduction follows for the intersection search alone, down to eight electrons in eight orbitals on the basis of the same preliminary calculation showing that four occupied and four unoccupied pi orbitals suffice where the two states are nearly degenerate. This one is validated after the fact rather than before: the intersection was optimized in the eight-orbital space, then a ten-orbital calculation was performed at that geometry and the gap between the two states confirmed small enough to still be an intersection. Optimizing in a small space and verifying in a larger one at the located point is a cheap and honest way to use a reduced space for a geometry search, and the authors draw the right conclusion, that the larger space would give a similar structure rather than that it would give the same one. The whole scheme rests on a symmetry constraint that is itself a modelling choice: calculations are confined to Cs, so a planar structure has the full two-fold symmetry while nonplanar distortions are permitted only within the mirror plane. Since the central question is whether the intersection is nonplanar in the seven-membered ring, constraining the allowed distortions is a substantive restriction, and the paper devotes an appendix to defending it. A second appendix defends the basis: polarization functions on the skeletal carbons are stated to be necessary to obtain a reasonable intersection at all for this family of molecules, so the intersection geometry is sensitive to the one-electron basis as well as to the space. Dynamical correlation enters only as single-point corrections at several conformations, with all valence and virtual orbitals included in the perturbation, so the surfaces that were scanned and the geometries that were optimized carry no correlation beyond the ten-orbital space.

method: CASSCF potential energy surface scans and geometry optimizations, with second-order multireference Moller-Plesset perturbation corrections computed at several conformations including all valence and virtual orbitals; the conical intersection was optimized in a reduced space and verified in the larger one

active_space_protocol: Reduced in two stages from the fourteen-electron fourteen-orbital full pi space, declared desirable but unrealistic for surface scanning. The ten-orbital space serves the scans and the minima; an eight-orbital space, justified by the same preliminary calculation, was used for the conical intersection search and then checked by a ten-orbital calculation at the located geometry confirming the state gap remained small enough. All work is confined to Cs symmetry, so a planar structure has C2v symmetry and nonplanar distortion is allowed only within the mirror plane.

electronic_structure_description: The point at which radiationless relaxation from the first excited singlet to the ground state occurs. It is reached from the excited state minimum, and the non-adiabatic transition there returns the molecule to the ground state geometry. Whether such intersections in this family take a nonplanar structure in the seven-membered ring, which has been proposed to explain strong oscillations in the observed decay, is the question the study addresses; the authors note that no earlier experimental or computational work supports nonplanar intersections of this kind.
Other: The space here is arrived at by a two-stage reduction from a stated ideal, with each stage justified numerically rather than by assertion, and the criterion is occupation numbers taken from an independent calculation. The desirable space is named first: fourteen electrons in fourteen orbitals, since the molecule has fourteen pi electrons, ten from the bicyclic skeleton and four from the nitrile group. That is declared unrealistic for scanning potential energy surfaces, so a configuration interaction calculation including up to triple excitations was run over all seven occupied and the lowest seven unoccupied pi orbitals, and the resulting occupation numbers used to prune. The lowest two occupied orbitals came out above 1.98 and the highest two unoccupied below 0.02, so those four were dropped, leaving ten electrons in ten orbitals. The crucial detail is that the occupation criterion was checked for all sampled conformations, not just at equilibrium -- a space pruned on occupation numbers at one geometry can easily fail elsewhere on a surface that runs to a conical intersection, and the authors closed that gap explicitly. Using triple excitations rather than a cheaper diagnostic to generate the occupations is also worth noting, since the orbitals being judged are the ones whose importance a lower-level method would be least able to assess. A second reduction follows for the intersection search alone, down to eight electrons in eight orbitals on the basis of the same preliminary calculation showing that four occupied and four unoccupied pi orbitals suffice where the two states are nearly degenerate. This one is validated after the fact rather than before: the intersection was optimized in the eight-orbital space, then a ten-orbital calculation was performed at that geometry and the gap between the two states confirmed small enough to still be an intersection. Optimizing in a small space and verifying in a larger one at the located point is a cheap and honest way to use a reduced space for a geometry search, and the authors draw the right conclusion, that the larger space would give a similar structure rather than that it would give the same one. The whole scheme rests on a symmetry constraint that is itself a modelling choice: calculations are confined to Cs, so a planar structure has the full two-fold symmetry while nonplanar distortions are permitted only within the mirror plane. Since the central question is whether the intersection is nonplanar in the seven-membered ring, constraining the allowed distortions is a substantive restriction, and the paper devotes an appendix to defending it. A second appendix defends the basis: polarization functions on the skeletal carbons are stated to be necessary to obtain a reasonable intersection at all for this family of molecules, so the intersection geometry is sensitive to the one-electron basis as well as to the space. Dynamical correlation enters only as single-point corrections at several conformations, with all valence and virtual orbitals included in the perturbation, so the surfaces that were scanned and the geometries that were optimized carry no correlation beyond the ten-orbital space.

electronic_structure_description: Vertical energies in eV as reference level, single-state and multistate perturbation theory: the covalent 2Ag- state at 4.46, 4.23 and 3.70 with dipole 5.79 D; the 1Bu- state at 5.33, 5.15 and 4.34 with dipole 5.04 D; a further state at 5.95, 5.71 and 5.15; and the ionic 1Bu+ state at 5.97, 3.96 and 5.87 with a dipole of 9.43 D and reference oscillator strength 2.56. The ground state dipole is 4.63 D. After the multistate treatment the state ordering is entirely different from the reference: the lowest excited state at 3.70 eV carries oscillator strength 1.55 and is 0.84 of the reference ionic state mixed with 0.16 of the covalent one, while the second at 4.34 eV is the complementary 0.84/0.16 mixture.
Other: Two separate sensitivities are documented here, and the second is the more alarming. The space itself is twelve electrons in twelve orbitals for both molecules, but it is reached by subtraction rather than selection: two occupied and two virtual pi orbitals were removed from the complete pi space of the smaller compound and four of each from the larger one. The same nominal space therefore covers a substantially different fraction of the conjugated system in the two molecules, so the comparison between them -- which is the point of using the smaller one as a model -- rests on spaces of equal size but unequal completeness. That the excluded orbitals are the outermost of the pi manifold is the usual justification, and the absence of n-pi* character was checked separately with a cheaper method, but the asymmetry is worth knowing before transferring conclusions from the model to the target. The second sensitivity is to the number of states averaged, and the authors state the mechanism plainly: possibly large interactions of the reference wave functions at the multistate level make the results sensitive to how many states enter the state-averaged reference. They tested this at both ground and excited state geometries and settled on eight states, choosing the point at which not only the energies but the configuration state function compositions become stable. Requiring composition stability rather than energy stability alone is the stricter and more meaningful criterion, since energies can plateau while the character of the states is still shifting. The tables show why this matters so much. At the reference level the bright state lies highest of those computed, 5.97 eV for the model compound and 4.62 for the target; after the multistate treatment the lowest excited state falls to 3.70 and 3.10 eV and carries most of the oscillator strength. Single-state perturbation theory puts the bright state at 3.96 and 3.21 eV, a shift of about 2 eV and 1.4 eV from the reference values. More than a shift, the state identities do not survive: the lowest perturbatively modified state is 0.84 of one reference state plus 0.16 of another for the model compound and 0.61 plus 0.36 for the target, so the reference labels are not preserved and the two lowest excited states are strong mixtures of the covalent and ionic characters that the reference keeps separate. The mixing is markedly heavier in the larger molecule, which is also the one whose space is more severely truncated. Anyone reading a state label off a CASSCF calculation on a polyene of this length would be reading the wrong state. The authors are explicit that double excitations play a relevant role here, which is why the cheaper single-reference route is described as inadequate despite the size of the system, and they characterize the final states through natural orbital occupancies of the perturbatively modified functions rather than through the reference configurations. Technical settings carried forward: all valence electrons correlated with the complete Fock matrix in the zeroth-order Hamiltonian, an imaginary level shift of 0.2 against intruder states, carbon and oxygen core orbitals frozen, and transition moments computed from the perturbatively modified functions rather than the raw reference ones.
