active_space_protocol: The same twelve-orbital space is used for both methods being compared, so the only variable is how the configuration expansion within it is truncated. In the generalized scheme the orbitals are partitioned into disconnected subspaces, one per bonding-antibonding pair, with at most two electrons excited within a pair and no interspace excitations - the separated-pairs approximation. This reduces the configuration interaction expansion by a factor of twenty.
nroots_per_mult: one, the ground state
electronic_structure_description: The standard hard case for multiconfigurational methods, owing to its formally sextuple bond and severe static correlation. Dissociation energies from the truncated expansion agree with those from the complete expansion to within 0.16 eV despite the twentyfold reduction in the size of the configuration interaction expansion, and the two potential energy curves track each other closely along their whole length. Changing the IPEA shift moves both curves by similar amounts, since both use the same size of space; a value of 0.45 gives the best agreement with experiment, well away from the usual default of 0.25.
Other: This paper is about the active space itself rather than about a molecule, and the chromium dimer is the hardest available test bed for it. The space is the full valence -- twelve electrons in the twelve orbitals formed from the 4s and 3d orbitals of each atom -- and it is held IDENTICAL between the two methods being compared, so the only variable is how the configuration expansion inside it is truncated. In the generalized scheme each bonding/antibonding pair is confined to its own subspace, only two electrons may be excited within a pair, and NO EXCITATIONS BETWEEN SUBSPACES are allowed -- a separated-pairs approximation. The result is that the configuration expansion shrinks by a FACTOR OF TWENTY while the dissociation energy stays within 0.16 eV of the untruncated result. That ratio is the whole point: for a molecule whose complete space is already at the practical ceiling of about eighteen electrons in eighteen orbitals, a twentyfold reduction is what makes larger spaces reachable at all. Two further observations are more interesting than the headline. First, the authors note that perturbation theory at second order is NOT oversensitive to the reference, since curves from the truncated and untruncated references track each other closely -- a reassuring result, because a correction that amplified reference error would make any truncation scheme useless. Second, and more pointed, they separate two things usually conflated: the IPEA shift moves both curves by similar amounts because the space is the same size in both, and they argue that the need for such a shift is a symptom of a space that is too small rather than a defect of the perturbation theory, so that being able to use larger spaces should make the method LESS EMPIRICAL. The value giving best agreement with experiment for this molecule is 0.45, far from the usual default of 0.25, which is itself a warning about treating that parameter as transferable. The argument is then closed off by a case that cannot be explained by the shift at all: an alternative perturbation theory with no such parameter still depends on the same reference wave function, and going to third order in it introduces large deviations. From this the authors conclude that the inaccuracy lies in the REFERENCE rather than in the zeroth-order Hamiltonian -- a conclusion that reframes years of IPEA tuning as compensation for an inadequate space. Practical details reinforce how delicate the system is: D2h symmetry was imposed, restricted Hartree-Fock orbitals seeded the optimizations only near equilibrium, and every other point on the curve was started from the converged orbitals of its neighbour, since a curve this flat and multireference cannot be converged pointwise from scratch.

geometry_source: Ground-state geometries optimized from the two crystallographic conformations, using both density functional methods and a single-state CASSCF(12,11)/6-31G(d) calculation; excited-state geometries and the conical intersection optimized with a two-root state-averaged reference
method: Single-state CASSCF for ground-state geometry, state-averaged CASSCF over five equally weighted roots for vertical excitations and over two roots for excited-state optimizations, with CASPT2 single points on the CASSCF geometries; branching-space gradient-difference and nonadiabatic-coupling vectors computed to characterize the intersection topology. electronic_structure_description: Vertical excitation energies of 3.40 and 4.18 eV to the two lowest singlet excited states at the uncorrected level, with oscillator strengths of 0.023 and 0.552, falling to 2.72 and 3.00 eV with the perturbative correction, with strengths 0.018 and 0.396; the excited-state minimum lies at 2.49 eV uncorrected and 1.46 corrected. The lowest excited state has twisted intramolecular charge-transfer character. The anilino torsion is computed at 48.3 degrees against a crystallographic 9.3, while the torsion between the two cyanovinyl fragments is computed at 98 plus or minus 1 degrees against a crystallographic 107.8. Other: Three distinct sensitivities show up here and they point in different directions, which makes this a useful entry. The authors diagnose the cause rather than splitting the difference -- the two methods treat correlation differently, with the functional predicting stronger pi conjugation between the aniline and butadiene fragments and hence a flatter structure. Neither computed value matches the crystal, and the authors note that short-range intermolecular interactions are known to matter in these crystals, so the gas-phase comparison is not decisive. What is notable is that on the OTHER torsion, between the two cyanovinyl fragments, the two methods agree closely with each other and with experiment: 98 plus or minus 1 degree against a crystallographic 107.8 for one conformer, and 73.4 against 78.0 for the other. So the disagreement is confined to the coordinate carrying the conjugation, exactly where the correlation treatment should matter. Second, the perturbative correction is LARGE and unequal between states: the first excitation drops from 3.40 to 2.72 eV and the second from 4.18 to 3.00, so their separation collapses from 0.78 to 0.28 eV. Since the whole photophysical argument concerns which state is populated and how it decays, a correction that compresses the gap between the two lowest excited states by nearly two-thirds is not a refinement but a change of picture; the corrected first excitation also lands close to the functional's value, from the opposite side. Third, and cleanly reported, the NUMBER OF AVERAGED ROOTS is chosen per task rather than fixed: five equally weighted roots for vertical excitations, but only two for excited-state geometry optimization. Averaging over more states than the optimization needs would compromise the state being optimized, and averaging over too few would misplace the vertical energies -- splitting the choice by purpose is right, at the cost that geometries and vertical energies come from different references. The space itself, twelve electrons in eleven orbitals, is used single-state for ground-state optimization and state-averaged elsewhere. A scope limit is stated plainly: for the larger of the two molecules studied, a comprehensive multiconfigurational treatment was NOT FEASIBLE, especially for state-averaged calculations, so that compound is treated only by density functional methods and no multireference result exists for it. ligand_set: the protein-derived first coordination sphere of the mononuclear nonheme iron site, with noncoordinating residues removed
geometry_source: A density functional structure computed with Gaussian 09 was used for the multiconfigurational calculation, with noncoordinating residues removed for computational efficiency; a single-point BP86 calculation in ORCA provided the starting orbitals
method: CASSCF with the active orbitals constructed by orbital rotation from a density functional starting calculation, used to compute the zero-field splitting tensor via the Breit-Pauli operator over a wide manifold of spin states; the electric field gradient and hyperfine tensors were taken from density functional theory instead, because the state-averaged potential needed for the splitting produces nearly vanishing field gradients

basis_set: TZVP with auxiliary TZVP/C for the CASSCF calculations; TZVP with auxiliary TZVP/J for the density functional starting calculation
relativistic_treatment: Spin-orbit coupling through the Breit-Pauli operator
active_space_orbital_description: Six electrons in the five iron 3d orbitals, the 3d6 configuration of the high-spin iron(II) centre. The active orbitals were built explicitly using the program's orbital-rotation routine from a density functional starting calculation rather than selected automatically.
active_space_protocol: The minimal space capable of describing the problem: the complete metal d shell and nothing else. The zero-field splitting was computed over 5 quintet, 18 triplet and 13 singlet roots. electronic_structure_description: A high-spin iron(II) centre in a low-symmetry environment. Mossbauer spectroscopy gives a quadrupole doublet with a splitting of 3.28 mm/s and an isomer shift of 1.22 mm/s for the resting state, and for the enzyme-substrate complex a zero-field splitting near -8 reciprocal centimetres with a rhombicity close to the limiting value of one third. The magnetization axis of the integer-spin system is nearly parallel to the symmetry axis of the doubly occupied ground orbital deduced from the field gradient and hyperfine tensors - an alignment that crystal-field theory informed by density functional results cannot rationalize. The multiconfigurational calculation gives a splitting of -8.5 reciprocal centimetres and a rhombicity of 0.27, and places the eigenvector of the negative eigenvalue approximately along the molecular axis, reproducing the observed alignment.
Other: The space here is the minimum that can describe the problem -- six electrons in the five metal 3d orbitals -- and the paper is an unusually clear case of a MINIMAL space succeeding exactly where a single-determinant method fails. The quantity at issue is the zero-field splitting of a high-spin iron(II) site, and the experimental observation that resists explanation is geometric rather than energetic: the magnetization axis of the integer-spin system lies nearly parallel to the symmetry axis of the doubly occupied ground orbital deduced independently from the electric field gradient and hyperfine tensors. Crystal-field reasoning informed by density functional results cannot rationalize that alignment; the multiconfigurational calculation reproduces it, giving a splitting of -8.5 reciprocal centimetres and a rhombicity of 0.27 against experimental values of -8 and 0.37, and putting the eigenvector of the negative eigenvalue approximately along the molecular axis, as experiment requires. Getting a tensor ORIENTATION right, not just a magnitude, is the stronger test, since a magnitude can come out right by cancellation while an axis cannot. The authors say explicitly that they were prompted to try this approach by a published case on an iron protein where the multiconfigurational values agreed well with experiment while density-functional ones were substantially off. Two protocol details deserve recording. The active orbitals were not obtained by a standard selection but CONSTRUCTED BY ROTATION from a density functional starting calculation, using the program's orbital-rotation facility to build the five 3d orbitals explicitly -- a necessary step for a metal site where an automatic selection would not reliably find the d shell. And the splitting was computed over a wide manifold, 5 quintet, 18 triplet and 13 singlet roots, using the Breit-Pauli operator. The most instructive limitation is a genuine incompatibility the authors hit and report: the STATE-AVERAGED potential required to obtain reliable solutions across that wide range of states produces NEARLY VANISHING electric field gradient tensors, so the same calculation cannot supply both properties. They therefore take the splitting from the multiconfigurational treatment and the field gradient and hyperfine tensors from density functional theory. That is a real and rarely stated cost of heavy state averaging -- it degrades one-electron properties of the ground state even as it stabilizes the manifold -- and it forces a hybrid in which two tensors compared for their relative orientation come from different methods. The model was also truncated, with noncoordinating residues removed for efficiency, so the space sits in a smaller cluster than the enzyme site.

ligand_set: 1,4,8,11-tetramethyl-1,4,8,11-tetraazacyclotetradecane in its RSRS isomer, with an acetylide ligand in the apical position
geometry_source: A model compound built from the single-crystal X-ray structure, optimized and confirmed as a local minimum by vibrational frequencies at the density functional level in Gaussian 03
method: CASSCF followed by CASPT2, run alongside density functional theory for comparison
software: MOLCAS 7.9 for the CASSCF and CASPT2 calculations; Gaussian 03 for the density functional work

active_space_orbital_description: Sixteen electrons in thirteen orbitals: the four acetylide pi orbitals of gerade and ungerade symmetry, their four antibonding partners, and the five nickel 3d orbitals. The sixteen electrons are the eight of the d8 metal plus the eight in the four doubly occupied acetylide pi orbitals. The lowest-lying metal d orbital does not survive orbital optimization and leaves the space.
active_space_protocol: The space is composed to let ligand pi density and metal d density compete on equal terms, so that any multiconfigurational character in the metal-acetylide bond would show up. The basis sets are deliberately unbalanced by element, concentrating quality on the metal and coordinating nitrogens where the bonding question lies.
electronic_structure_description: A distorted square-pyramidal nickel(II) centre with the acetylide apical and the macrocycle in its RSRS isomer. The ground state is a triplet, consistent with room-temperature magnetic measurements across the family, and the two singly occupied orbitals are metal-centred, of dz2 and dx2-y2 character. The wave function is dominated by a single configuration at 87 percent, with every other configuration below one percent, so the system is effectively single-reference and the multiconfigurational and density functional descriptions agree. The orbitals immediately below the singly occupied pair are the ungerade acetylide pi orbitals, whose occupation numbers are lower than those of the gerade set, consistent with their higher energy.
Other: The space is built by naming what could plausibly mix rather than by choosing a size: the four acetylide pi orbitals of both symmetries and their four antibonding partners, plus the complete metal 3d shell, giving thirteen orbitals holding sixteen electrons -- eight from the metal's d8 configuration and eight from the four doubly occupied acetylide pi orbitals. That composition is designed to let ligand pi density and metal d density compete on equal footing, which is exactly the question when an acetylide binds a first-row metal. The result is that they do NOT compete: one configuration accounts for 87 percent of the wave function and every other configuration contributes under one percent each, so the system is effectively single-reference and the density functional description is confirmed rather than overturned. That is a negative result, and it is worth recording as such -- a space chosen to detect multiconfigurational character in the metal-acetylide bond found essentially none, which is the useful outcome for anyone deciding whether this class of compound needs multireference treatment at all. The active space also PRUNED ITSELF during optimization: the metal d orbital lying lowest in energy does not remain in the space once the orbitals are optimized, mirroring the density functional finding that it sits well below the frontier region. An orbital leaving the space of its own accord is a cleaner signal that it was unnecessary than any external selection criterion. Two further pieces of information come from occupation numbers rather than energies: the orbitals immediately below the singly occupied pair are the ungerade acetylide pi orbitals, and their occupation numbers are lower than those of the gerade set, consistent with their being higher in energy -- a correspondence between occupancy and orbital energy that would not be visible in a single-determinant picture at all. The calculation confirms the two singly occupied orbitals are metal-centred, which is what underwrites the assignment of a spin-one ground state to the whole family from magnetic measurements. The usual caveats are stated: only one of the four synthesized compounds was treated multiconfigurationally, and it was treated as a truncated model built from a crystal structure, with basis sets deliberately unbalanced by atom -- triple-zeta quality on the metal and the coordinating nitrogens, double-zeta on carbon and a minimal set on hydrogen -- so the description is concentrated where the bonding question lies. Scalar relativistic effects enter through a Douglas-Kroll-Hess Hamiltonian and Cholesky decomposition with local exchange screening reduces the integral cost.
reference_short: Tyler, Natoli, Vlaisavljevich, Fanwick & Ren, Inorg. Chem. 2015, 54, 10058
notes: One of four synthesized acetylides and the only one treated multiconfigurationally; the others were handled by density functional theory on models built from their crystal structures. compound_name: Sulfur dioxide radical cation, ground and excited doublet states
point_group: C2v for the equilibrium calculations; Cs for the dissociation curves
geometry_source: Equilibrium geometries and the two symmetric vibrational frequencies obtained by CASSCF optimization in the larger basis; all excitation energies are perturbatively corrected single points on those geometries
method: CASSCF geometry optimization and frequencies, with CASPT2 single points computing the first-order wave function and second-order energy in the full configuration interaction space
basis_set: Two contracted atomic natural orbital sets: S[6s4p3d1f]/O[5s3p2d1f] and S[4s3p2d]/O[3s2p1d]
active_space_orbital_description: Eleven electrons in thirteen orbitals, formed from the full valence space of the neutral parent by deleting the three lowest valence orbitals - the gap between the highest deleted and the lowest retained exceeding 5 eV - and adding four virtual orbitals lying above the highest valence orbital. Quoted as an orbital count per irreducible representation in both point groups used.
active_space_protocol: Built by subtraction and addition from the full valence rather than taken as the full valence: low-lying orbitals removed on an explicit 5 eV energy-gap criterion, and virtual orbitals added because five of the eight excited states have shake-up character and cannot be represented without them. The same space is used for all eleven states so that their relative energies are strictly comparable.
nroots_per_mult: eleven states in total: the ground state and ten excited states
electronic_structure_description: Eleven electronic states were characterized: the ground state and ten excited doublets. Five of the eight excited states studied in detail have shake-up ionization character, involving simultaneous ionization and excitation. The corrected adiabatic ordering of the eight is, in increasing energy, 1 2B1, 2 2B1, 2 2A2, 2 2A1, 3 2A1, 2 2B2, 3 2B2 and 3 2B1. The ground state has an S-O distance of 1.439 Angstrom and an O-S-O angle of 127.7 degrees. On this basis the three disputed photoelectron bands are assigned: the C state to 1 2B1 and the D state to 2 2A1. Six earlier studies had proposed three mutually incompatible assignments for these bands, with each of the three symmetry labels having been assigned to each band by some group.
Other: The space here is constructed by SUBTRACTION AND ADDITION from the full valence, with each move justified by a stated number rather than by taste. Starting from the twelve valence orbitals of the neutral parent, three low-lying orbitals are DELETED on an explicit energetic criterion -- the gap between the highest deleted orbital and the lowest retained one exceeds 5 eV, so those orbitals cannot participate at the energies of interest -- and four VIRTUAL orbitals lying above the last valence orbital are ADDED. The resulting eleven electrons in thirteen orbitals is therefore neither the full valence nor a truncation of it but a deliberate reshaping, and adding virtuals beyond the valence matters here because five of the eight excited states studied have SHAKE-UP character, meaning they involve simultaneous ionization and excitation and simply cannot be represented without unoccupied orbitals in the space. A conventional full-valence space would have been the wrong choice for exactly the states the paper exists to assign. The space is quoted twice more, once per symmetry group used, as an orbital count per irreducible representation for both the higher-symmetry equilibrium calculations and the lower-symmetry dissociation curves, so a reader can reproduce it in either setting -- a level of specification that is rare and genuinely useful. The purpose is an assignment problem where the literature disagrees: six previous studies, experimental and theoretical, had proposed three mutually incompatible orderings for the three bands in question, with each of the three symmetry labels having been assigned to each of the three bands by someone. Resolving that requires not accuracy in any one energy but a consistent treatment of eleven states at once, which is what the fixed space provides. The protocol keeps geometry and energy strictly separated and says so: geometries and vibrational frequencies come from the uncorrected reference in the larger basis, while all excitation energies are perturbatively corrected single points on those geometries. Three distinct energy quantities are reported rather than conflated -- adiabatic values at each state's own optimized geometry, vertical values at the ground-state ion geometry, and relative values at the NEUTRAL molecule's geometry -- which matters because a photoelectron band is measured from the neutral geometry while a spectroscopic term value refers to the ion's own minimum. Reporting all three separately avoids the usual ambiguity about which number a computed excitation energy should be compared with. Two basis sets of different quality are used throughout, and for the dissociation curves a Jacobi coordinate system is adopted so that elongating one bond is described properly.
reference_short: Li & Huang, J. Phys. Chem. A 2004, 108, 6901
notes: Three distinct energy quantities are reported separately rather than conflated: adiabatic excitation energies at each state's own optimized geometry, vertical excitation energies at the ground-state geometry of the ion, and relative energies computed at the geometry of the neutral parent molecule. For some states the geometries found lie at lower corrected energy than the nominal equilibrium geometries of those states. Dissociation potential energy curves were computed in a Jacobi coordinate system with the second bond length and angle held fixed at 1.4489 Angstrom and 120 degrees.
correlation_correction: CASPT2 single points on the CASSCF geometries, computed in the full configuration interaction space

ligand_set: three hexafluoroacetylacetonate ligands and a tetrathiafulvalene-fused dipyridophenazine
geometry_source: Single-crystal X-ray structures determined in this work; ligand-truncation models were built by simplification without subsequent geometry optimization
method: State-averaged CASSCF followed by a perturbative correction on the spin-free wave functions, then spin-orbit mixing by restricted-active-space state interaction, with magnetic properties and g tensors of the lowest states obtained in a pseudospin one-half formalism
software: MOLCAS, using the RASSI-SO and SINGLE-ANISO routines, with Cholesky decomposition of the two-electron integrals
basis_set: ANO-RCC throughout, graded by proximity to the metal: [8s7p4d3f2g1h] for dysprosium and [8s7p4d3f2g] for ytterbium, [4s3p2d] for the directly coordinated oxygen and nitrogen, [4s3p] for sulfur, [3s2p] for carbon, nitrogen and fluorine, and [2s] for hydrogen
relativistic_treatment: Relativistically contracted atomic natural orbital basis; spin-orbit coupling by state interaction over the spin-free states
active_space_orbital_description: The seven 4f orbitals of the lanthanide ion.
nroots_per_mult: all 21 sextets, all 224 quadruplets and 300 of the 490 doublets averaged, of which 21 sextets, 128 quadruplets and 107 doublets were carried into the spin-orbit step
electronic_structure_description: A mononuclear complex showing slow relaxation of the magnetization, with a pre-exponential factor of 4.14e-6 seconds and an energy barrier of 39 kelvin from an Arrhenius fit of the alternating-current susceptibility between 2 and 15 K under a 1 kOe field. The ground multiplet splits into eight Kramers doublets, whose energies and g tensors were computed. Three progressively truncated ligand models were built to test the effect of the conjugated system, and increasing pi conjugation was found to have no significant influence on either the multiplet splitting or the ground-state g tensor.
Other: For an f-element the active space is not really a choice -- it is the 4f shell, seven orbitals holding whatever the oxidation state dictates, nine electrons for one metal here and thirteen for the other -- so the interesting decisions all concern HOW MANY STATES are carried, and this paper is unusually explicit about a limit imposed by the software rather than by the physics. For the nine-electron case the averaging covers all 21 sextets and all 224 quadruplets but only 300 of the 490 doublets, and the authors state the reason plainly: software limitations. The truncation is then compounded at the next stage, where the spin-orbit step mixes 21 sextets, 128 quadruplets and 107 doublets -- fewer of each than were averaged. So two different truncations apply in sequence, and neither is a converged choice; a reader comparing this study to another must know that roughly two-fifths of the doublet manifold never entered the calculation at all. By contrast the thirteen-electron case is COMPLETE: all seven doublets are averaged and all seven enter the spin-orbit step, so that metal's treatment is exact within the space while the other metal's is not. Comparisons between the two ions in this paper therefore rest on calculations of unequal completeness, which is worth knowing even though the physics of the two shells differs anyway. The genuinely useful active-space result is a NEGATIVE one obtained by systematic ligand truncation: three progressively simplified models of the ligand were built, cutting back the conjugated system without reoptimizing geometry, and the conclusion is that increasing pi conjugation has no significant influence on either the splitting of the ground multiplet or the g tensor of the ground state. That is the right experiment for the question -- if the extended conjugation mattered, the magnetic anisotropy would move as the ligand is cut back -- and finding that it does not tells anyone modelling such systems that the expensive full ligand can be replaced. Holding the geometry fixed while truncating is what makes the test clean, since any change could then only come from the electronic effect. Basis quality is deliberately graded by distance from the metal, from a large set on the lanthanide down to a minimal two-function set on the peripheral hydrogens, concentrating description where the 4f shell can feel it. Dynamical correlation enters as a perturbative correction applied on top of the spin-free wave functions, before the spin-orbit mixing, and Cholesky decomposition reduces the integral cost.
reference_short: Pointillart, Jung, Berraud-Pache, Le Guennic, Dorcet, Golhen, Cador, Maury, Guyot et al., Inorg. Chem. 2015, 54, 5384
notes: The ligand is a tetrathiafulvalene-fused dipyrido[3,2-a:2',3'-c]phenazine, which acts both as a sensitizer for lanthanide luminescence and as a redox-active structural component; the metal binds at its bischelating nitrogen site. active_space_protocol: The reference space is enlarged specifically by lone pairs for the correlated step, so that n-pi-antibonding states can be balanced against pi-pi-antibonding ones. The IPEA shift is deliberately not applied, in contrast to the same group's related work on another chromophore where the default 0.25 was used; an imaginary shift of 0.2 is used against intruder states.
nroots_per_mult: five states treated: the ground state and the lowest pi-pi-antibonding and n-pi-antibonding states of each multiplicity
electronic_structure_description: Vertical excitation energies at the ground-state minimum are 3.57 eV to the bright pi-pi-antibonding singlet and 3.90 eV to the dark n-pi-antibonding singlet in the smaller basis, but 3.53 and 3.35 eV respectively in the larger basis, so the ordering of the two lowest singlets inverts with basis. The triplets lie at 2.99 and 3.24 eV in the smaller basis and 2.94 and 2.98 in the larger. The experimental value for the bright state is 3.27 eV; both perturbative results are close to it and to a published multireference configuration interaction result, while a range-separated functional overestimates by more than 0.5 eV. Three energetically feasible pathways populate the lowest triplet from the initially excited bright singlet: direct intersystem crossing at a singlet-triplet crossing point, an indirect route relayed by the dark singlet state through a conical intersection, and a third relayed by the n-pi-antibonding triplet. The carbonyl bond lengths in solution, 1.191 and 1.185 Angstrom, are close to their gas-phase values.
Other: Two spaces of different size are used for different purposes, and a third factor -- the basis set -- turns out to matter more than either. Geometries, intersections and crossing points come from a space of fourteen electrons in ten orbitals, itemized as twelve pi electrons in nine pi and pi antibonding orbitals plus two lone-pair electrons in one n orbital; the perturbative energies are then recomputed in a LARGER space of sixteen electrons in twelve orbitals, adding a second lone pair. Enlarging specifically by lone pairs is the right move for a molecule whose photophysics runs through n-pi-antibonding states, since those states cannot be balanced against pi-pi-antibonding ones unless every relevant lone pair is active. The striking result, though, is how STATE-DEPENDENT the basis sensitivity is. Going from a split-valence polarized basis to a triple-zeta correlation-consistent one barely moves the bright pi-pi-antibonding state, 3.57 to 3.53 eV, but moves the dark n-pi-antibonding state by 0.55 eV, from 3.90 down to 3.35. The consequence is not a shift but an INVERSION: in the smaller basis the bright state lies 0.33 eV BELOW the dark state, and in the larger basis the dark state lies 0.18 eV below the bright one. Since the paper's central mechanism is a relay in which the bright state decays first to the dark state and only then crosses to a triplet, the identity of the lower state is the mechanism, and it is decided here by the one-electron basis rather than by the active space or the correlation treatment. The same pattern holds in the triplet manifold, where the n-pi-antibonding state moves 0.26 eV against 0.05 for the pi-pi-antibonding one. Lone pairs are simply harder to describe than pi systems, and a space enlarged to include them does not by itself fix a basis too small to represent them. A second point worth recording is a parameter inconsistency within one group's own practice: the IPEA shift is NOT APPLIED here, whereas the same authors used the default 0.25 in closely related work on another chromophore. Given how much that parameter has been shown to move state gaps elsewhere, excitation energies from the two studies are not directly comparable, and the choice is stated rather than defaulted, which is what allows the discrepancy to be seen at all. An imaginary shift of 0.2 guards against intruder states and Cholesky decomposition handles the integrals. Against the experimental value of 3.27 eV for the bright state, both perturbative results are close while a range-separated functional overestimates by more than 0.5 eV.
reference_short: Chang, Xie, Lin & Cui, J. Phys. Chem. A 2016, 120, 6129
notes: The molecule is of interest because it shows a small fluorescence quantum yield and a large intersystem-crossing yield; the three relay mechanisms proposed all end in the lowest triplet, which is consistent with that behaviour.
correlation_correction: Multistate CASPT2 in the enlarged sixteen-electron twelve-orbital space, with no IPEA shift and an imaginary shift of 0.2
